ERLEADA INDICATIONS AND IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION

INDICATIONS

ERLEADA (apalutamide) is an androgen receptor inhibitor indicated for the treatment of patients with:

· Metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC)

· Non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC)

IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION

WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS

Cerebrovascular and Ischemic Cardiovascular Events, including events leading to death, occurred in patients receiving ERLEADA. Monitor for signs and symptoms of ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disorders. Optimize management of cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia. Consider discontinuation of ERLEADA for Grade 3 and 4 events.

In a randomized study (SPARTAN) of patients with nmCRPC, ischemic cardiovascular events occurred in 3.7% of patients treated with ERLEADA and 2% of patients treated with placebo. In a randomized study (TITAN) in patients with mCSPC, ischemic cardiovascular events occurred in 4.4% of patients treated with ERLEADA and 1.5% of patients treated with placebo. Across the SPARTAN and TITAN studies, 4 patients (0.3%) treated with ERLEADA and 2 patients (0.2%) treated with placebo died from an ischemic cardiovascular event.

Patients with history of unstable angina, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, stroke, or transient ischemic attack within 6 months of randomization were excluded from the SPARTAN and TITAN studies.

In the SPARTAN study, cerebrovascular events occurred in 2.5% of patients treated with ERLEADA and 1% of patients treated with placebo. In the TITAN study, cerebrovascular events occurred in 1.9% of patients treated with ERLEADA and 2.1% of patients treated with placebo. Across the SPARTAN and TITAN studies, 3 patients (0.2%) treated with ERLEADA and 2 patients (0.2%) treated with placebo died from a cerebrovascular event.

Fractures occurred in patients receiving ERLEADA. Evaluate patients for fracture risk. Monitor and manage patients at risk for fractures according to established treatment guidelines and consider use of bone-targeted agents.

In a randomized study (SPARTAN) of patients with nmCRPC, fractures occurred in 12% of patients treated with ERLEADA and in 7% of patients treated with placebo. In a randomized study (TITAN) of patients with mCSPC, fractures occurred in 9% of patients treated with ERLEADA and in 6% of patients treated with placebo.

Falls occurred in patients receiving ERLEADA with increased frequency in the elderly. Evaluate patients for fall risk.

In a randomized study (SPARTAN), falls occurred in 16% of patients treated with ERLEADA compared with 9% of patients treated with placebo. Falls were not associated with loss of consciousness or seizure.

Seizure occurred in patients receiving ERLEADA. Permanently discontinue ERLEADA in patients who develop a seizure during treatment. It is unknown whether anti-epileptic medications will prevent seizures with ERLEADA. Advise patients of the risk of developing a seizure while receiving ERLEADA and of engaging in any activity where sudden loss of consciousness could cause harm to themselves or others.

In two randomized studies (SPARTAN and TITAN), five patients (0.4%) treated with ERLEADA and one patient treated with placebo (0.1%) experienced a seizure. Seizure occurred from 159 to 650 days after initiation of ERLEADA. Patients with a history of seizure or, predisposing factors for seizure, or receiving drugs known to decrease the seizure threshold or to induce seizure were excluded. There is no clinical experience in re-administering ERLEADA to patients who experienced a seizure.

Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions — Fatal and life-threatening cases of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), including Stevens‑Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN), and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) occurred in patients receiving ERLEADA.

Monitor patients for the development of SCARs. Advise patients of the signs and symptoms of SCARs (eg, a prodrome of fever, flu-like symptoms, mucosal lesions, progressive skin rash, or lymphadenopathy). If a SCAR is suspected, interrupt ERLEADA until the etiology of the reaction has been determined. Consultation with a dermatologist is recommended. If a SCAR is confirmed, or for other Grade 4 skin reactions, permanently discontinue ERLEADA [see Dosage and Administration (2.2)].

Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)/Pneumonitis — Fatal and life-threatening interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis can occur in patients treated with ERLEADA.

Post-marketing cases of ILD/pneumonitis, including fatal cases, occurred in patients treated with ERLEADA. Across clinical trials (TITAN and SPARTAN, n=1327), 0.8% of patients treated with ERLEADA experienced ILD/pneumonitis, including 0.2% who experienced Grade 3 events [see Adverse Reactions (6.1, 6.2)].

Monitor patients for new or worsening symptoms indicative of ILD/pneumonitis (eg, dyspnea, cough, fever). Immediately withhold ERLEADA if ILD/pneumonitis is suspected. Permanently discontinue ERLEADA in patients with severe ILD/pneumonitis or if no other potential causes of ILD/pneumonitis are identified [see Dosage and Administration (2.2)].

Embryo-Fetal Toxicity — The safety and efficacy of ERLEADA have not been established in females. Based on findings from animals and its mechanism of action, ERLEADA can cause fetal harm and loss of pregnancy when administered to a pregnant female. Advise males with female partners of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose of ERLEADA [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1, 8.3)].

Interference with Immunoassay Measurement of Digoxin

ERLEADA can interfere with certain digoxin immunoassays (e.g., Chemiluminescent Microparticle Immunoassays), resulting in falsely elevated digoxin plasma concentration results. Notify the laboratory conducting the digoxin plasma concentration assay to use an appropriate method in patients receiving ERLEADA and digoxin [see Drug Interactions (7.3)].

ADVERSE REACTIONS

The most common adverse reactions (≥10%) that occurred more frequently in the ERLEADA-treated patients (≥2% over placebo) from the randomized placebo-controlled clinical trials (TITAN and SPARTAN) were fatigue, arthralgia, rash, decreased appetite, fall, weight decreased, hypertension, hot flush, diarrhea, and fracture.

Laboratory Abnormalities — All Grades (Grade 3-4)

Hematology — In the TITAN study: white blood cell decreased ERLEADA 27% (0.4%), placebo 19% (0.6%). In the SPARTAN study: anemia ERLEADA 70% (0.4%), placebo 64% (0.5%); leukopenia ERLEADA 47% (0.3%), placebo 29% (0%); lymphopenia ERLEADA 41% (1.8%), placebo 21% (1.6%)

Chemistry — In the TITAN study: hypertriglyceridemia ERLEADA 17% (2.5%), placebo 12% (2.3%). In the SPARTAN study: hypercholesterolemia ERLEADA 76% (0.1%), placebo 46% (0%); hyperglycemia ERLEADA 70% (2%), placebo 59% (1.0%); hypertriglyceridemia ERLEADA 67% (1.6%), placebo 49% (0.8%); hyperkalemia ERLEADA 32% (1.9%), placebo 22% (0.5%)

Rash — In 2 randomized studies (SPARTAN and TITAN), rash was most commonly described as macular or maculopapular. Adverse reactions of rash were 26% with ERLEADA vs 8% with placebo. Grade 3 rashes (defined as covering >30% body surface area [BSA]) were reported with ERLEADA treatment (6%) vs placebo (0.5%).

The onset of rash occurred at a median of 83 days. Rash resolved in 78% of patients within a median of 78 days from onset of rash. Rash was commonly managed with oral antihistamines and topical corticosteroids, and 19% of patients received systemic corticosteroids. Dose reduction or dose interruption occurred in 14% and 28% of patients, respectively. Of the patients who had dose interruption, 59% experienced recurrence of rash upon reintroduction of ERLEADA.

Hypothyroidism — In 2 randomized studies (SPARTAN and TITAN), hypothyroidism was reported for 8% of patients treated with ERLEADA and 1.5% of patients treated with placebo based on assessments of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) every 4 months. Elevated TSH occurred in 25% of patients treated with ERLEADA and 7% of patients treated with placebo. The median onset was at the first scheduled assessment. There were no Grade 3 or 4 adverse reactions. Thyroid replacement therapy, when clinically indicated, should be initiated or dose adjusted.

DRUG INTERACTIONS

Effect of Other Drugs on ERLEADA

ERLEADA Strong CYP2C8 or CYP3A4 Inhibitors

Reduce the ERLEADA dose as recommended for adverse reactions [see Dosage and Administration (2.2)]. Co-administration of a strong CYP2C8 or CYP3A4 inhibitor is predicted to increase the steady‑state exposure of the active moieties (sum of unbound apalutamide plus the potency‑adjusted unbound N-desmethyl-apalutamide).

Effect of ERLEADA on Other Drugs

Substrates of CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, P-gp, BCRP, or OATP1B1

Refer to the Prescribing Information for these substrates. Consider alternative agents when possible or evaluate for loss of activity of the substrate if concomitant use cannot be avoided.

Apalutamide is a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2C19, a weak inducer of CYP2C9, and an inducer of P-gp, BCRP, and OATP1B1. Apalutamide decreases exposure of substrates of CYP3A4, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, P-gp, BCRP, or OATP1B [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3)], which may decrease the effectiveness of these substrates.

USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS

The recommended ERLEADA dosage in patients with (Child-Pugh C) is lower than the recommended dosage in patients with normal hepatic function. No dosage modification is recommended for patients with mild (Child-Pugh A) or moderate (Child-Pugh B) hepatic impairment.

INDICATIONS FOR RYBREVANT FASPRO AND RYBREVANT

RYBREVANT FASPRO (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) and RYBREVANT (amivantamab-vmjw) are indicated:

· in combination with LAZCLUZE (lazertinib) for the first-line treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R substitution mutations, as detected by an FDA-approved test.

· in combination with carboplatin and pemetrexed for the treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R substitution mutations, whose disease has progressed on or after treatment with an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

· in combination with carboplatin and pemetrexed for the first-line treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations, as detected by an FDA-approved test.

· as a single agent for the treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations, as detected by an FDA approved test, whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy.

IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION FOR RYBREVANT FASPRO AND RYBREVANT

CONTRAINDICATIONS

RYBREVANT FASPRO is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to hyaluronidase or to any of its excipients.

WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS

Hypersensitivity and Administration-Related Reactions with RYBREVANT FASPRO

RYBREVANT FASPRO can cause hypersensitivity and administration-related reactions (ARR); signs and symptoms of ARR include dyspnea, flushing, fever, chills, chest discomfort, hypotension, and vomiting. The median time to ARR onset is approximately 2 hours.

RYBREVANT FASPRO with LAZCLUZE

In PALOMA-3 (n=206), all Grade ARR occurred in 13% of patients, including 0.5% Grade 3. Of the patients who experienced ARR, 89% occurred with the initial dose (Week 1, Day 1).

Premedicate with antihistamines, antipyretics, and glucocorticoids and administer RYBREVANT FASPRO as recommended. Monitor patients for any signs and symptoms of administration-related reactions during injection in a setting where cardiopulmonary resuscitation medication and equipment are available. Interrupt RYBREVANT FASPRO injection if ARR is suspected. Resume treatment upon resolution of symptoms or permanently discontinue RYBREVANT FASPRO based on severity.

Infusion-Related Reactions with RYBREVANT

RYBREVANT can cause infusion-related reactions (IRR) including anaphylaxis; signs and symptoms of IRR include dyspnea, flushing, fever, chills, nausea, chest discomfort, hypotension, and vomiting. The median time to IRR onset is approximately 1 hour.

RYBREVANT with LAZCLUZE

In MARIPOSA (n=421), IRRs occurred in 63% of patients, including Grade 3 in 5% and Grade 4 in 1% of patients. IRR-related infusion modifications occurred in 54%, dose reduction in 0.7%, and permanent discontinuation of RYBREVANT in 4.5% of patients.

RYBREVANT with Carboplatin and Pemetrexed

Based on the pooled safety population (n=281), IRRs occurred in 50% of patients including Grade 3 (3.2%) adverse reactions. IRR-related infusion modifications occurred in 46%, and permanent discontinuation of RYBREVANT in 2.8% of patients.

RYBREVANT as a Single Agent

In CHRYSALIS (n=302), IRRs occurred in 66% of patients. IRRs occurred in 65% of patients on Week 1 Day 1, 3.4% on Day 2 infusion, 0.4% with Week 2 infusion, and were cumulatively 1.1% with subsequent infusions. 97% were Grade 1-2, 2.2% were Grade 3, and 0.4% were Grade 4. The median time to onset was 1 hour (range: 0.1 to 18 hours) after start of infusion. IRR-related infusion modifications occurred in 62%, and permanent discontinuation of RYBREVANT in 1.3% of patients.

Premedicate with antihistamines, antipyretics, and glucocorticoids and infuse RYBREVANT as recommended. Administer RYBREVANT via a peripheral line on Week 1 and Week 2 to reduce the risk of IRRs. Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of IRRs in a setting where cardiopulmonary resuscitation medication and equipment are available. Interrupt infusion if IRR is suspected. Reduce the infusion rate or permanently discontinue RYBREVANT based on severity. If an anaphylactic reaction occurs, permanently discontinue RYBREVANT.

Interstitial Lung Disease/Pneumonitis

RYBREVANT FASPRO and RYBREVANT can cause severe and fatal interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis.

RYBREVANT FASPRO with LAZCLUZE

In PALOMA-3, ILD/pneumonitis occurred in 6% of patients, including Grade 3 in 1%, Grade 4 in 1.5%, and fatal cases in 1.9% of patients. 5% of patients permanently discontinued RYBREVANT FASPRO and LAZCLUZE due to ILD/pneumonitis.

RYBREVANT with LAZCLUZE

In MARIPOSA, ILD/pneumonitis occurred in 3.1% of patients, including Grade 3 in 1.0% and Grade 4 in 0.2% of patients. There was one fatal case of ILD/pneumonitis and 2.9% of patients permanently discontinued RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE due to ILD/pneumonitis.

RYBREVANT with Carboplatin and Pemetrexed

Based on the pooled safety population, ILD/pneumonitis occurred in 2.1% of patients with 1.8% of patients experiencing Grade 3 ILD/pneumonitis. 2.1% discontinued RYBREVANT due to ILD/pneumonitis.

RYBREVANT as a Single Agent

In CHRYSALIS, ILD/pneumonitis occurred in 3.3% of patients, with 0.7% of patients experiencing Grade 3 ILD/pneumonitis. Three patients (1%) permanently discontinued RYBREVANT due to ILD/pneumonitis.

Monitor patients for new or worsening symptoms indicative of ILD/pneumonitis (e.g., dyspnea, cough, fever). Immediately withhold RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE (when applicable) in patients with suspected ILD/pneumonitis and permanently discontinue if ILD/pneumonitis is confirmed.

Venous Thromboembolic (VTE) Events with Concomitant Use with LAZCLUZE

RYBREVANT FASPRO and RYBREVANT in combination with LAZCLUZE can cause serious and fatal venous thromboembolic (VTE) events, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Without prophylactic anticoagulation, the majority of these events occurred during the first four months of treatment.

RYBREVANT FASPRO with LAZCLUZE

In PALOMA-3 (n=206), all Grade VTE occurred in 11% of patients and 1.5% were Grade 3. 80% (n=164) of patients received prophylactic anticoagulation at study entry, with an all Grade VTE incidence of 7%. In patients who did not receive prophylactic anticoagulation (n=42), all Grade VTE occurred in 17% of patients. In total, 0.5% of patients had VTE leading to dose reductions of RYBREVANT FASPRO and no patients required permanent discontinuation. The median time to onset of VTEs was 95 days (range: 17 to 390).

RYBREVANT with LAZCLUZE

In MARIPOSA (n=421), VTEs occurred in 36% of patients including Grade 3 in 10% and Grade 4 in 0.5% of patients. On-study VTEs occurred in 1.2% of patients (n=5) while receiving anticoagulation therapy. There were two fatal cases of VTE (0.5%), 9% of patients had VTE leading to dose interruptions of RYBREVANT, and 7% of patients had VTE leading to dose interruptions of LAZCLUZE; 1% of patients had VTE leading to dose reductions of RYBREVANT, and 0.5% of patients had VTE leading to dose reductions of LAZCLUZE; 3.1% of patients had VTE leading to permanent discontinuation of RYBREVANT, and 1.9% of patients had VTE leading to permanent discontinuation of LAZCLUZE. The median time to onset of VTEs was 84 days (range: 6 to 777).

Administer prophylactic anticoagulation for the first four months of treatment. The use of Vitamin K antagonists is not recommended.

Monitor for signs and symptoms of VTE events and treat as medically appropriate. Withhold RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE based on severity. Once anticoagulant treatment has been initiated, resume RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE at the same dose level at the discretion of the healthcare provider. In the event of VTE recurrence despite therapeutic anticoagulation, permanently discontinue RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT. Treatment can continue with LAZCLUZE at the same dose level at the discretion of the healthcare provider. Refer to the LAZCLUZE Prescribing Information for recommended LAZCLUZE dosage modification.

Dermatologic Adverse Reactions

RYBREVANT FASPRO and RYBREVANT can cause severe rash including toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), dermatitis acneiform, pruritus and dry skin.

RYBREVANT FASPRO with LAZCLUZE

In PALOMA-3, rash occurred in 80% of patients, including Grade 3 in 17% and Grade 4 in 0.5% of patients. Rash leading to dose reduction occurred in 11% of patients, and RYBREVANT FASPRO was permanently discontinued due to rash in 1.5% of patients.

RYBREVANT with LAZCLUZE

In MARIPOSA, rash occurred in 86% of patients, including Grade 3 in 26% of patients. The median time to onset of rash was 14 days (range: 1 to 556 days). Rash leading to dose interruptions occurred in 37% of patients for RYBREVANT and 30% for LAZCLUZE, rash leading to dose reductions occurred in 23% of patients for RYBREVANT and 19% for LAZCLUZE, and rash leading to permanent discontinuation occurred in 5% of patients for RYBREVANT and 1.7% for LAZCLUZE.

RYBREVANT with Carboplatin and Pemetrexed

Based on the pooled safety population, rash occurred in 82% of patients, including Grade 3 (15%) adverse reactions. Rash leading to dose reductions occurred in 14% of patients, and 2.5% permanently discontinued RYBREVANT and 3.1% discontinued pemetrexed.

RYBREVANT as a Single Agent

In CHRYSALIS, rash occurred in 74% of patients, including Grade 3 in 3.3% of patients. The median time to onset of rash was 14 days (range: 1 to 276 days). Rash leading to dose reduction occurred in 5% and permanent discontinuation due to rash occurred in 0.7% of patients. Toxic epidermal necrolysis occurred in one patient (0.3%).

When initiating treatment with RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE, prophylactic and concomitant medications are recommended to reduce the risk and severity of dermatologic adverse reactions. Instruct patients to limit sun exposure during and for 2 months after treatment. Advise patients to wear protective clothing and use broad spectrum UVA/UVB sunscreen.

If skin reactions develop, administer supportive care including topical corticosteroids and topical and/or oral antibiotics. For Grade 3 reactions, add oral steroids and consider dermatologic consultation. Promptly refer patients presenting with severe rash, atypical appearance or distribution, or lack of improvement within 2 weeks to a dermatologist. For patients receiving RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT in combination with LAZCLUZE, withhold, reduce the dose, or permanently discontinue both drugs based on severity. For patients receiving RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT as a single agent or in combination with carboplatin and pemetrexed, withhold, dose reduce or permanently discontinue RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT based on severity.

Hepatotoxicity

LAZCLUZE in combination with amivantamab can cause severe hepatotoxicity (including increased ALT and AST).

RYBREVANT with LAZCLUZE

In MARIPOSA, based on adverse reaction data, hepatotoxicity occurred in 49% of patients treated with LAZCLUZE, including Grade 3 in 9.3% of patients and Grade 4 in 0.5%. LAZCLUZE was interrupted for an adverse reaction of hepatotoxicity in 8% of patients, the dose was reduced in 1.4% and permanently discontinued in 0.2%.

Perform liver function tests (including ALT, AST, and total bilirubin) before initiation of LAZCLUZE and during treatment, as clinically indicated. Withhold, reduce the dose, or permanently discontinue LAZCLUZE and amivantamab based on severity.

Ocular Toxicity

RYBREVANT FASPRO and RYBREVANT can cause ocular toxicity including keratitis, blepharitis, dry eye symptoms, conjunctival redness, blurred vision, visual impairment, ocular itching, eye pruritus and uveitis.

RYBREVANT FASPRO with LAZCLUZE

In PALOMA-3, all Grade ocular toxicity occurred in 13% of patients, including 0.5% Grade 3.

RYBREVANT with LAZCLUZE

In MARIPOSA, ocular toxicity occurred in 16%, including Grade 3 or 4 ocular toxicity in 0.7% of patients.

RYBREVANT with Carboplatin and Pemetrexed

Based on the pooled safety population, ocular toxicity occurred in 16% of patients. All events were Grade 1 or 2.

RYBREVANT as a Single Agent

In CHRYSALIS, keratitis occurred in 0.7% and uveitis occurred in 0.3% of patients. All events were Grade 1-2.

Promptly refer patients presenting with new or worsening eye symptoms to an ophthalmologist. Withhold, dose reduce or permanently discontinue RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT and continue LAZCLUZE based on severity.

Embryo-Fetal Toxicity

Based on animal models, RYBREVANT FASPRO, RYBREVANT and LAZCLUZE can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. Verify pregnancy status of females of reproductive potential prior to initiating RYBREVANT FASPRO and RYBREVANT. Advise pregnant women and females of reproductive potential of the potential risk to the fetus. Advise patients of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose of RYBREVANT FASPRO or RYBREVANT, and for 3 weeks after the last dose of LAZCLUZE.

ADVERSE REACTIONS

RYBREVANT FASPRO with LAZCLUZE

In PALOMA-3 (n=206), the most common adverse reactions (≥20%) were rash (80%), nail toxicity (58%), musculoskeletal pain (50%), fatigue (37%), stomatitis (36%), edema (34%), nausea (30%), diarrhea (22%), vomiting (22%), constipation (22%), decreased appetite (22%), and headache (21%). text:
Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is “off the charts”, Business Insider reported. His company has put more than $170bn on the line for them and other large customers, according to an analysis of its filings by The Information.

The publication also reported that Nvidia is in talks to back one more. Firmus, an Australian AI cloud company, pulled its stock market listing this month.

The total includes as much as $164.5bn in guarantees and other commitments to support new data centres, Shane Burke and Phoebe Liu reported. The figures run to Nvidia’s July quarter. Among them are promises to pay landlords if tenants default on leases, and promises to buy computing capacity. Nvidia has also invested, or agreed to invest, more than $7bn directly in AI cloud providers.

Neoclouds are companies that borrow heavily to buy Nvidia’s chips and rent out the computing power. Nvidia already holds $99bn in shares of companies that buy its chips. It has also talked to insurers about loans backed by them.

Firmus after the failed float

Nvidia is discussing an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus, The Information reported. It cited people familiar with the talks. Nvidia is already an investor in the company. TNW has not independently verified the reports.

Firmus dropped its planned ASX float earlier this month after it struggled to win over global investors. It had sought to raise as much as $5.5bn, Bloomberg reported. The deal would have valued Firmus at about $30bn.

John Pearce, chief investment officer of one of Australia’s largest pension funds, explained why his fund stayed out of the offering, Axios reported.

“We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn’t have a compelling valuation,” Pearce said.

Other neoclouds are under pressure too. South Korea’s Elice sank 32% on debut on Tuesday. CoreWeave’s shares have fallen 50% in six months, Business Insider reported.

Huang: demand is ‘off the charts’

Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, made his case in the CNBC interview.

“The demand for the neoclouds is off the charts. Their capabilities are extraordinary,” Huang told CNBC.

He said the sector’s problem was a shortage of capital, not of customers. Nvidia is working to make its computing hardware an asset that lenders will finance, he said. Last week, Huang said CoreWeave needed no backstop.

“It is now becoming an asset class,” Huang said.

‘Strategically super smart’

Huang has also defended Nvidia’s practice of investing in its own customers. In London last week, where he announced stakes in five UK startups, he told Fortune that Nvidia invests only “a small percentage” of what those companies have to raise.

“It is also strategically super smart to do because everybody we invest in is connected into Nvidia’s ecosystem, and so we’re making our platform more vibrant, and we’re able to reach into new markets we otherwise couldn’t,” Huang said.

On stage in a converted church, he channelled Oprah Winfrey, as Axios put it.

Barclays plans to cut around 5,000 jobs, equivalent to about 5% of its global workforce, as the British lender simplifies its operating model and increases its use of artificial intelligence (AI), according to multiple news reports.

The bank has reportedly already eliminated around 1,000 roles, with the remaining 4,000 reductions expected to be completed by the end of the year.

Around 60% of the cuts are expected to fall on support functions, including developer roles, while the cost-reduction exercise will also focus on the bank’s UK retail operations. A significant proportion of the affected back-office roles is expected to be based in India.

Barclays Chief Financial Officer Anna Cross told reporters that the workforce changes form part of plans to deliver more than £1.1bn in savings in 2027, adding that AI is helping employees become more productive.

Chief Executive CS Venkatakrishnan was cited as saying the bank has been making “deep investments” in technology to simplify and improve its business.

“AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said. “We will employ AI at scale. But AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake.”

The bank employed about 93,000 people globally at the end of 2025.

Según L'Oréal, la empresa de cosméticos más grande del mundo, el auge de los fármacos para adelgazar está impulsando las ventas de productos de belleza y cuidado de la piel.

Algunos de los productos de la compañía están diseñados específicamente para combatir algunos de los efectos secundarios de perder de peso rápidamente.

Nicolas Hieronimus, director ejecutivo, dijo que el mercado de la belleza está demostrando ser resiliente en un contexto global desafiante, y que el uso de GLP-1 (conocido popularmente por marcas como Ozempic, Wegovy o Mounjaro) ha sido "un fenómeno muy importante para nosotros".

En una conferencia telefónica con inversores, Hieronimus señaló que el aumento en su uso estaba "teniendo un impacto en el consumo de productos de belleza y, en particular, en el consumo de productos para el cuidado de la piel".

L'Oreal, propietaria de otras marcas populares como Maybelline y La Roche-Posay, anunció este jueves que sus ventas aumentaron un 7,7% en el tercer trimestre del año y superaron las expectativas de los analistas.

La fiebre del GLP-1

El GLP-1 se volvió increíblemente popular en los últimos años, después de que se descubriera que, además de tratar la diabetes, también provocaba una pérdida de peso significativa al suprimir el apetito.

Si bien no es causada directamente por los fármacos GLP-1, la pérdida rápida de peso puede, en algunas personas, tener como efecto secundario la flacidez de la piel, incluso en el rostro.

Hieronimus dijo que las marcas SkinCeuticals y Kiehl's, de L'Oreal, cuentan con productos "diseñados para funcionar conjuntamente con el GLP-1 y contrarrestar sus efectos secundarios sobre la flacidez de la piel" y otros efectos relacionados con la pérdida rápida de peso.

text:
The Turin-based start-up CarpeCarbon and Michelin Italiana have signed an agreement to develop a project for the capture and utilisation of atmospheric CO₂ at the multinational’s tyre factory in Cuneo. This involves the construction of CarpeCarbon’s first industrial plant, which utilises its proprietary direct air capture (DAC) technology and integrates it into a production process, following the completion in December 2025 of the pilot plant at its headquarters in Caselle, near Turin.

The project with Michelin

Under the agreement, the project will make CO₂ captured directly from the atmosphere available for specific industrial applications at the site, helping to replace a portion of the carbon dioxide that Michelin receives from external suppliers. In addition, the portion of captured CO₂ that is not supplied to Michelin will be managed independently by CarpeCarbon and will be used for storage and the generation of carbon credits (in this case, certified as CO₂ equivalent removals).

The plant, representing an investment of two million euros, will have a nominal capacity of 300 tonnes of CO₂ per year. It is scheduled to come into operation in the second half of 2027.

The outlook

CarpeCarbon aims to increase its total carbon capture capacity to 5,000 tonnes per year by 2028–2029 and to 50,000 tonnes by 2030, through a growth model based on modular systems that can be integrated directly into existing industrial sites, powered at low temperatures (for example, by waste heat available on site), and on stand-alone modular systems powered exclusively by solar heat, again with low energy requirements.

The plant

“We have developed a proprietary technology, covered by three patents, and invested in the construction of a pilot plant. Being able to start implementing this plan alongside a leading industrial player such as Michelin Italiana is important for accelerating the subsequent phases of the technology’s industrial development. We are working to ensure that this serves as the starting point for extending the model to many other manufacturing companies in Italia, Europe and around the world,” emphasises Giuliano Antoniciello, co-founder and CEO of CarpeCarbon.

Global computing developer NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) has acquired a strategic minority equity stake in Cambridge-based quantum error correction (QEC) startup Riverlane. Announced alongside corporate investments in four UK artificial intelligence ventures, the deal strengthens NVIDIA’s alignment with Riverlane’s physical QEC decoder stack (Deltaflow QEC) and expands its broader $250 million UK computing commitment.

Coinciding with the strategic investment, Riverlane and NVIDIA revealed an expanded technical collaboration demonstrating the use of NVIDIA H100 GPUs to accelerate real-time QEC decoder recalibration workflows. By adapting Riverlane’s Local Clustering Decoder (LCD) for high-throughput GPU parallel processing, a surface code training cycle that previously took 3 minutes on a single CPU core was reduced to 2.8 seconds. The H100 GPU processed over 4 million surface code error syndromes per second (compared to ~59,000 on CPU), enabling routine, pre-experiment decoder recalibration to mitigate dynamic qubit drift and hardware defects.

Mitigating Dynamic Qubit Drift via High-Throughput GPU Calibration

A primary bottleneck in scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) is hardware instability: qubit frequencies shift, two-qubit gate fidelities fluctuate, and physical defects appear over time. Standard QEC decoders rely on pre-computed error likelihood weights; as physical qubit behavior drifts, these weights become inaccurate, degrading logical qubit fidelities.

By leveraging NVIDIA GPUs to process large batches of experimental syndrome data in parallel, Riverlane’s AI-driven calibration loop dynamically updates the decoder’s physical noise model in real time without manual tuning. The integration creates a tightly coupled QPU-GPU control loop where classical GPU acceleration continuously recalibrates low-latency hardware decoders (such as Riverlane’s ASIC/FPGA matrix chips), establishing a foundation for reliable, multi-modal utility-scale quantum systems.

text:
GOOCHLAND, Va. (WWBT) - Pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly broke ground Thursday on a $5 billion manufacturing facility in Goochland County’s West Creek area, marking a major step forward for one of Central Virginia’s largest economic development projects.

The facility, located along West Creek Parkway, is expected to bring approximately 1,800 construction jobs to the region, followed by 650 permanent positions once manufacturing operations begin.

The company announced the $5 billion project in September 2025, during former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration.

Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who attended Thursday’s ceremony, acknowledged the work of her predecessor’s administration in bringing the project to Virginia.

Spanberger also revealed that the company’s original plans called for a significantly smaller investment.

“The original plans that Lilly put forward called for a $2.1 billion investment. And they have more than doubled it,” Spanberger said.

Part of a nationwide manufacturing expansion

The Goochland project is part of Eli Lilly’s broader $50 billion commitment to expand pharmaceutical manufacturing in the United States.

Ricks said the Richmond-area facility is one of 10 new U.S. manufacturing sites announced by the company and one of five focused on producing active pharmaceutical ingredients — the components responsible for a medicine’s therapeutic effects.

The company has experienced rapid growth, fueled in part by demand for its diabetes and weight-loss medications, Mounjaro and Zepbound.

However, those medications will not be the focus of the Goochland facility.

Instead, the company plans to manufacture advanced biologic medicines, including therapies being developed to treat cancer and potentially autoimmune diseases.

A first-of-its-kind facility for Lilly

According to company leaders, the Goochland site will be Lilly’s first fully integrated manufacturing facility dedicated to its emerging bioconjugate platform and monoclonal antibody portfolio.

The facility will handle the process from producing active pharmaceutical ingredients to manufacturing finished medicines at a single location.

Ricks said that approach will give the company greater control over production while reducing its reliance on foreign suppliers.

“What makes this site unique is that it will bring API production together with finished medicine,” Ricks said. “So it will literally run the whole process here at Richmond.”

Among the treatments planned for the facility are antibody-drug conjugates, or ADCs, which combine an antibody designed to target cancer cells with a powerful cancer-fighting drug.

The goal is to deliver treatment more precisely to tumors while limiting damage to surrounding healthy tissue and potentially reducing side effects.

The facility is also expected to incorporate artificial intelligence, machine learning and advanced analytics into its manufacturing operations. Lilly is targeting LEED Gold certification, an environmental building standard.

Alongside the manufacturing project, Lilly announced a $40 million commitment to the Virginia Center for Advanced Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, a workforce development initiative involving industry, government and higher education partners.

The initiative will include a hands-on pharmaceutical manufacturing training center in Goochland County, targeted to open in 2028.

The training is intended to help Virginians develop skills for careers in pharmaceutical manufacturing, including people who have never worked in the industry.

The facility’s permanent positions are expected to include engineers, scientists, manufacturing operators and laboratory technicians.

“In Virginia, we have made workforce development a top priority because the jobs being created by this project, they will need to be filled, and they need to be filled by Virginians,” Spanberger said.

Lilly officials said work to prepare the site and recruit employees has already begun.

While the project promises significant economic investment, company leaders acknowledged that construction could cause temporary disruptions for people living and traveling near West Creek.

Ricks said the scale of the project could affect traffic patterns and create other disturbances as construction progresses.

“Let me begin by apologizing for any disturbance,” Ricks said. “Progress takes some of that from time to time.”

He thanked neighbors for their patience and said Lilly wants to hear community feedback as work continues.

The company expects construction of the facility to be completed by 2030.

Additional commissioning and regulatory approvals will be necessary before full manufacturing operations can begin.

3 things going right for Eli Lilly that this headline doesn't cover.

How does the Richmond ADC facility reshape Eli Lilly's business model?

The Richmond site links active ingredient production and finished-dose manufacturing for antibody drug conjugates on one campus, which tightens control over a complex supply chain. That integrated setup can reduce coordination risk across contractors and gives Eli Lilly more flexibility to match future oncology and autoimmune demand with in house capacity.

Does this Richmond and METiS news change the Eli Lilly Narrative?

It leans into the existing Narrative rather than rewriting it. Analysts already frame incretin drugs as the earnings engine, with big U.S. manufacturing projects and non incretin portfolios in oncology and immunology as supporting catalysts. Richmond requires large up front capital and a highly skilled workforce, so construction delays, hiring gaps or regulatory setbacks could push out when that ADC capacity becomes usable. On the METiS side, technical hurdles in tissue specific lipid nanoparticles or safety issues in early programs would limit how quickly those delivery platforms can feed into commercial candidates.

The clearest checkpoint is whether Richmond hits its targeted operational timeline around 2028 with ADC output ramping as planned, alongside at least one METiS partnered LNP program advancing into later stage trials. If capital spend climbs without those concrete milestones, the case for this build out as a long term earnings support weakens.

text:
Microsoft says its medical AI system can diagnose difficult cases more than twice as accurately as practicing doctors.

Dubbed the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), the system “substantially outperformed practicing generalist physicians” in diagnostic accuracy while ordering fewer tests and procedures, according to a newly published paper.

The Microsoft study, titled “Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models,” was first posted online last year on arXiv as a non-peer-reviewed preprint. On Thursday, the findings were finally published in the peer-reviewed journal Science.

That’s a major step toward validating the findings, but any real-world deployment would still require clinical testing, Microsoft’s AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told The Verge. Microsoft already has plans for that: the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, told the publication that testing will begin at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts, within the next couple of months.

In tests involving complex medical cases published in The New England Journal of Medicine, DxO achieved 83.2% diagnostic accuracy, compared with 36.1% for generalist physicians who had access to reference materials. When physicians were denied those resources, their accuracy dropped to roughly 22%, making DxO nearly four times as accurate. In a separate test involving emergency department admissions, Microsoft’s AI again outperformed generalist physicians, though by a narrower margin of 80.3% to 46.8%. The system achieved its strongest results using OpenAI’s GPT-5, with additional testing showing improvements using GPT-5.5.

“It also manages to do this at half or even one third of the cost, getting to the right diagnosis with fewer tests and procedures,” Microsoft said in a blog post Thursday. Those savings, however, are based on estimated costs in simulated cases rather than actual medical expenses. The researchers admitted that they “would expect the performance gap to narrow” if DxO were compared with expert specialists rather than generalists.

Notably, DxO works sequentially, meaning patients don’t simply present the system with a comprehensive list of symptoms, medical history, and test results. Instead, it starts with a chief complaint and must determine which follow-up questions to ask and tests to order before arriving at a diagnosis. That’s much closer to how doctors actually diagnose patients. The researchers say benchmarks have previously failed to evaluate LLMs’ diagnostic capabilities sequentially and propose a new benchmark called the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark, or SDBench.

DxO “simulates a panel of physicians,” the paper explains, “continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests.” The system assigns different roles to AI agents that propose diagnoses, select tests, challenge assumptions, and weigh costs. Researchers suggest this approach can help counter some of the cognitive biases that affect individual physicians, such as anchoring on an initial diagnosis or overlooking alternative explanations.

Similar claims have been made about other companies’ AI tools. Earlier this year, researchers from Harvard University and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center found that OpenAI’s o1-preview reasoning model outperformed physicians in diagnosing emergency room patients during triage.

text:
Is KDP a good stock to buy? We came across a bullish thesis on Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. on Astute Optics - US's Substack. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on KDP. Keurig Dr Pepper Inc.'s share was trading at $34.47 as of October 21st 2026. KDP's trailing and forward P/E were 32.08 and 12.45 respectively according to Yahoo Finance.

This isn't the first time we see a beverage company pitched as a great investment. KDP shares gained 25.12% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Coca-Cola Consolidated (COKE) and The Coca-Cola Company (KO) gained 64.19% and 32.51%, respectively, during the same period. Familiar brands and repeat purchases can attract investors, but rising share prices also raise expectations. Does KDP still offer an attractive buying opportunity after its rally, or have investors already priced in much of the upside?

Pixabay/Public Domain

In June, we published an article about the 10 Undervalued Counter Cyclical Stocks to Buy Now and KDP ranked #1 in that article. KDP gained 7.71% since then. So, hedge funds were right about their #1 pick. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on KDP. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much.

Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. (NASDAQ:KDP) owns and distributes a broad range of non-alcoholic beverages while also running one of the largest single-serve coffee systems through Keurig brewers and K-Cup pods. Its brands include Dr Pepper, Canada Dry, Snapple, Ghost, Electrolit, and Green Mountain Coffee Roasters, and the April 2026 acquisition of JDE Peet's greatly expanded its global coffee business. The central investment debate is whether that acquisition and the planned split of the company can boost earnings and create enough value to make up for the large debt taken on to pay for the deal.

Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich

Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential

Over the past twelve months, revenue reached $20.1 billion, up 27.5% from a year earlier, though much of that growth came from adding JDE Peet's rather than from the existing business growing on its own. Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. trades at about 31.7 times its past earnings, well above the peer median of 18.4 times, but that drops to roughly 13.7 times when looking at expected future earnings. This gap suggests investors are not paying only for today's business, they are betting that the acquisition and separation will produce a much stronger earnings base.

The optimistic view rests mainly on the $18.4 billion JDE Peet's deal and the idea that the combined company can create more value once it splits into two independent businesses. Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. completed the purchase in April 2026, adding coffee brands such as Jacobs, L'OR, and Peet's, while steady demand for Dr Pepper, Ghost energy drinks, and Electrolit hydration products continues to support the beverage side. Management plans to separate the company into a standalone refreshment beverage business and a standalone global coffee business by early 2027, giving investors two distinct companies instead of one.

Management expects 2026 net sales of $25.9 billion to $26.4 billion, which shows how much larger the business is set to become with the coffee operations and U.S. refreshment beverages combined. If Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. can bring JDE Peet's smoothly into the fold, capture cost savings, and keep up momentum in energy, hydration, functional, and zero-sugar drinks, bulls believe each business will have a clearer strategy and a more focused approach to spending its cash. If that happens, earnings should recover meaningfully from today's depressed level, which is why the earnings multiple looks far cheaper on future profits than on past ones. The company also generated $1.5 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2025, which gives management some room to pay down debt before the split.

Analysts are also supportive. Their average 12-month price target of $36.21 implies about 15% upside from the $31.39 share price, while the median target is $38 and individual estimates range from $29 to $42. Those targets rest on expected earnings per share of $2.29, which is more than double the $0.99 the company earned over the past twelve months. Put simply, the targets assume Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. will be valued at a fairly ordinary level once profits rebound. Because the gap between past and expected earnings is so large, investors should watch closely whether the benefits of the deal and operating improvements actually show up, as a slower recovery would make these targets harder to justify.

The latest quarter shows why integration and debt are the key risks. The JDE Peet's deal is adding a lot of revenue, so you would expect profits to hold up as the business grows, but they have not. Gross margin, which shows how much of each sales dollar is left after the direct cost of making products, fell sharply from a year earlier, and both operating income and earnings per share dropped noticeably. At the same time, interest costs have climbed almost twofold, since Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. carries about $28.5 billion of net debt after the deal. Shrinking margins, rising interest costs, and heavy debt just before a major split raise real questions about how well management can execute. You can check out whether Keurig Dr Pepper's $925 million exit from Chobani is a smart reset here.

Another risk for the stock is weakening demand within Keurig's single-serve coffee system. Its recurring pod sales depend on households continuing to use its brewers and buy compatible coffee. In 2025, U.S. K-Cup pod volumes fell 4.8%, while brewer volumes dropped 19.9%, reflecting price sensitivity and other pressures. Weaker brewer sales could slow household adoption, although replacement purchases and retailer inventory changes also affect those figures. If consumers buy fewer pods or switch brewing methods, coffee sales could struggle even with successful acquisition integration. Price increases may support revenue temporarily while masking lower consumption. In our opinion, this could limit KDP's price multiples if its expanded coffee business lacks sustained underlying demand growth.

Hedge fund positioning shows a mixed signal. As per our database, 47 hedge fund portfolios held Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. at the end of the second quarter, up from 43 in the previous quarter. This modest rise suggests institutional investors are still fairly optimistic about the integration, the planned separation, and the earnings recovery, despite concerns over debt and margins. By comparison, The Coca-Cola Company (NYSE:KO) was held by 90 hedge funds, up from 76, while PepsiCo, Inc. (NASDAQ:PEP) was held by 68 hedge funds, down from 72, and Coca-Cola Consolidated, Inc. (NASDAQ:COKE) was held by 33, up from 31. Overall, institutions grew most confident in The Coca-Cola Company, interest in Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. also improved, PepsiCo, Inc. lost some support, and Coca-Cola Consolidated, Inc. saw only a small gain relatively.

Short interest data also paints a somewhat cautious picture for Keurig Dr Pepper Inc., with 6.03% of its shares available for trading sold short, well above The Coca-Cola Company at 1.24% and PepsiCo, Inc. at 1.90%. It is, however, slightly below Coca-Cola Consolidated, Inc., where 6.79% of shares are sold short. This suggests the integration, debt, margin pressure, and planned split are drawing more scrutiny for Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. than for The Coca-Cola Company and PepsiCo, Inc., though negative sentiment is still a little milder than for Coca-Cola Consolidated, Inc.

Valuation Analysis

KDP's EV/EBITDA is 16.74x. The Coca-Cola Company, Coca-Cola Consolidated, Inc., and PepsiCo, Inc. trade at EV/EBITDA multiples of 20.48x, 13.72x, and 12.12x, respectively. KDP's own EV/EBITDA was 15.41x on December 31, 2025, approximately 9% below its current multiple, although the JDE Peet's acquisition limits comparability because trailing EBITDA includes only part of the acquired business's earnings. We believe the current valuation reflects expectations that acquisition savings and the planned separation will improve profitability, balanced against concerns about debt and weakening coffee demand. Key insights from management’s remarks

Management attributed the quarter’s results to disciplined cost controls, improved Medicaid rate alignment, and expanded adoption of Carelon’s integrated solutions, which together drove better operating performance in several core business lines.

Medicaid margin stabilization: Recent rate increases and targeted clinical management actions helped stabilize Medicaid margins and set up the segment for improvement in 2027. Management noted ongoing efforts to align rates with cost trends and proactively address behavioral health utilization.

CarelonRx and value-based care: Strong operating performance in CarelonRx was driven by integration of medical and pharmacy benefits, with members in integrated plans experiencing fewer emergency room visits and significant per-member-per-month savings. The introduction of specialized programs, like the Oncology Center of Excellence, has enhanced patient outcomes and operational efficiency.

Commercial segment pricing discipline: The Commercial business benefited from prudent pricing and a focus on affordable, integrated solutions. Medicare Advantage repositioning: Deliberate changes in product and market focus for Medicare Advantage led to improved quality mix and operating margins. Management is prioritizing HMO plans and dual-eligible members, aiming to further increase the share of members in higher-rated plans.

AI and analytics in cost management: The company is increasingly leveraging AI-enabled analytics to identify abnormal utilization patterns, particularly in behavioral health and payment integrity. These efforts have contributed to early identification of cost drivers and expedited corrective actions, with notable impact on claims management and fraud detection.

Medicaid margin improvement: Management expects Medicaid margins to begin recovering in 2027 as state rates better reflect underlying cost trends and targeted interventions in behavioral health and care management take hold. Carelon external growth and integration: The company is scaling Carelon’s offerings beyond affiliated health plans, focusing on external client wins in behavioral health, pharmacy, and post-acute care. Leadership highlighted high retention rates and a robust sales pipeline, supporting expectations for Carelon to become a larger contributor to enterprise earnings.

Commercial and ACA market discipline: In the Commercial segment, pricing for stability amid elevated cost trends is a priority, while ACA market performance benefits from product mix shifts and disciplined rate filings. Management cautions that the risk pool in ACA will take more than one cycle to normalize as enhanced subsidies expire.

Catalysts in upcoming quarters

In the coming quarters, the StockStory team will watch (1) the pace of Medicaid margin recovery as rate adjustments and care management initiatives progress, (2) Carelon’s success in expanding its external client base and executing on integrated value-based care, and (3) the commercial segment’s ability to maintain pricing discipline amid cost trend pressures. text:
Eli Lilly and Company broke ground Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, on a $5 billion manufacturing facility in Goochland County, Virginia, just west of Richmond, moving its first fully integrated plant for active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished medicines from plan to construction. The Indianapolis-based drugmaker said the site will focus on antibody-drug conjugates, a class of targeted cancer treatments, and is expected to employ about 650 people once running, with roughly 1,800 workers needed during construction.

How antibody-drug conjugates are made

Antibody-drug conjugates combine a monoclonal antibody, which seeks out a specific marker on a cell, with a potent drug payload attached through a chemical linker. The design aims to deliver a cell-killing agent directly to tumor cells while limiting exposure to healthy tissue. Lilly said in its announcement that these medicines are being developed for cancer and are also being explored for autoimmune diseases and other conditions.

Producing them is technically demanding because it joins two very different manufacturing worlds. The antibody comes from large-scale biologics production in living cells, while the payload and linker are small-molecule chemistry, often involving highly potent compounds that require containment. The conjugation step that links them, followed by purification and fill-finish, adds further handling and quality requirements. Many developers split these steps across several plants or outside contractors, which makes Lilly's decision to house API and drug product in one facility the central operational feature of the Virginia project.

When Lilly first announced the site in September 2025, it described the plant as its first dedicated, fully integrated site for its bioconjugate platform and monoclonal antibody portfolio and said it expected construction to be completed within five years.

Industry implications

The groundbreaking turns a commitment Lilly first disclosed in 2025 into physical construction. Lilly framed the project as one of 10 new U.S. manufacturing sites it has announced since 2020, including five that will produce API: Richmond; Huntsville, Ala.; Houston; and two sites in Lebanon, Ind. Its other new U.S. sites cover injectable medicines and devices in Research Triangle Park and Concord, N.C., Kenosha, Wis., and Lehigh Valley, Pa., plus a genetic medicines site in Lebanon.

For the broader drug industry, the Virginia plant signals that targeted oncology biologics are now being treated as volume products that justify dedicated domestic capacity, rather than niche therapies made in small batches. Lilly's emphasis on digital tools for "right-first-time execution" also reflects a shift toward data-driven quality control in complex biologics, where batch failures carry high costs.

The project also lands amid federal pressure to reshore drug production. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spoke at the event and tied the investment to the resilience of the American economy, underscoring the policy weight now attached to domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Competitive and supply chain implications

Integrating API and finished product under one roof reduces the number of handoffs between facilities, a common source of delay and risk for complex biologics. For Lilly, that could mean tighter control over timelines and quality as its oncology pipeline advances. For contract development and manufacturing organizations that specialize in conjugation and high-potency handling, a large in-house plant from a major drugmaker may limit some future outsourcing opportunities, even as demand from smaller developers continues.

The build also creates near-term demand for suppliers of bioreactors, chromatography systems, containment equipment, automation software and cleanroom construction. Lilly has not disclosed equipment vendors or contractors for the site. Rivals that rely heavily on overseas or third-party capacity for antibody-drug conjugates may face pressure to explain their own domestic supply plans to regulators and payers.

Workforce availability is a practical constraint. Highly potent compound handling and biologics operations require specialized technicians, which helps explain Lilly's $40 million commitment to a statewide training network rather than relying solely on local hiring.

Regional implications

The facility strengthens the Richmond region's emerging biopharmaceutical manufacturing base. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger called the investment a powerful vote of confidence in the state, and Goochland County Board of Supervisors Chairman Jonathan Christy described the groundbreaking as an exciting step forward for the community.

The training center planned for 2028 gives the region a pipeline for skilled operators that could also serve other drug manufacturers. In its 2025 announcement, Lilly said job creation support would come in part through the Virginia Talent Accelerator Program and that its investment and job figures exceeded what it first committed in its state incentive application. The roughly 1,800 construction jobs will add near-term activity for regional trades and contractors.

What comes next

Site construction in Goochland County, with Lilly hiring for permanent roles in the Richmond area as building progresses.

Opening of the Virginia Center for Advanced Pharmaceutical Manufacturing training center in Goochland County, targeted for 2028.

Equipment installation, commissioning and validation ahead of regulatory approval for commercial supply, within the five-year completion window Lilly outlined in 2025.

Further construction milestones at Lilly's other new U.S. API sites, including Huntsville and Houston.

Updates on the antibody-drug conjugate programs that the facility is designed to supply.

Eli Lilly and Company: Lilly announces plans to build $5 billion manufacturing facility in Virginia (Sept. 16, 2025)

text:
L'Oreal said Thursday its third quarter sales rose by double digits as the French cosmetics giant appeared to have dodged the stagnation affecting much of the luxury industry.

The company, whose brands include Garnier, Lancome and Maybelline, said its sales came in at 11.6 billion euros ($13.0 billion) in the three months to the end of September, handily beating analyst expectations.

That is an 11.9-percent increase from the same period last year, with growth in all divisions, including the luxury unit.

Chief executive Nicolas Hieronimus called L'Oreal's third quarter performance "exceptional".

"The global beauty market, once again, proved its resilience in a challenging context -- and we continued to significantly outpace it," he said.

He reaffirmed his confidence that L'Oreal will manage to increase its sales and profits again this year, but did not provide any figures.

Sales rose in all regions, including in the company's North Asia region.

It said China had been the key driver, its sales there advancing nearly three times faster than the overall market, with the luxury segment also growing.

China was the main driver of growth in the luxury market until recent years.

L'Oreal has largely been able to avoid the troubles that luxury groups have faced thanks to its products aimed at the mass market and professionals.

text:
This story was originally published on Banking Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Banking Dive newsletter.

Barclays is cutting roughly 5,000 full-time employees, or 5% of its workforce, this year – with heavy impact expected in "support functions" such as developers – as artificial intelligence boosts productivity, the bank's CFO, Anna Cross, said Thursday.

The announcement came as the British bank reported its third-quarter earnings, which revealed, among other metrics, a 19% year-over-year drop in revenue from fixed income and currency trading.

The job cuts stole the show, though. Barclays reduced its workforce by about 1,000 employees in the first half of the year, so the remaining 4,000 jobs are expected to be shed by December.

"The changes that we're making in the third and fourth quarters of this year are sizable," Cross told analysts on a call Thursday. "They relate both to the simplification of the organization and to some of the impacts that we're starting to see from AI."

Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan, colloquially known as Venkat, noted the bank intends to "employ AI at scale."

"But AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake," Venkat said.

Barclays is far from the only bank this year to hang workforce cuts on the rise of AI.

HSBC in March was reported to have been considering shedding as many as 20,000 mostly middle- and back-office jobs over the next five years in favor of AI.

Standard Chartered in May said it would eliminate more than 7,800 "corporate functions" jobs, such as human resources, risk management and regulatory compliance, by 2030.

But StanChart CEO Bill Winters' description of the jobs that would be replaced rankled some observers.

"It's not cost cutting; it's replacing, in some cases, lower-value human capital with the financial capital and the investment capital we're putting in," Winters said during the bank's May investor day. "We don't have job losses, but we do have job role reductions in favor of the machines, and that will accelerate as we go forward into AI."

Winters later apologized amid public criticism that he appeared to be assigning value to the workers inhabiting those roles.

"Where roles do fall away, it reflects changes in the work, not the value of our people," Winters said in a memo the next day.

Barclays' Venkat, as it turns out, offered a more tempered assessment of Winters' comments as the StanChart blowback grew.

"What people do are jobs, and a job is much more than a collection of tasks," Venkat told Bloomberg in May. "Now you've just got to take tasks and make them more productive."

Roughly 60% of the Barclays jobs on the chopping block are so-called support functions. The bank said it had spent £307 million ($410.5 million) over the first nine months of 2026 on a restructuring that has included staff reductions, investments in technology and a broader overhaul of operations. Barclays expects to incur another £300 million in restructuring costs by the end of December, the bank said.

The total, more than £600 million, is roughly double the bank's earlier estimate. Barclays, however, is sticking to its cost estimates for 2027 and 2028, Cross said.

On the earnings front, Venkat said he is "disappointed" by the dip in fixed income.

"This is always the house that fixed income built," he said. "You can be sure this will get my attention."

Not all of Barclays' earnings news should come as negative, though. The bank reported third-quarter profit of $3.1 billion, a 12% increase from a year ago.

Barclays' equities traders, meanwhile, posted a 47% jump in revenue.

text:
The only constant is change, as the saying goes, and workers are wearing thin because of it.

Organizational change isn’t new, but many companies have undergone great upheaval since the Covid-19 pandemic: navigating hybrid work and return-to-office mandates, mass layoffs, restructurings and the consequent reshuffling of responsibilities, and AI adoption.

“Everybody is feeling change fatigue,” Lorraine “Lo” Stomski, Walmart’s chief talent officer, told CNBC Make It at Forbes’ Future of Work Summit in New York City on Oct. 6. “The environment is changing so rapidly.”

Managers and employers should be thinking about “really helping their employees to navigate through that,” she adds.

Change fatigue is a state of exhaustion workers may experience after going through many changes at their employer. It can show up as resistance, apathy, or resignation to changes, and research indicates it can predict increased strain and burnout, as well as lower employee commitment and performance.

Many employees are hit with curveball after curveball with little time to adjust. Roughly 73% of employees said their organization had experienced some level of disruptive change within the past year in a Gallup survey of over 22,000 U.S. workers published in December 2024. “The more disruption that employees have experienced, the more likely they are to feel burned out today,” the report says.

“Change is stressful, particularly if it’s not managed well,” says Peter Cappelli, management professor and director of the Center for Human Resources at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School. “Every transition creates stress and requires energy from people, and they just get worn out from doing it.”

Employers can take some steps to make changes feel more manageable, including “giving workers agency” and “equipping them with tools,” said Stomski.

That could mean getting their input on a restructuring ahead of time. Letting them apply for other jobs internally if their current role will be eliminated also helps, Cappelli adds: “You should certainly tell people what you’re trying to do, and then say we want to involve you in the process.”

Communicating clearly through the change, including specifying why it’s happening and how it will affect employees, can mitigate anxiety around it. When it comes to introducing new technologies, like AI, training can help things go over more smoothly.

“A lot of resistance comes from people who feel they’re going to fail in the new context,” Cappelli says. If you can demonstrate what it looks like and practice what they should do with it, that can help smooth the transition.

As for employees, while they likely won’t have much sway in the matter, they should focus on what they can control. They can also ask their direct managers for more answers and clarity that can ease the transition, Cappelli says. But organizations should expect some workers may also resort to looking for work elsewhere.

“Employees who are confronted with this kind of change, without a story about where it’s going, without any sense that they’re going to be involved in the process, without any control over it — I wouldn’t be surprised to find that they’re all going to be looking for another job,” Cappelli says.

text:
Barclays is cutting roughly 5,000 full-time employees, or 5% of its workforce, this year – with heavy impact expected in “support functions” such as developers – as artificial intelligence boosts productivity, the bank’s CFO, Anna Cross, said Thursday.

The announcement came as the British bank reported its third-quarter earnings, which revealed, among other metrics, a 19% year-over-year drop in revenue from fixed income and currency trading.

The job cuts stole the show, though. Barclays reduced its workforce by about 1,000 employees in the first half of the year, so the remaining 4,000 jobs are expected to be shed by December.

“The changes that we’re making in the third and fourth quarters of this year are sizable,” Cross told analysts on a call Thursday. “They relate both to the simplification of the organization and to some of the impacts that we’re starting to see from AI.”

Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan, colloquially known as Venkat, noted the bank intends to “employ AI at scale.”

“But AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake,” Venkat said.

Barclays is far from the only bank this year to hang workforce cuts on the rise of AI.

HSBC in March was reported to have been considering shedding as many as 20,000 mostly middle- and back-office jobs over the next five years in favor of AI.

Standard Chartered in May said it wouldeliminate more than 7,800 “corporate functions” jobs, such as human resources, risk management and regulatory compliance, by 2030.

But StanChart CEO Bill Winters’ description of the jobs that would be replaced rankled some observers.

“It’s not cost cutting; it’s replacing, in some cases, lower-value human capital with the financial capital and the investment capital we’re putting in,” Winters said during the bank’s Mayinvestor day. “We don’t have job losses, but we do have job role reductions in favor of the machines, and that will accelerate as we go forward into AI.”

Winters later apologized amid public criticism that he appeared to be assigning value to the workers inhabiting those roles.

“Where roles do fall away, it reflects changes in the work, not the value of our people,” Winters said in a memo the next day.

Barclays’ Venkat, as it turns out, offered a more tempered assessment of Winters’ comments as the StanChart blowback grew.

“What people do are jobs, and a job is much more than a collection of tasks,” Venkat told Bloomberg in May. “Now you’ve just got to take tasks and make them more productive.”

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Banking Dive free daily newsletter

Roughly 60% of the Barclays jobs on the chopping block are so-called support functions. The bank said it had spent £307 million ($410.5 million) over the first nine months of 2026 on a restructuring that has included staff reductions, investments in technology and a broader overhaul of operations. Barclays expects to incur another £300 million in restructuring costs by the end of December, the bank said.

The total, more than £600 million, is roughly double the bank’s earlier estimate. Barclays, however, is sticking to its cost estimates for 2027 and 2028, Cross said.

On the earnings front, Venkat said he is “disappointed” by the dip in fixed income.

“This is always the house that fixed income built,” he said. “You can be sure this will get my attention.”

Not all of Barclays’ earnings news should come as negative, though. The bank reported third-quarter profit of $3.1 billion, a 12% increase from a year ago.
