text:
ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.

This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.

Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.

"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."

The companies were drawn to the region with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give these data centers a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population. This order gives them the power to expropriate land, strips local mayors of veto powers, and restricts the time the public has to object to 23 working days. (For the recent Amazon Web Services development, the regional government opened the window to oppose the project over the Christmas period. Opponents of the project believe they did this to try to push it through at a time when people would be paying less attention, though the government denies this.)

The rapid approval process for these large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly impact their region and lives.

"It's going to be like living beside a prison"

The first time Silvia Baselga and her family learned of the data center soon to tower over their home was when they noticed the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. "When we saw this, we went to the city hall and said, 'OK, we want information. This is really close to our house.'" But the local council told them they had no information. Only when the planning documents were later made public did they learn that the outer perimeter of the data center is to be built within 300 feet of their home in the hilltop village of Botorrita. The plans showed that the complex will be larger than the village itself.

Baselga's parents retired here for the tranquility of a life spent in a tight-knit village community. Their home looks out over fields and gently rolling hills. To try to block the noise the data center will emit, Baselga believes the company will build a 20-foot-high wall, as happened in a nearby village. "We're going to open the window and see nothing," she said. Friends regularly visit at night to gaze at the stars in this rural setting. Baselga said the center's 24-hour security lights will block out the night sky. "It's going to be like living beside a prison."

Centers like these are set to be built across Aragon — 27 in total, according to official documents — some by Spanish and other firms, but most by American companies, taking up about 7 square miles of land. At least one is built partly on ground originally classified as protected for natural ecosystems. The companies promise employment. Amazon Web Services told NPR it will create 6,200 permanent jobs once these centers are built. But many residents fear they will also deliver an environmental crisis.

Economic development "at the cost of the environment"

The data centers will consume many times the current electricity needs of the region and require large amounts of water to cool their servers in one of Spain's driest regions, one that's been repeatedly blighted by drought.

Julio Enfedaque drives across the parched land his family has farmed for generations. This year it barely rained for four months, and the government cut the amount of water available for irrigation by two-thirds. "Even if they say the data centers won't take the water that we need for agriculture, I am sure it's going to become very complicated to farm like my ancestors used to." Enfedaque has advised his nephews to find different careers and leave the land.

Amazon Web Services says its data centers will draw water only after temperatures hit 86 degrees Fahrenheit and that they are investing millions of dollars to help fix leaking water pipes and working with farmers to use AI technology to make their water use more efficient. "We're trying to not only use as less [sic] water as possible, but also to help those communities where we operate have the best infrastructure," David Blázquez, Amazon's head of public policy for Spain and Portugal, told NPR.

But the company remains opaque about how much water each center will use. Blázquez said it's "a company policy not to publish water usage per site." Regional figures show Amazon's three existing data centers, which are much smaller than what is planned, used 68 million liters — 48% more than the company had originally told regional officials they would need.

Endangering valuable habitat for rare and migratory birds

Perhaps an even bigger problem is the energy these centers need to run. Unlike many data centers in the U.S., which are powered by natural gas, companies in Aragon say they will rely mainly on renewable sources (though they also have diesel generators on site). Blázquez says Amazon Web Services has secured "a hundred renewable projects in Spain," including 17 in Aragon.

While that energy is carbon-free, ecologists and biologists warn that additional wind projects could have their own devastating consequences for the environment.

The region is full of hunting grounds for vultures and other birds of prey and an important stop for migrating birds.

"The vultures look for the thermal air currents to lift them. But they run straight into the windmills — for them it's like flying through knives," explained José Antonio Pinzolas, an ornithologist.

Aragon's own environmental agency has warned that wind farms in this area pose a high risk of collision to the endangered red kite and other protected raptors, and has documented an increase in bird and bat deaths in recent years as the renewable sector expands.

"I've collected ospreys, golden eagles, kestrels by the dozen, black vultures," said Juan Ballesteros, a nature protection officer for the local government.

Ballesteros used to love his job for its access to wildlife. Now, he said, he spends his days placing the corpses of birds killed by turbine blades into body bags. Ballesteros met NPR as he arrived to collect the body of a young Eurasian black vulture that lay dead on the ground, its wings splayed in the dirt at the foot of a wind turbine.

Blázquez told NPR, of the damage to this important habitat that the expansion of wind and solar farms causes, that Amazon Web Services "definitely shares those concerns." He said they work with renewable energy companies that comply with environmental legislation. But Pinzolas said the growing number of bird deaths shows the current protections in place are not working.

Environmental groups say the overall impact of wind turbines on birds isn't being properly assessed.

Several groups have crowdfunded together to mount a legal action to try to stop Amazon Web Services' expansion in Aragon. The court case challenges the Aragon government's fast-tracked approvals of the plans. "We have concerns about water consumption, about energy consumption, the impact on some other industries and on the environment," said Luis García,, an activist with Ecologistas En Accion, one of the organizations involved in the case. He said the economic benefits of data centers are not great enough to justify the "huge damage they do to the environment."

Locals fight to preserve nature for future generations

One recent weekend in the region's capital, Zaragoza, an avenue filled with demonstrators protesting against a new data center to be built at the edge of a forest by the city. Residents fear the heat and noise of the complex will destroy a tranquil space that is a haven during the hot summer months.

"This is a worthy fight as all the worlds invades us, to save this pine forests, to save the environment, against this voracious capitalism that thinks only of economic interests and not of people," said Marian Rams, a local resident with white hair dyed in hues of pink, green and blue. "They want to swap nature for data centers."

Nearby, a little girl no older than 5 chanted along with the demonstrators. Her mother, Ana Domezian, walked alongside her with her second child, a baby, nestled in a carrier against her chest. "If we don't fight now for what we have," she asked, "what are we going to leave to them in the future?"

text:
Most web pages run using an open-source programming language called PHP. That language is maintained by the PHP Foundation. Today, the foundation disclosed two “critical” software vulnerabilities and issued an emergency patch, urging websites to implement it immediately or take down their websites until they are able to. The vulnerabilities are named CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively called “php2shell.”

As reports broke late on Oct. 20 of the vulnerabilities ahead of the patch’s official release, some opportunistic attackers tried to exploit it. Cloudflare, a global cybersecurity company that helps secure millions of websites, saw “tens of thousands” of exploit attempts within 45 minutes of the word getting out. That number jumped to “hundreds of thousands” within two hours, and millions by the evening of Oct. 21, according to seeing “early attacks,” according to its co-founder and CEO Matthew Prince.

Amazon Web Services also reported on Oct. 21 that the vulnerability is “now being broadly exploited in the wild.” The company said that it had seen some attempts by hackers to use the exploit in the days prior to the vulnerability being disclosed on Oct. 20, raising the possibility that the news about the flaw had leaked to hackers prior to the official announcement from PHP.

One startup owner reported that the PHP bug is “real bad” and says everyone should be “afraid” after hackers allegedly stole their source code, exposed cookie data, and leaked legal documents.

Multiple governments have decided to take websites offline as a safety precaution, including some agencies in the Netherlands and Finland, Reuters reported. The FBI’s cyber division and the National Security Agency both issued statements urging potentially affected organizations to update their services, as did the prime minister of Japan, the European Union’s computer emergency response team, and several other national agencies.

“The impact of the PHP vulnerabilities is massive, [and] can expose a large number of websites to immediate attacks if not patched in time,” Gang Wang, associate professor of computer science at the University of Illinois’s Grainger College of Engineering, told Fortune. The bugs allow bad actors to remotely execute code on flawed, not-yet-patched PHP systems. Attackers can use that as an “entry point into the network hosting that machine, and from there potentially carry out attacks that cause significant damage,” Wang’s colleague, David Nicol, director of the Information Trust Institute at Grainger College, told Fortune.

Among the most well known sites that run on PHP is WordPress, which powers roughly 40% of all websites, according to Reuters. But PHP is ubiquitous across the web, having started as a small project back in 1994 and grown up with the modern internet. For example, Facebook launched in 2004 as a PHP website, although in 2020 the company embarked on a major effort to update to different software. Other popular sites using PHP include Microsoft.com, Wikipedia.org, Archive.org (now temporarily offline), TheGuardian.com, and Baidu.com, according to W3Techs. An initial analysis by cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks identified 22.6 million potentially vulnerable instances.

OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman said PHP was his “first programming language,” in a post about the vulnerability discovery. OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as well as other AI tools, played a key role in finding the vulnerabilities.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said in a blog post. “It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”

The backstory: Three parties discovered different elements of the bug

Multiple security organizations independently found the issue around the same time, in August. All of them used AI to help find the vulnerabilities. They then banded together in a coordinated effort with the PHP Foundation to develop fixes and coordinate the disclosure of the vulnerabilities and rollout of the patch, OpenAI said.

Technically, the first to discover part of the issue was the California-based AI red-teaming firm Calif. OpenAI had invited Calif to join its Patch the Planet initiative, an effort to proactively find and patch security vulnerabilities in digital infrastructure. Calif decided to investigate PHP because it “stood out as a high-impact target,” the company says. It reached out to Volker Dusch at the PHP Foundation, and then “got to work hacking PHP.”

The Calif team was “not expecting to find anything critical” since PHP has been highly scrutinized by the cybersecurity community for years. In fact, the bug they eventually found had “been present in PHP for 14 years,” OpenAI’s Brockman pointed out in his post. “A limited version of it had been discovered in 2024 and wasn’t considered significant at the time.” But now that AI models can run attack sequences autonomously, almost no vulnerability is too difficult to exploit.

“Php2shell shows how AI can help uncover buried flaws and turn complex exploit chains into practical attacks, increasing the potential risk,” TJ Sayers, senior director of threat intelligence at the Center for Internet Security, told Fortune.

On Aug. 1, Calif found the first issue using GPT-5.6 Sol. It then informed OpenAI, which looked into the issue on its own and found additional elements of the bug. This made the discovery more comprehensive, but almost made clear that the flaw was more serious than Calif had originally realized, an OpenAI spokesperson told Fortune.

Then OpenAI began chatting with the PHP Foundation about the issue. Through those conversations, OpenAI learned that Wiz, a Google-owned cybersecurity company, was also talking to the foundation about the issue.

Researchers at Wiz had independently found the vulnerabilities in August. They decided to investigate PHP in the first place because it’s “the backbone of the internet,” a Wiz spokesperson tells Fortune, acknowledging that the parallel initiative may seem like a “coincidence,” but the Wiz team’s charter is to investigate high-impact digital infrastructure, and PHP was top of mind. The Wiz team identified the first issue on Aug. 19, using a combination of Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, and Wiz Atlas.

“With 70% of the internet affected, the impact of php2shell cannot be overstated,” Wiz said in a blog post announcing its findings. “It marks an AI inflection point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade–what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit.”

OpenAI then decided to bring all the parties together, leading a “coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address [the] critical vulnerabilities,” the company said. That included Wiz, Calif, PHP, Cloudflare, and multiple U.S. government agencies, among others. Cloudflare’s blog post also names the French cybersecurity company Quarkslab as part of the effort.

title: BKT ties up with Pirelli for premium car tyres as rivals commit ₹8600 crore to expansion
description:
BKT will separately pay Pirelli in euros for testing and technical services covering its own passenger-car, SUV and two-wheeler tyres.
Apollo accounts for ₹5,810 crore, CEAT ₹1,314 crore, Bridgestone approximately ₹750 crore ($85 million) and Michelin nearly ₹686 crore.
BKT targets ₹23,000 crore in revenue by FY30, with on-highway tyres contributing approximately 20 per cent, or ₹4,600 crore.
BKT and Pirelli expect India’s premium car-tyre market to grow almost fivefold between 2025 and 2030, without disclosing its starting size.
For Pirelli, the partnership offers Indian manufacturing capacity; for BKT, the challenge is building a profitable passenger-car tyre business against established competitors.
text:
Balkrishna Industries (BKT) on Thursday announced a partnership with Italian tyre maker Pirelli to manufacture premium passenger car and SUV tyres at its Bhuj plant in Gujarat, targeting annual production of up to 8 lakh Pirelli-branded tyres by 2030. The companies have not disclosed when production will begin.

Rajiv Poddar, BKT’s Joint Managing Director, said the partnership would accelerate its existing plans to enter new tyre categories, describing Pirelli’s decision as “a recognition of the manufacturing strength, quality and expertise we have built over decades”.

Under three agreements signed on October 22, the companies plan a 50:50 joint venture to establish a new tyre factory in India, sharing manufacturing capacity equally. BKT will separately pay Pirelli in euros for testing and technical services covering its own passenger-car, SUV and two-wheeler tyres. The venture’s incorporation is targeted by December 31, 2030, although investment, capacity and commissioning details remain undisclosed.

The partnership comes as Bridgestone, Michelin, CEAT and Apollo Tyres have announced combined investments of approximately ₹8,600 crore to expand Indian production. Apollo accounts for ₹5,810 crore, CEAT ₹1,314 crore, Bridgestone approximately ₹750 crore ($85 million) and Michelin nearly ₹686 crore.

BKT has separately outlined a ₹6,800 crore investment programme through FY29 covering off-highway and on-highway tyres, carbon black and infrastructure. Whether the Pirelli venture requires additional investment remains unclear.

India’s premium tyre opportunity extends beyond luxury cars. SUVs account for more than half of passenger-vehicle sales, driving demand for larger 17-inch to 22-inch tyres. Electric vehicles require tyres designed for greater weight, higher torque and reduced noise, while the expanding vehicle population supports replacement demand.

Manufacturing orders, technology support

Under the initial offtake agreement, Pirelli has committed to minimum annual purchases, although year wise quantities, contract value and margins remain undisclosed. Pricing will reflect actual raw-material and conversion costs, providing demand visibility without guaranteeing profitability.

The arrangement gives BKT, traditionally an off-highway tyre specialist serving agriculture, mining and construction, an established premium customer while it develops its own passenger-car brand. Pirelli’s trademark and specified know-how can be used only for tyres supplied to Pirelli and its affiliates.

Marco Tronchetti Provera of Pirelli, said India’s economic development and growing demand for technologically advanced tyres made it important to the company’s international strategy.

BKT targets ₹23,000 crore in revenue by FY30, with on-highway tyres contributing approximately 20 per cent, or ₹4,600 crore.

Competition builds capacity

Bridgestone, which reported around 20 per cent of India’s passenger-vehicle replacement tyre market in 2024, plans to add 11 lakh tyres annually at Pune by 2029. CEAT plans another 35 lakh annually at Chennai by FY28, while Michelin is expanding premium-car tyre production and Apollo is adding passenger-car and commercial-vehicle capacity.

BKT and Pirelli expect India’s premium car-tyre market to grow almost fivefold between 2025 and 2030, without disclosing its starting size.

For Pirelli, the partnership offers Indian manufacturing capacity; for BKT, the challenge is building a profitable passenger-car tyre business against established competitors.

text:
Disciplined execution and tangible progress on the Group's strategic priorities in a challenging environment

Focused action plan to restore Gucci desirability and rebuild foundations for sustainable growth

Solid momentum at Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta, Brioni, Kering Jewelry and Kering Eyewear, with clear action plans to further unlock their full potential

Revenue : €3,345 million

Stable on a reported basis, -1% on a comparable basis

“Third-quarter revenue reflects the phasing we anticipated, in a softer macroeconomic environment.

The recovery of Gucci remains our defining priority. We are steadily strengthening desirability and advancing our product development at pace. Reflecting the complementarity of our portfolio, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta and Brioni, as well as Kering Eyewear and Kering Jewelry, continue to extend their strong trajectory and we are doubling down on the renewal of Balenciaga and Alexander McQueen.

Unlocking the Group's full potential requires restoring momentum at Gucci, accelerating on product excellence, delivering our action plan in China, realizing the full benefits of our Group platform and embedding a culture of execution across the organization.

The transformation of Kering is a multi-season undertaking, but the improvements we are seeing across the Group, notably in desirability and key operating indicators, reinforce our confidence in the direction we have set, and the determination of our teams to deliver it.”

Luca de Meo, Directeur général de Kering

Kering revenue in the third quarter of 2026 amounted to €3,345 million, stable as reported and down 1% on a comparable basis year-on-year. The change in reported revenue included a positive currency effect of 1 percentage point and no scope impact.

Third-quarter revenue reflected the anticipated second-half phasing and a more difficult comparison base, compounded by softer macroeconomic trends. Traffic remained the main constraint, while conversion, average price and average ticket remained supportive across most Houses, helped by stronger product execution and improved client engagement.

By channel, in the third quarter:

• Sales from the directly operated retail network, including e-commerce, declined by 3% on a comparable basis, remaining uneven across regions and Houses.

• Wholesale and Other revenues were up 3% on a comparable basis.

In the first nine months of 2026, the Group generated revenue of €10,565 million, down 2% as reported and stable on a comparable basis, while advancing the optimization of its store network. Following 75 net store closures in 2025, Kering completed a further 105 net store closures during the first nine months of the year, including 128 closures and 23 openings, thereby exceeding its full-year objective of 100 net closures ahead of schedule. The Group now plans at least 125 net closures for the full year 2026.

Kering Fashion & Leather Goods

In the third quarter of 2026, Kering Fashion & Leather Goods revenue amounted to €2,743 million, down 1% as reported and 3% on a comparable basis.

The performance of Gucci, which is part of this segment, is detailed in a dedicated section.

Sales in the directly operated retail network were down 4% on a comparable basis. Excluding Gucci, retail sales increased by 2%, driven by continued growth at Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta and Brioni, underscoring the increasing breadth of the Group’s portfolio.

• Saint Laurent growth was notably driven by sustained momentum in North America and Western Europe, and strong engagement from VICs (Very Important Clients) and Core clients.

• Bottega Veneta again outperformed across key markets, supported by sustained brand desirability, strong momentum in leather goods and successful product introductions. The House also advanced its diversification strategy, notably in ready-to-wear, while benefitting from strong engagement among VICs.

• Balenciaga remained resilient in leather goods, while its ready-to-wear and shoes categories were still challenged.

• Alexander McQueen pursued its repositioning, sharpening its British tailoring identity, enhancing its product offering and streamlining its distribution footprint as part of its turnaround plan.

• Brioni maintained strong growth, supported by its highly personalized client relationship and the strength of its bespoke offer.

Wholesale and Other revenues of the segment increased by 4% on a comparable basis.

of which Gucci

Gucci recorded revenue of €1,291 million in the third quarter, down 4% as reported and down 6% on a comparable basis.

The performance of Gucci reflected a more demanding comparison base and a less pronounced newness effect than in the second quarter. While traffic remained the main constraint, conversion, average price and average ticket improved further, supported by the progressive rollout of new collections.

The House pressed ahead with its product transformation agenda, further refining its product and pricing architecture, enhancing quality and improving time to market. Handbags were at the forefront of these efforts, supported by a richer offering, while ready-to-wear and shoes remain key areas of focus.

Sales from the directly operated retail network declined by 9% on a comparable basis. North America remained the House’s most resilient market against a more demanding comparison base, while lower traffic weighed on performance in Asia Pacific, particularly in Mainland China, and in Japan.

Wholesale and Other revenues were up 35% on a comparable basis in the third quarter. Wholesale, which amounted to €120 million, or 9% of the quarterly sales, was up 45% on a comparable basis, reflecting a low comparison base and order-book effects as new collections came through.

Kering Jewelry

In the third quarter of 2026, Kering Jewelry delivered another strong performance against a more demanding comparison base. Revenue amounted to €239 million, up 12% as reported and 11% on a comparable basis, reflecting the strength of the division’s complementary Houses.

Boucheron maintained strong momentum, supported by the enduring appeal of its iconic collections Quatre and Serpent Bohème and good performance in Japan and South Korea. Pomellato continued to build momentum, particularly in Japan, driven by sustained demand for Nudo, Iconica and Together. Performance at DoDo and Qeelin was mixed, though the Houses moved forward with their product initiatives, notably with Qeelin’s successful launch of Wulu Purple Jade.

Sales in the directly operated retail network increased by 18% on both a reported and a comparable basis, while Wholesale and Other revenues decreased by 6%.

Kering Eyewear

In the third quarter of 2026, Kering Eyewear revenue amounted to €373 million, up 6% as reported and up 4% on a comparable basis, reflecting the resilience of the business despite the anticipated phasing effects between the third and fourth quarters. Performance was supported by ongoing innovation and strong commercial execution across the portfolio, with growth across all regions. Key developments during the quarter included the launch of the Fall Winter 2026 collection of Maui Jim, initiatives celebrating the fortieth anniversary of Lindberg, as well as successful sales and marketing campaigns across key markets.

Corporate & Other

In the third quarter of 2026, revenue from Corporate & Other amounted to €27 million, down 5% on a reported and a comparable basis, primarily reflecting the end of rental income following the real estate transactions.

Within the segment, Ginori 1735 delivered strong double-digit growth, reflecting the steady progress in brand development and desirability across key markets.

Outlook

Kering is fully mobilized on the execution of its strategic plan. The Group continues to prioritize the quality of its revenue and the depth of its transformation, with progress on both fronts: several Houses are showing strong momentum and the recovery at Gucci is gradually taking shape.

While short-term revenue trends reflect a more challenging macroeconomic environment, Kering confirm its objective of improving its recurring operating margin in 2026, supported by the efficiency measures under way, while maintaining strong investment in the desirability of its Houses.

HIGHLIGHTS AND ANNOUNCEMENTS DURING THE THIRD QUARTER

Gucci and L’Oréal entered a 50-year exclusive beauty license, one year ahead of schedule

On July 7, 2026, Gucci and L’Oréal entered into a 50-year exclusive beauty license agreement, expected to become effective in mid-2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals and the early redemption of the existing agreement between Gucci and Coty. By combining the global desirability and distinctive creative vision of Gucci with the unparalleled expertise of L’Oréal in beauty, innovation capabilities and worldwide distribution network, the partnership aims to unlock significant long-term growth opportunities across fragrance and beauty.

Romain Spitzer appointed Chief Executive Officer of Bottega Veneta

On July 15, 2026, Romain Spitzer was appointed Chief Executive Officer of Bottega Veneta, effective since September 1, 2026. He reports to Luca de Meo and joins the Executive Committee of Kering. He brings more than thirty years of international experience in the luxury industry, with extensive expertise in brand

stewardship, retail excellence, and client experience.

Kering Jewelry leadership appointments

of Kering Jewelry. These appointments support Kering Jewelry's ambition to further unlock the growth potential of its Houses while reinforcing their distinctive identities.

Sabina Belli appointed President of Kering Italia

On September 1, 2026, Sabina Belli was appointed President of Kering Italia, effective since September 15, 2026, reporting to Luca de Meo, Chief Executive Officer of Kering. In her new role, she represents Kering in Italy and strengthens the Group’s dialogue with public institutions, luxury industry associations and key stakeholders. In addition, she continues to oversee the Kering Accademia per le Eccellenze.

Sophie Maddaloni appointed General Secretary of Kering

On September 1, 2026, Sophie Maddaloni was appointed General Secretary of Kering, effective immediately, joining the Group Executive Committee and reporting to Jean-Marc Duplaix, in his capacity as Group Chief Operating Officer. In her new role, she is responsible for the Group's governance and for

safeguarding its interests, as well as for upholding the highest standards of compliance. She oversees the Legal, Internal Control, Internal Audit, and Security departments, working closely with Executive Management and the Board of Directors.

The House will soon announce its new creative leadership.

Alexander McQueen. The House will soon announce its new creative leadership.

Kering is a global, family-led luxury group, home to people whose passion and expertise nurture creative Houses across couture and ready-to-wear, leather goods, jewelry, eyewear and beauty: Gucci, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta, Balenciaga, Alexander McQueen, Brioni, Boucheron, Pomellato, DoDo, Qeelin, Ginori 1735, as well as Kering Eyewear. text:
First Lilly site to produce both active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished medicines in a fully integrated facility

Site will create 650 high-wage jobs

INDIANAPOLIS, Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE: LLY) broke ground today on a new $5 billion manufacturing facility just west of Richmond, Virginia, in Goochland County, one of 10 new U.S. manufacturing sites announced since 2020 and one of five among them that will produce active pharmaceutical ingredients (API). As part of the company's more than $50 billion push to expand medicine production in the U.S., the Richmond site will be Lilly's first to produce both API and finished medicines in a fully integrated facility, with dedicated API capacity for bioconjugate and large-molecule medicines.

The facility will produce antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), targeted cancer treatments designed to combine the precision of antibodies with potent cytotoxic medicines to attack diseased cells directly while limiting exposure to healthy tissue. ADCs are also being explored for autoimmune diseases and other conditions.

David A. Ricks, Lilly Chair and CEO: "We are developing a new generation of medicines designed to target cancer cells with greater precision, yielding more powerful treatments with potentially fewer side effects. This $5 billion investment means we can make them right here in America. Lilly Richmond will help make sure this innovative science can reach the people who need it."

Building a talent pipeline in Richmond

Making advanced medicines in the U.S. requires a highly skilled workforce. Lilly is building that workforce in Virginia, offering long-term careers where people can grow close to home. Lilly has committed $40 million to support the Virginia Center for Advanced Pharmaceutical Manufacturing, a statewide network of industry, government, and higher education partners that will prepare Virginians for those careers. The network will include a pilot-scale, hands-on training center in Goochland County, with a targeted opening in 2028.

Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger: "Lilly's investment is a powerful vote of confidence in Virginia, our people, and our ability to compete for the industries and good jobs that will shape our future. Today's groundbreaking marks an exciting milestone in this partnership, and we are proud that Virginia will play an important, durable role in Lilly's continued global growth and innovation."

Lilly is currently hiring in Richmond and expects the new facility to create 650 high-wage jobs like engineers, scientists, operations personnel, and lab technicians – along with approximately 1,800 construction jobs as the site is built and brought online. Visit the Lilly Richmond career page for open positions or join Lilly's talent community for future opportunities.

Jonathan Christy, Chairman of the Goochland County Board of Supervisors: "Lilly's groundbreaking marks a significant investment in Goochland County and an exciting step forward for our community. We proudly welcome Lilly and the opportunities this project will create for quality jobs, economic growth, and lifesaving innovation."

By pairing a highly skilled workforce with advanced technologies and specialized manufacturing, the Richmond site will help support a reliable supply of safe, high-quality medicines. It will use state-of-the-art technologies, including machine learning, AI, digitally integrated systems and advanced data analytics, to drive right-first-time execution, with digital automation embedded throughout the site to streamline operations.

The Richmond facility will be built and operated to the highest standards for safety, quality and environmental stewardship, and Lilly is committed to being a good neighbor in Goochland County and a trusted partner across Virginia. The site is targeting a Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Gold certification, demonstrating Lilly's focus on sustainable performance as it expands advanced manufacturing in the U.S.

Lilly has announced 10 U.S. sites since 2020:

Five will produce API:

Richmond, Virginia; Huntsville, Alabama; Houston, Texas; and two sites in Lebanon, Indiana – Lebanon API and Lilly Medicine Foundry, which will also focus on new production methods and making medicines for clinical trials

Four will make injectable medicines and manufacture devices:

Research Triangle Park and Concord, North Carolina; Kenosha, Wisconsin; and Lehigh Valley, Pennsylvania

One will make genetic medicines in Lebanon, Indiana; Lebanon Advanced Therapies

Additional quotes for media use

Ambassador Jamieson Greer, U.S. Trade Representative: "President Trump's America First Trade Policy is accelerating our nation's reindustrialization, incentivizing companies to proudly build, invest, and expand their operations domestically. Lilly's new Richmond facility will ensure that life-saving medicines are manufactured on American soil. Today's groundbreaking stands as a powerful testament that there is no substitute for the resilience of the American economy and the skill of the American worker."

About Lilly

Lilly is a medicine company turning science into healing to make life better for people around the world. We've been pioneering life-changing discoveries for 150 years, and today our medicines help tens of millions of people across the globe. Harnessing the power of biotechnology, chemistry and genetic medicine, our scientists are urgently advancing new discoveries to solve some of the world's most significant health challenges: redefining diabetes care; treating obesity and curtailing its most devastating long-term effects; advancing the fight against Alzheimer's disease; providing solutions to some of the most debilitating immune system disorders; and transforming the most difficult-to-treat cancers into manageable diseases. With each step toward a healthier world, we're motivated by one thing: making life better for millions more people. That includes delivering innovative clinical trials that reflect the diversity of our world and working to ensure our medicines are accessible and affordable. text:
Two of the leading AI labs are choosing divergent fundraising paths. Anthropic, which developed the Claude family of large language models (LLMs), is planning an initial public offering (IPO) as early as mid-November and could file for it as soon as Friday, according to media reports on Wednesday.

By contrast, OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, had been planning an IPO in 2026, but has decided to postpone that and is now in talks to hold another private funding round instead. That's a big change for a company that was previously racing toward the public-market finish line.

Here's why Anthropic is still aiming to IPO by the end of the year and why OpenAI decided to wait.

Anthropic has an open window and its best numbers yet

Anthropic confidentially submitted a draft S-1 to the SEC on June 1, and it was reportedly planning to IPO in October. It held off to show prospective investors its third-quarter financial results first, which it did at an official investor day on Oct. 14.

Revenue reached $16.8 billion in Q3, up from $11.5 billion in Q2 and $4.7 billion in Q1. The AI lab said that it had achieved adjusted profitability in the second consecutive quarter and positive free cash flow. Anthropic also generated $1.70 in revenue per $1 spent on computing power in Q3, indicating a compute margin of more than 40%.

The timing also works out well for Anthropic. Space Exploration Technologies went public in June, so enough time has now passed to build up demand in the market for another high-profile IPO. With OpenAI punting on its IPO for the time being, Anthropic stock can enjoy all the attention.

Why OpenAI is waiting

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spoke to Fortune in September and provided a few reasons why his company won't IPO in 2026. He said he believes this "would be an ill-advised moment to go public" due to the growing concerns about the risks posed by AI development. He also mentioned OpenAI's split between nonprofit and for-profit governance, explaining that the company may make decisions that run counter shareholders' financial interests. That becomes more complicated for a publicly traded company.

Although both are legitimate reasons to wait, OpenAI hasn't performed as well as Anthropic, based on the financial metrics each has reported recently. Based on their latest funding rounds, Anthropic's valuation surpassed OpenAI's this year, and Anthropic has reached profitability on an adjusted basis, while OpenAI's operating loss widened to $12.3 billion in Q2.

Anthropic also topped it in Q2 revenue ($11.6 billion for Anthropic vs. $6.7 billion for OpenAI). In fairness, OpenAI reports net revenue and claims that Anthropic reports all contracts sold through cloud partners as revenue, so this may not be an apples-to-apples comparison.

For now, OpenAI prefers to raise money privately. It's also aiming to do so quickly, seeking about $30 billion at a valuation of $1.4 trillion before Anthropic goes public, according to Reuters. That plan has some onlookers speculating that OpenAI wants to lock in its next batch of funding before Anthropic's audited financials are available for comparison.

What to watch

The next major event in this saga will be the arrival of Anthropic's public S-1 (possibly this week), which will allow would-be investors to review its audited financials. The market has only gotten snippets of information so far. A full balance sheet and financial statements will provide a much better picture of Anthropic's business. The S-1 needs to be public at least 15 days before Anthropic's roadshow, which is currently expected to start Nov. 9. If the S-1 isn't available by Oct. 25, then the IPO may be delayed again.

text:
Barclays shares edged lower in London after the bank said on Thursday it would cut around 5,000 jobs, including around 1,000 already cut in the first half of the year.

The announcement came alongside an earnings update that showed Barclays’ net profit grew 13% in the third quarter, helped by surging income in its equities division.

Barclays said in an earnings presentation that it was implementing “organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI”.

About 60% of the job cuts affect support functions, including developers, as AI makes staff more productive, according to the bank.

Will Howlett, a financial analyst at Quilter Cheviot, said the announcement illustrates "just how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said, adding that "Barclays expects its efficiency measures to deliver more than £1.1 billion (€1.31bn) of savings, which should help bring down costs and improve profitability."

The bank’s profit attributable to shareholders rose to £1.65 billion (€1.97 billion) in the third quarter from £1.46 billion (€1.74 billion) in the July–September period a year earlier.

Barclays chief executive C. S. Venkatakrishnan said he was pleased with the bank’s operational and financial momentum, and said the investment bank division “delivered strong equities performance”.

Income from equities jumped 47% year-on-year, while total group income for the quarter climbed 3% to £7.37 billion (€8.79 billion).

"The investment bank was weaker, particularly in fixed income trading, but Barclays remains on track against its longer-term targets," said Howlett. He added that "the question is increasingly whether Barclays can turn technological investment and a smaller workforce into sustainably lower costs without compromising growth." If it can, he said, "there is still considerable scope for improved returns.”

The bank also announced a £500 million (€596 million) share buyback.

The AI “announcement comes as the company failed to match expectations with its third-quarter performance — with the unveiling of a healthy share buyback failing to entirely ease investors’ disappointment”, noted AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.

He added that while costs increased across the wider group, there are two "major clouds over the business".

“The first being a widely expected increase in tax on the sector in next week’s (UK) budget and the other being a reported probe into possible misrepresentation of risks in its private credit portfolio,” Mould said.

According to the FT, the Bank of England was examining claims that Barclays had understated risks linked to financing for private credit funds. The concern is whether Barclays made these exposures look less risky in its books, allowing it to hold less capital to cover potential losses.

Barclays has said its private credit exposure is treated in line with accounting and regulatory capital requirements.

text:
AXA XL, Convex, Marsh, RenaissanceRe, Tokio Marine, and Travelers join Moody’s as founding members, representing six founding organizations spanning the insurance value chain.

NEW YORK, October 22, 2026— Moody’s has announced the launch of Moody’s Casualty Risk Intelligence Group (MCRIG), formed with the participation of six founding firms.

The newly formed group aims to support the advancement of the global casualty (re)insurance market by contributing research and analytical perspectives that encourage the development of independent, science-led, forward-looking approaches to risk assessment, underwriting, and portfolio management.

The casualty industry faces increasing complexity, ranging from longstanding tort exposures and mass litigation to emerging risks such as artificial intelligence liability, as firms navigate a rapidly evolving landscape. Against this backdrop, casualty (re)insurers increasingly recognize the benefits of using forward-looking risk assessment and analytics to help understand, price, and manage casualty risk with greater precision and confidence.

MCRIG was formed to create an open dialogue between industry leaders and Moody’s to discuss areas where new approaches to risk assessment and analytics can help advance the casualty (re)insurance industry. These focus areas could range from exploring the standardization of exposure, loss, and claims data and enhancing portfolio transparency to developing new approaches to forward-looking litigation intelligence that can help clarify where risk is heading.

Joe Melly, Managing Director, Head of Casualty and Financial Lines, Moody’s, said: “Casualty insurance is the next frontier for risk analytics, and Moody’s is committed to leading that transformation. The casualty industry carries enormous economic weight and growing complexity. It is ready to move toward new data standards, litigation intelligence, and decision-grade analytics to help firms understand and manage their exposure.

The formation of MCRIG is Moody’s route to achieving this goal. By engaging with a range of participants, MCRIG aims to support the enhancement of independently developed analytical frameworks and insights intended to advance risk understanding.

We are proud to launch the MCRIG in New York and to do so with such a strong and diverse group of founding participants.”

Noel Richardson, Chief Risk Officer, AXA XL, said: “Casualty insurance faces significant complexity from emerging risks such as PFAS and AI liability, yet the industry relies largely on backward-looking analysis. Through MCRIG, we have an opportunity to develop the data standards, litigation intelligence, and forward-looking analytics that are currently missing. By working with peers and Moody's, we can build the tools casualty underwriting genuinely needs—and create real value in how we assess, price, and manage risk.”

Christopher Ross, Global Casualty Leader, Marsh Re, said: “Marsh believes strongly in the benefits of a collaborative approach to exploring emerging risk issues and welcomes the opportunity to work with our fellow MCRIG members to develop data-driven insights that empower our clients with new and cutting-edge views of risk. The casualty (re)insurance market has undergone significant changes over the past several years in response to the evolving nature of risk. The advent of AI and its downstream implications will only accelerate change, and we will lead the industry in evaluating and creating solutions that enable our clients to succeed in this market.”

Fiona Walden, SVP, Chief Underwriting Officer, Casualty & Specialty, RenaissanceRe, said: “We are proud to be a founding member of the MCRIG and look forward to contributing our expertise and partnering with Moody's and our fellow members to advance casualty analytics and data standards across the industry. This group reinforces our efforts to bring greater transparency and forward-looking insight around emerging casualty trends, supporting our clients and the long-term health of the casualty market.”

Don Mahoney, Vice President, Enterprise Underwriting, Casualty, Travelers, said: “We are pleased to join Moody’s and this exceptional group of partners. This initiative will provide better visibility into casualty exposures in an ever-changing environment and a stronger foundation for risk managers and underwriters across the industry.”

Alongside the launch of MCRIG, Moody’s has announced a significant increase in investment in casualty data, analytics, and modeling. Casualty and Financial Lines at Moody’s, which includes the Praedicat, Inc. acquisition in 2024, together with sustained investment in people, data, and technology, reflects a clear mission: to bring casualty to the same level of analytical rigor that catastrophe modeling brought to property more than three decades ago.

To deliver casualty-specific, decision-grade intelligence, the team uses Moody’s comprehensive, globally renowned commercial data estates, spanning firmographics, financials, credit risk, M&A activity, directors’ and officers’ data, litigation records, cyber risk scores, and satellite-derived analytics across hundreds of millions of entities worldwide.

END

About Moody’s Casualty Risk Intelligence Group

Moody’s Casualty Risk Intelligence Group (MCRIG) operates as a research and thought leadership initiative with appropriate safeguards to ensure compliance with applicable competition laws. Participation is voluntary and non-exclusive, and members act independently at all times in relation to their commercial activities. The group does not involve the exchange of confidential or competitively sensitive information or any alignment or harmonization of pricing, underwriting practices, market conduct, or business strategies. Any outputs are derived from aggregated, anonymized, or publicly available data and are intended to support independent decision-making by market participants.

About Moody’s

In a world shaped by increasingly interconnected risks, Moody’s (NYSE: MCO) data, insights, and innovative technologies help customers develop a holistic view of their world and unlock opportunities. With a rich history of experience in global markets and a diverse workforce of approximately 16,000 across more than 40 countries, Moody’s gives customers the comprehensive perspective needed to act with confidence and thrive.

Maruti Suzuki has partnered with Adobe to modernise its digital customer experience platforms, integrating content, customer data and digital journeys across marketing, sales, service and vehicle ownership.

The collaboration aims to establish a common digital platform for customer interactions across the automaker’s businesses. The initiative involves integrating legacy systems, improving data connectivity and updating its websites to support more personalised and consistent experiences throughout the vehicle ownership journey.

Sunil Kakkar, Director of Corporate Planning and Executive Committee Member at Maruti Suzuki, said the collaboration had helped the company respond to market changes, accelerate innovation and create customer experiences suited to the evolving digital landscape.

Shobhit Mittal, Executive Vice President, Digital Enterprise at Maruti Suzuki, highlighted legacy system integration as a key challenge during the website revamp. He said Adobe’s proof of concept demonstrated how the technology could support complex integrations, maintain data consistency and deliver personalised experiences at scale.

Website Migration & Customer Data Integration

Maruti Suzuki has used Adobe Experience Manager Sites as a Cloud Service, supported by Edge Delivery Services, to migrate and update several brand websites.

According to the company, its NEXA and ARENA platforms now feature sub-second page loads and 3D showrooms. The websites have also been enhanced to support search engine optimisation and customer engagement.

Adobe Experience Platform is being used to unify customer profiles in real time. Maruti Suzuki plans to use the platform to coordinate media and non-media campaigns, loyalty programmes and service journeys across its businesses.

Exploring AI-led Customer Engagement

Maruti Suzuki is also exploring Adobe’s capabilities in real-time customer journey orchestration, next-best-action triggers and content supply chain optimisation to support personalised engagement.

Additional tools under evaluation include Adobe Brand Visibility, formerly known as Adobe LLM Optimizer, Adobe Brand Concierge and AI agents. The company is considering these technologies for customer personalisation and improving internal efficiency.

Dr Tapan Sahoo, Senior Executive Officer of Digital Enterprise at Maruti Suzuki, said the partnership enabled teams to collaborate around a shared vision and co-create value for customers.

Implementation Support

Adobe Professional Services and Adobe Ultimate Success have supported the implementation, governance and scaling of the digital platforms.

The partnership combines Maruti Suzuki’s digital operations with Adobe’s content management and customer experience technologies, with the aim of improving customer interactions across the vehicle ownership lifecycle.

Medtronic plc (IE00BTN1Y115) stock was at EUR 82.78 at Lang & Schwarz on October 22, 2026, 9.22 percent below the EUR 91.19 52-week high recorded on October 21, 2026. The company had received CE Mark approval for five Vitalis pacemakers on October 19, adding a product launch to a share-price picture shaped by legal and operating developments.

Three events shape the picture

Medtronic's recent chronology combines growth, regulatory risk and product expansion. On September 1, 2026, the company reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of USD 9.76 billion, up 13.70 percent year over year, while adjusted earnings per share reached USD 1.45 against a USD 1.39 consensus estimate, according to MarketBeat.

On October 17, 2026, a recall involving 3,746 biopsy kits linked to Medtronic Navigation was reported by Boerse Express. On October 19, 2026, Medtronic announced the CE Mark for its five-device Vitalis portfolio through Medtronic.

What does the approval add?

The CE Mark covers ReSyncra CSP, Restoria CSP, Refina CSP, Effectra and Confirma pacemakers. Medtronic said the portfolio is designed for conduction system pacing, which works through the heart's natural electrical pathways, and includes options for patients who may not benefit from conventional cardiac resynchronization therapy.

The commercial significance is the breadth of the launch rather than a disclosed revenue contribution. Five devices give European clinicians a broader set of pacing options, while the fiscal first-quarter revenue increase of 13.70 percent shows that the company entered the product announcement from a measurable growth base.

Legal risk offsets product progress

The product approval does not resolve the separate insulin-pump litigation described in the October 17 report. For investors, the relevant contrast is concrete: a five-device cardiac launch sits alongside a recall affecting 3,746 biopsy kits, while the latest reported quarter delivered USD 9.76 billion in revenue.

Stock stays below its yearly high

At EUR 82.78, the Lang & Schwarz price was 9.22 percent below Medtronic's EUR 91.19 52-week high as of October 21, 2026. The quote was in pre-market trading under the Xetra session model at 9:19 a.m. CEST, so the price view remains separate from the company's NYSE closing data.

text:
In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool contributors Travis Hoium, Rachel Warren, and Lou Whiteman discuss:

Dots are here!

Should Muse worry?

Anthropic's prospectus leak.

What we're looking for in the S-1.

Aura's IPO delay.

A closing window.

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

A full transcript is below.

This podcast was recorded on Sept. 30, 2026.

Travis Hoium: The Dots are here, and Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool and Gems Investing. I'm Travis Hoium. I'm joined today by Rachel Warren and Lou Whiteman. Guys, Meta's Muse had the market's attention for nearly a month. But that's long enough in the world of artificial intelligence. Dots are here. This is a Muse-like product from OpenAI. Can operate within ChatGPT. Rachel, they're all bringing out these interesting characters. They want us to be using agents all the time and interacting on an ongoing basis with Muse, with Dots. What do you think about OpenAI's play into this world?

Rachel Warren: I think this is the continued push for durable monetization for OpenAI. There's been a lot of experimentation to see what works. I think this is the next iteration of that. Dots, there's a $ 200-a-month plan. There's also a $ 500-a-month tier for the really heavy corporate users. This is not for a casual consumer use case. This is very much for digital power users, really, you know, highly technical professionals, thinking data analysts that might be running massive sets across systems, software engineers running continuous background code tests. There are applications here. This isn't a chatbot. It's really an advanced workflow infrastructure layer.

What's interesting, though, as I was reading that OpenAI is already cutting compute limits on the $200 tier because running the background agents is obviously wildly expensive. That could be a bit of an issue in terms of execution. As you noted, with Meta's views, it held the spotlight for a few weeks. Then OpenAI has jumped in with dots. I think one of the big takeaways for me here is we're seeing that, at least algorithmically speaking, moats don't exist right now. The moment one of these companies invents a new feature, a competitor clones or improves it within weeks. No one is sitting on a lead in terms of those types of products.

Travis Hoium: Lou, that seems to be a big piece here is that whatever somebody creates, no matter how awesome it is, somebody can just copy it, and it only takes about 30 days.

Lou Whiteman: Weren't we just talking about this two weeks ago when we were talking about why we shouldn't be too excited about Meta on this? Yeah, sure enough. Look, congratulations on the modernization strategy at $200 a month. All they need is what? About 200 million users annually to pay for their compute spend. I don't know what they're doing here. It feels like maybe they were annoyed with Meta's valuation because it doesn't feel like that there is a real chance for monetization here. There's no chance normals are going to say, let me sign up to pay $200 a month to find out if this is any good. That's just not going to happen. I guess you could give it away for free and hope people get addicted.

But again, they have use down the street, and with the compute costs, I don't know if that's a good idea. This is neat, this is fun, this is still not answering any of the questions that we have about this company. It's a great proof of concept, but if it's not a revenue producer, OpenAI still got big questions. If this is an add-on to a $200 subscription plan? I've still got big questions. I don't know what problem they're solving here other than saying, Look what we can do.

Travis Hoium: Lou, I wanted to touch on that because that seems like the interesting thing with all of these products, and we keep coming back to this over and over again. This is amazing. I think it's great that we can do all of these things. I've found great use cases in Muse. They're not massive use cases, but just small improvements to my life, and yet I'm not going to pay for them. It's great that Muse is free. Is this the fundamental problem with these companies is people are getting some use out of it, but when you say, Hey, you got a pony up even $20 a month, most people aren't paying that.

Lou Whiteman: I want to be careful with my words here because we're early days, and there's plenty of paths that we can take to get there. But we've said it before, not with OpenAI and Anthropic because they don't have a history, but all of these companies basically from the valley. These guys are used to double digit return on invested capital numbers. If you look at the amount of capital that they are spending on this, there's massive amounts of revenue. There was one, was it Apple? Who said, we need a couple trillion in revenue in the years to come to justify all of what's going on here, and I still don't see how these things are going to get there if they're commoditized. Now, that we just have two. Wait, Gemini hasn't entered the chat yet. They might, but now that we have two, how does anyone have pricing power here? Just the same basic questions. Again, I'm not going to sit here and say they can't answer them. I'm not going to be that Luddite. But as far as investible, there is nothing about this that changes versus two months ago what we would think about these companies. This is a neat feature that shows the potential of the technology, but it still doesn't feel like a business plan.

Travis Hoium: Rachel, do you think any of these products have people moving to a different service? I think that we've learned that the big players in the industry are going to remain the big players in the industry. Instinct has come out, but I don't know, it seems like they're already past their peak. But as we look at Meta's products now, OpenAI's products, Lou mentioned it, Gemini is probably going to come out with something. I would be shocked if Apple doesn't integrate these features into the iPhone that I have sitting in my pocket all the time. Do you think that anyone is actually going to move to a different platform, move their data, move the way that they're interacting? Or is this all just entrenching the incumbents even further?

Rachel Warren: I think it could risk just entrenching the incumbents even further. Like I said earlier, I think OpenAI is really looking for a monetization strategy that sticks, and I don't think they found it. It doesn't mean they won't. But that's part of the problem. You could easily see Microsoft, Alphabet's Google, Apple could build these tools into an operating system for free. OpenAI's achieved advantage is the brand momentum. That early user data. There's a real consumer edge there in the sense that that's where a lot of your average users who first got introduced to Generative AI went. But if Meta is giving away a similar product for free, really to protect its Ad model, opening eyes paywall, it looks flimsy. The real lasting moat is probably going to be those who weave these agents deepest into the enterprise systems. But I think we are seeing a time where that flat monthly subscription doesn't make sense long term if you have a power user's continuous usage costs. The company way more than they pay in fees. Could we see a model that pivots to a consumption-based utility model? That could be really interesting to think about. I don't think that this is going to be the end-all, be-all for OpenAI. I think it's the experimentation phase. I think we should expect to see more of that. That's good. But this is not going to be the solution to their cash burn and profitability problems.

Lou Whiteman: The issue is, at the end of the day, it's neat when something auto-fills your calendar, but you're really going to pay to not have the type of things. Anthropic's IPO is expected in the next month or so, and we're starting to get more leaks. This is a company that has leaked a lot of its numbers in the past. The reporting earlier this week was that we got some information about what their 2025 numbers are and what their commitments are for 2027. But Lou, what did we actually get, because it's not the real full filing?

Lou Whiteman: No, we haven't gotten really anything. We've got somebody leaked something to a couple of sources, is the best we can tell. Reuters and the Financial Times both have some information. It's select information. It's not the most recent information, which is weird. If it was a third party that just had the documents, why would you just copy and paste the old stuff that isn't interesting? With all these things, we can get into what's there. This is true with M&A all the time, I think it's true here. Who's leaking it, why they're leaking it? Why now, to me, is almost more interesting than the numbers. The numbers, we can get into it. There's some things there, but it's mostly just confirming everything we thought.

Travis Hoium: Rachel, what are the numbers that we need to keep an eye on at least from what we learned so far? Then I do want to get to how that translates to what we should be looking at when the official S1 comes out.

Rachel Warren: There's a few key numbers to look at. I mean, some of this is from 2025, and then we, of course, expectations for 2026. Anthropic spent more than $7 billion on infrastructure in 2025 alone, and they have disclosed commitments to spend $518 billion on Claude computing power over the next decade. There's a couple other things I want to hit here. They're seeking a $2 trillion valuation. You put that on their $4.6 billion 2025 revenue, that's a 434 price-to-sales multiple. Now, their exit run rate for the end of 2026 is supposed to hit anywhere between $100 billion and $120 billion.

Let's say they hit the lower end of that range, $100 billion in revenue. That $2 trillion valuation comes down to a 20 times forward price-to-sales multiple. But most of that funding is coming from big tech, private credit packages, venture capital. Google and Amazon, they give billions to Anthropic. Anthropic immediately hands those billions back. It's a circular wheel of funding, which is something I've talked about on prior episodes. I am very curious what the final prospectus is actually going to look like. But these are some real numbers that we're looking at, and I think it paints at least a story where we still have way more questions than answers.

Travis Hoium: Lou, just some context on that $518 billion number. That is commitment over the next decade. It's not just a single year, but Alphabet generated $446 billion in revenue over the past year. We're talking about Anthropic saying, Hey, we're going to be one of the biggest companies in the world relatively quickly.

Lou Whiteman: It's a Mark Twain line. There's lies, damn lies, and statistics. Numbers without context are just numbers. Again, we're talking to investors here. As investors, I don't think there is anything in any of this that is actionable. Now, it's a good thing because we're going to have to see the S1 before we can take action. But look, there are other numbers floating around online that I can't give any credibility to either, because, again, we're not seeing them, but that would imply that the recent few months' revenue growth does not look like what they had hoped for, maybe even when they were writing the S1.

Travis Hoium: This goes from they were flying high late in 2025 and early in 2026 when everybody suddenly was using Claude, when it was being integrated into. It was the coding one that all programmers were using, and then suddenly, Chaim tea and OpenAI catch up, Gemini gets this act together a little bit. That's the context behind what you're saying.

Lou Whiteman: This is bubblegum. This is stuff that people like us love to just chew on for a while, and it makes for great headlines and great fodder. But really, we don't know anything other than, okay, some of my prayers seem to be confirmed, and some of them maybe, things are going differently. Let's just wait and see the S1 and judge that because, again, a number without context, a number without a historical trend, is just a number, and there's just not much here that I think we can draw conclusions from.

Travis Hoium: Speaking of upcoming IPOs, we had one that was pushed back this week. Talk about that in a month.

Welcome back to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing. We learned that Aura's IPO has been pushed off. This is the ring company helping track your health, getting data all the time about your heart rate and things like that. They were looking for a $15 billion valuation that's more than 10 times sales. They were supposedly oversubscribed. They were supposed to go public earlier this week, but Lou, they did not. Why does this happen? What does it say about the IPO market right now?

Lou Whiteman: I think it says what we already know. Look, it's weird. Well, in some sense, the markets are near an all-time high, but if you look at volatility and specifically single-stock volatility, one thing you can look at is a form of the VIX. VIX is a measure of volatility. Looking at single stocks versus the VIX, and that is at a spread that is very unusual, which I think speaks to the choppiness in the market. We'll talk about AA. We can talk about Holtech, SB Energy, Inspire Brands, the Dunkin' Donuts owner, Bamboo Insurance, and about a dozen more who have delayed IPOs citing market conditions. There are other reasons. The last month or so, that's just from my syndicate list, just looking at it.

This is not a great time. Volatile times are the worst times to take a company public. The mechanisms of going public is you have to build your order book. You have to build buyers and sellers ahead of the launch, and they have to commit, and when you commit, you don't want volatility. You're putting your money out of your hands for 72 hours in some cases. It is really hard for the banks behind an offering to manage an offering, keep it stable when things are volatile right now. I don't even know if this is AA's decision. It could be the banks just saying, Look, IPOs, they really love to make them control. They really like it to be orderly. It's almost like trying to go fishing in a hurricane. You may be fine. It might turn out you can probably get your hook in the water, but it's not going to be a smooth sail. I think that this is just a simple case of the bankers recognizing the market. They're pulling them left and right here and saying, Let's just wait until the volatility goes down, and then we can do a more controlled offering.

Travis Hoium: Rachel, what do you think about this in relation to some of the bigger IPOs that we may have not only in the next month but in the next six months, because Anthropic, like we mentioned earlier, hoping to go public in the next month. Although there was talk that it may have already been public by now. OpenAI's, the other one talking about early 2027, those are maybe bigger. Maybe don't have quite as volatile IPO with a $1 trillion valuation than you do with a $15 billion valuation. But it seems like a strange time in the market given the fact that we are near all-time highs, but companies are saying, we're going to wait until things are even better.

Rachel Warren: I think what's happened with [inaudible] and some of these other companies that have delayed their IPOs. I think it's a very different story than the interest and likely hype and excitement we'll see in the markets around IPOs, like the anticipated ones of OpenAI and Anthropic. I think, if anything, if you're an AI-focused company right now, the window is wide open, I think, but for everyone else, it's narrowed significantly. It's interesting [inaudible] had just launched their IPO plan last week, so there's a very sudden pullback. The deal was reportedly four times oversubscribed. Institutional buyers were fighting on the price, and it forced demand at the bottom of the range. I think there's an understanding that investors are not willing to pay the favorable multiples of years gone by for consumer hardware companies, essentially. We're seeing, of course, rising sovereign debt yields, surging borrowing costs are impacting investors, and I think demanding wide pricing discounts to offset rising interest rates. There's, I think, a lot of concern about how that impacts some of these private companies entering the public markets.

s Lou noted, there's been a string of other IPO delays and withdrawals. I think there's also the idea that some of these companies, pulling their listings essentially close to the finish line. They might struggle to find another open window to return to the public markets anytime soon. I think it also highlights this idea that, whereas once a really strong consumer brand, a popular flagship product. In this case, or are the profitable, revenues growing favorably. They have millions of users. That's not enough to guarantee a successful public debut, at least not in this market. I think the interest, the real tailwinds, are centered on the AI companies right now, and I think at least for the foreseeable future, that will probably remain the case.

Travis Hoium: Yeah, it'll be interesting to see how these companies are going to be able to finance themselves in the future, too. Not just Aura, but some of these companies are still burning money. It's easier to do that in public markets when you can go access public debt, which they can do as private companies, but also just sell a little bit more stock if you need to. We've seen that often. Even SpaceX did that shortly after their IPO, just to raise more funds. The options get a little bit fewer when you stay in those private markets. That's been OK for now, but I would like to see some of these companies go public to actually see what the real valuation ends up as.

description:

text:
I added to my Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) position again. Every earnings report gives me one more reason to buy. I hold it for retirement and I collect a dividend that keeps rising. I also watch management put cash into an AI infrastructure lead that I expect rivals to struggle to match before 2030.

Why I Keep Coming Back to the Buy Button

My thesis is simple. Microsoft is turning its capital spending into a toll road. The money that goes into data centers, chips, and models feeds products that enterprises already pay for every month. The company spent $115.95 billion on capex in fiscal 2026. Management expects spending to grow again in fiscal 2027, starting with over $50 billion in the first quarter alone. Competitors have to match that pace, and few of them start with a customer base the size of Microsoft’s.

Three Receipts Behind My Conviction

First, demand is running ahead of supply. Azure passed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time and grew 43% in the fourth quarter. On the July call, CFO Amy Hood said it directly: “Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity.” Management forecast first-quarter Azure growth to about 45% in constant currency.

Second, the backlog locks in years of revenue. Commercial remaining performance obligations reached $678 billion, up 84%. Excluding OpenAI, that backlog still grew 25%. Nearly 90% of full-year Microsoft Cloud revenue came from customers outside leading model companies.

Third, the spending builds a moat across the whole stack. Microsoft added 31 new data centers last quarter, bringing the total to 88 this year. Its in-house Maia 200 chip provides 30% better performance per dollar than the latest hardware in its fleet. Microsoft 365 Copilot runs on that infrastructure and now has over 30 million paid seats. GitHub Copilot has 50 million users. The hardware, the data centers, and the software all strengthen each other.

The balance sheet can carry the build. Operating margin stands at 46.78%, debt-to-equity at 0.29, and interest coverage at 50.88x. The quarterly dividend increases to $0.98 from $0.91, payable December 10, 2026. The yield is a low 0.67%. What I care about is how fast the payout grows. Two years ago it was $0.75 per quarter.

Why I Own the Landlord Instead of One Model

Plenty of investors go straight for the hottest AI model maker. I would rather own the platform those models run on. Microsoft’s catalog offers more than 11,000 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI, and its own MAI family. The number of customers building with models from multiple providers rose 5x since the start of the year. Microsoft also holds a roughly 27% stake in OpenAI and recorded a $3.2B gain on Anthropic in the fourth quarter. Whichever model wins, Microsoft gets paid for the compute. Hood put it this way: “think about that infrastructure as being pretty fungible.”

Free Cash Flow Pressure Is My Biggest Worry

Free cash flow fell 6.46% in fiscal 2026 to $66.99B. Fourth-quarter free cash flow dropped 23.19%. Should AI demand cool while capex remains high, returns could fall short. At about 30 times earnings, the stock leaves little room for error.

I can live with that risk because about two-thirds of CapEx goes to short-lived CPUs and GPUs. Hood explained: “if the demand environment changes, you just slow down what is, in fact, the largest component.” Operating cash flow rose 30% to $55.44B in the quarter, and management expects to remains free-cash-flow positive in fiscal 2027.

What Keeps My Buy Button Active

Microsoft expects another year of double-digit growth in both revenue and operating income in fiscal 2027, with operating margins down less than 1 point. Over ten years, the stock has returned 905.99%. Microsoft is building the infrastructure the next decade of business software will run on through what will easily reach $700 billion in capex, and I want to own more of it every year until 2030.
