text:
While the bank, in its statement today, did not explicitly give AI adoption as the prime driver of the change, the announcement is an example of how this technology affects the industry.

Barclays, which reported a rise in third-quarter profits today, confirmed that it is cutting its staff by around 5,000 jobs. The lender is introducing AI into more of its operations, a pattern seen in other banks.

The cuts are not being split by business segments, such as wealth management and private banking, this news service understands.

The cuts announcement came as the UK lender reported a 13 per cent year-on-year rise to Q3 attributable profit of £1.646 billion ($2.2 billion). Profit before impairment rose 4 per cent to £2.825 billion. “I am pleased with the ongoing momentum of Barclays' operational and financial performance, with RoTE [return on tangible equity] of 11.7 per cent in Q326 and 13.8 per cent year-to-date," CS Venkatakrishnan, group CEO said.

"Income of £7.4 billion is up 3 per cent from the same quarter last year…With one quarter to go before the end of our original three-year plan, we have either achieved or are on track to achieve all of our 2026 group targets," he said.

Shares in Barclays are down by around 11 per cent since the start of the year. In 2025, however, they surged almost 80 per cent.

Job reductions

Media reports quoted Barclays as saying that 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5 per cent of its global workforce.

Barclays’ move comes a few days it was revealed that HSBC intends to make large job cuts across its UK wealth management business, including cuts to financial advisors and specialist staff, as the UK/Hong Kong-listed group integrates AI.

“We are positioning Barclays for the future, building the workforce and skills needed to deliver our strategy and meet the evolving needs of our customers and clients,” it said in a statement emailed to this news service. “In doing so we are committed to helping our colleagues develop and build rewarding careers, while meeting the changing needs of customers and clients and ensuring Barclays continues to succeed in the years ahead.”

Reports said the bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back-office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall (source: BBC). The BBC quoted Barclays as saying the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the `icing on the cake' of its strategy.

Commenting on the implications of the Barclays announcement, George Holmes, managing director of business finance specialists Aurora Capital, said smaller businesses risk being left behind.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is arguably the most critical company in the artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystem, given the central role its chips and software play in powering AI workloads.

That deep expertise means Nvidia is well-suited to identifying other potential winners in the AI infrastructure market, so investors should pay attention to where the company keeps its money. Nvidia's capital allocation strategy can reveal opportunities that extend beyond its core chip business.

As of the second quarter, Nvidia had 80% of its investment portfolio concentrated in two AI stocks: 33% in Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) and 47% in Intel (NASDAQ:INTC). Here's what investors should know.

Image source: Getty Images.

Space Exploration Technologies: 33% of Nvidia's portfolio

SpaceX is a vertically integrated business whose operations span space, connectivity, and artificial intelligence. The company has an important economic moat in reusable rockets, which have made it much less expensive to launch payloads into orbit. That edge helped SpaceX build Starlink, the world's largest satellite internet service.

CEO Elon Musk wants to combine those proficiencies to build orbital (space-based) data centers, which could theoretically solve the power and cooling challenges associated with terrestrial data centers. In its SEC Form S-1, SpaceX states: "We believe we are the only company with a commercially viable path to building orbital AI compute at scale."

SpaceX reported encouraging third-quarter financial results. Revenue increased 161% to $14.6 billion, up from 92% revenue growth in the second quarter. The driving force behind the acceleration was momentum in the AI business, with revenue increasing by more than 800%. Investors have reason to think the company can maintain that momentum.

Earlier this year, SpaceX said it would rent data center capacity to Anthropic, Alphabet's Google, and Reflection AI in deals collectively worth $28 billion per year. More recently, the company said it had a fourth customer that will pay $13 billion per year, bringing the total annual commitments to $41 billion. For context, SpaceX reported about $3 billion in AI revenue in 2025.

However, SpaceX is a risky investment because the stock trades at 68 times sales, a rich valuation even for a company whose revenue is projected to increase at 150% annually through 2028. I think investors who are confident in the company's growth prospects can buy a few shares today, but I would keep the position small.

Intel: 47% of Nvidia's portfolio

Intel is the leader in central processing units (CPUs), with about 59% of the personal computer market and 54% of the data center server market as of the second quarter. The company benefits from vertical integration by designing and manufacturing its own chips, and it wants to expand its foundry operations by making chips for other companies.

Despite its market leadership, Intel has lost substantial market share over the last decade in PCs and servers due to execution missteps and missed opportunities. In particular, its slow transition to 10-nanometer technology allowed Advanced Micro Devices to bring more powerful, more power-efficient processors to market faster by working with Taiwan Semiconductor.

Intel is showing signs of a comeback under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. Revenue rose 25% to $16.1 billion in the second quarter, the fastest growth in more than 15 years. That was driven by strong momentum in the data center and foundry business segments. Intel also reported non-GAAP earnings of $0.42 per diluted share, up from a loss of $0.10 per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

However, Intel's impressive financial results say more about the strong demand for CPUs than about the company itself. Despite reporting its best revenue growth in years, Intel still ceded CPU market share to AMD and Arm in PCs and servers in the second quarter. Also, Intel's growth prospects in the foundry space remain questionable, as TSMC dominates the market.

Intel currently trades at 87 times adjusted earnings. That seemingly rich figure looks a little more palatable in context. Wall Street expects adjusted earnings to grow at 56% annually through 2027. Investors can buy a small position in Intel today, provided they understand the stock's high valuation could lead to substantial volatility in the future.

text:
Barclays said it's cutting 5,000 jobs, or around 5% of its full-time workforce, as it increases its reliance on AI.

The British bank said in its third-quarter earnings statement that it is "structurally reducing" its costs through "technology-enabled" head count reductions.

Barclays laid out the numbers in its accompanying earnings presentation, linking the cuts specifically to "organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI."

Around 60% of the cuts will impact support functions, including developers, according to the presentation. Coding has become one of the main business use cases for AI across industries, causing some companies to cut back on developers.

Anna Cross, Barclays' group finance director, said the layoffs come as "AI makes our people more productive."

"Nowhere in the bank is this more relevant than in Barclays UK, where we have taken more structural cost actions than planned in '26," she said on the earnings call.

Wall Street is grappling with how AI will impact head count for both back- and front-office roles, as much of junior bankers' technical, repetitive workload can be automated. Some executives have said they're looking for young people with sharp judgment and communication skills rather than just analytical brainpower, as AI places an even greater premium on client interactions.

Goldman Sachs said in a memo last year that it plans to "restrain head count growth," and JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon has said he will likely hire fewer bankers and more "AI people."

Barclays joins a growing list of companies that have announced AI-related layoffs this year, including Snap and Coinbase. Business Insider analyzed 15 layoff memos earlier this year and found that "AI" was the most commonly used term.

By Lawrence White

LONDON, Oct 22 (Reuters) – Barclays said it is cutting around 5,000 jobs or 5% of its workforce this year, as it uses technology such as AI to slash fixed costs and improve returns.

The job cuts were revealed as Barclays reported third-quarter profit of £2.3 billion ($3.08 billion), up ​12% from a year ago but undershooting analysts’ forecasts as its fixed income trading business underperformed.

“I ‌am disappointed, and you can be sure this will get my attention,” CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan said about the bank’s traditional strength of fixed income trading, blaming a volatile quarter and weak trading in rates and credit products in particular.

The bank said it had taken a further £201 million in “structural cost actions” in the third quarter, part of its longer-term plan to reduce expenses like staff costs through ‌greater ​use of technology.

Around 60% of the overall job cuts will impact staff ⁠in support functions such as developers, ⁠CFO Anna Cross told reporters, in one of the clearest signs yet from a big bank of how AI is enabling firms to reduce headcount in such roles.

Cross said 1,000 roles have already gone, with the remainder to be cut by the end of the year.

“The cuts illustrate just how significantly AI and ​automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years,” said Will Howlett, financials analyst at fund management business Quilter Cheviot.

Companies worldwide including tech giant Microsoft and HSBC have announced layoffs this year, as automation ⁠increasingly impacts employment.

Barclays shares slipped 0.1%, outperforming other lenders. The bank’s ⁠shares have fallen 12% so far this year, in line with European peers which ​have sold off after years of rallying as higher interest rates lifted profits.

Shore Capital said in a note that ​the results were weaker than expected due to the disappointing performance by the investment bank.

BUDGET ‌LOOMS

Barclays is the first major European lender to report its quarterly earnings, with British banks’ results likely to be overshadowed by finance minister John Healey’s first budget on October 28, where further taxes on banks may be levied.

Healey has refused to rule out hiking taxes on banks’ bumper profits despite intensive public and private lobbying by the industry ⁠in recent months, as the finance minister mulls higher taxes to help fund the Labour government’s policy agenda and as higher borrowing costs eat into the public purse.

Banks have argued they are already highly taxed compared with other ⁠jurisdictions and that any such levy would ‌curb lending.

text:
Artificial intelligence is already a huge business for Wall Street. But how is it playing on Main Street?

Goldman Sachs, as part of a philanthropic effort, is spending big in an attempt to help ensure smaller employers get in on it. The bank announced Thursday that it has launched the Small Business AI Institute as part of a $500 million expansion of its 10,000 Small Businesses, a program geared toward educating and supporting entrepreneurs. It said it would partner with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta to provide AI training and tools to entrepreneurs.

“You’ve got to embrace new technology always, because if you’re not embracing it, trying to figure out how it can make your businesses better, there’s a real chance that you can fall behind,” Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said in an exclusive interview for NBC News’ Business in America series.

It’s a pivotal moment for the AI wave and its financial backers, including Goldman. The technology is broadly available to consumers, and U.S. economic growth increasingly depends on the buildup of data centers.

“We believe AI will create the greatest boom in entrepreneurship and small businesses that the world has ever seen,” Sam Altman, CEO and co-founder of OpenAI, said in an announcement from Goldman Sachs. “This is an incredible moment for anyone with an idea for a new endeavor because the gap between imagining it and bringing it to life is getting much smaller.”

Yet the growth that AI is already driving has also helped push up prices for inflation-weary Americans. Anger at data centers is a rare point of bipartisan agreement among voters, and the midterm elections are days away.

In the finance world, critics say AI is an investment bubble that could burst and potentially wipe out companies and jobs. Cracks are forming in the AI trade in markets after Big Tech firms drove much of stocks’ recent surge to record highs.

Goldman Sachs, like much of Wall Street, is in the thick of it all.

The bank’s share price has approximately tripled over the past three years while AI-related companies pushed the stock market to record highs. Goldman helped lead the much-ballyhooed, record-breaking initial public offering for Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which counts xAI and Grok among its core businesses. Goldman is also reportedly working on the IPO of Anthropic, the startup behind the AI chatbot Claude.

“There is going to be a lot of financing to do,” Solomon said last week on an earnings call, “and we’re going to be in the middle of that.”

Goldman and other big firms are counting on small businesses, which make up more than 90% of all U.S. companies and drive most of America’s job growth, to buy in. It won’t be easy getting everyone on board, though.

A recent NBC News poll found that 79% of respondents believe the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI use. Sixty-seven percent disapprove of how President Donald Trump is handling the technology. Trump has said he favors lax AI regulation from the government.

Meanwhile, some small businesses that already embraced AI have faced backlash from the public, including restaurants that used AI-generated images of food that critics denounced as “slop.”

Still, according to Goldman, entrepreneurs are adopting the technology at a fast clip. A survey this year of more than 2,400 graduates of the company’s small business program found that 86% of respondents were using AI in their businesses, up from just 56% in 2024.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette and an alumna of the 10,000 Small Businesses program, told NBC News she sees AI as a tool to help her gin up more business with limited resources.

“I really treat my AI as my consigliere,” Balanzat said. “They are not there to replace your accountant and lawyer. They are not there to replace humans. However, it does help prep me to have much more meaningful questions when I am meeting with my accountant and with my lawyer.”

Despite the widespread use of AI among the Goldman program alumni, just 15% of them said they had fully integrated AI into their core operations, according to Goldman.

Mike DiMarino, who heads Linda Tool in Brooklyn, New York, was part of the inaugural class of Goldman’s program in 2010. The company makes precision machine components for the military and aerospace industries, and DiMarino thinks AI can help with planning, management and processes.

“I’m sure there’s a lot more it can do that I don’t know yet,” he said.

But DiMarino is also cautious about how Linda Tool uses the technology, especially given how much sensitive information the company handles for its work in defense, aerospace and manufacturing.

His concerns mirror broader cybersecurity fears about AI. In July, a swarm of about 700 AI agents created by OpenAI hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face. Last month, Google said Chinese hackers are using AI to automate their attacks.

In addition to the security risks, company leaders are also increasingly raising concerns about the cost of AI, especially relative to its concrete impact on the bottom line. After spending on AI tokens exploded in the past year, companies from Uber to Microsoft to Meta have all taken steps to limit or re-evaluate how their employees use AI compute power.

Americans are also concerned about what AI will do to the job market. A recent Gallup Poll found that a growing number of workers are worried that technology will make their jobs obsolete. Small businesses employ fewer people than large firms, which makes their workforces especially vulnerable to potential losses.

Balanzat and DiMarino told NBC News they want to use AI to support employees at their businesses, not replace them.

“Machines are expensive,” DiMarino said. “People are priceless.”

text:
Walmart wants your bot to shop.

The retail giant said Wednesday that it has two new tools to help third-party AI agents shop on customers' behalf: agent profiles and an agent gateway.

The agent profiles link all transactions to the bot that performed them, and allow Walmart customers to manage authorizations and spending limits as they would for an additional user on their credit card account, the company said.

With agent gateways, bots no longer have to navigate a website that is designed for humans. Instead, Walmart is granting access through a model text protocol that it says will help agents work more quickly and accurately.

Walmart's move contrasts with Amazon's approach, which recently blocked Meta's agent Muse from its site, saying agents violate Amazon's conditions of use. Amazon has also pushed back on other third-party agents, including a lawsuit against Perplexity and restrictions on agents from Google and OpenAI.

"As customers begin using agents to help them shop, we're building connections, permissions and options that complement those tools and support how customers want to use them," the company said in a statement.

The company also said the gateway protects the information that Walmart has about its customers, and only provides what is necessary for completing a given transaction. In particular, the gateway can share a relevant pattern or preference — such as a customer's favorite laundry detergent brand — without sharing their entire purchase history with the agent.

The company also laid out a set of terms and conditions regarding how AI agents are expected to operate when shopping.

Under the terms, the company said it will honor its usual returns policy and that agents will always see the same pricing that a human would see on Walmart.com.

text:
Pearson PLC on Thursday said it was restructuring its business into four divisions as it reported revenue growth accelerated in the third quarter.

The London-based education materials publisher said underlying group revenue increased 5% for the nine-months ended September 30, with growth accelerating to 6% in the third quarter, in line with expectations.

Growth picked up from 4% reported in both the first and second quarters of the year so far.

As a result, the FTSE 100-listing said it is on track to deliver 2026 guidance of mid-single digit underlying revenue growth with its adjusted operating profit range of £650 million to £675 million narrowed from £640 million to £685 million before.

In 2025, Pearson reported revenue of £3.58 billion and an adjusted operating profit of £614 million.

By division, Pearson said Assessment & Qualifications revenue increased 4% for the nine-month period, with growth accelerating to 10% in the third quarter, driven by new contracts and strong demand for the verification of AI skills.

Virtual Learning revenue increased 17% for the nine-month period, with growth of 13% in the quarter, while Higher Education revenue increased 2% in both the nine-month period and the quarter.

In US Higher Education, third quarter revenue growth was driven by a solid performance in core US Courseware, partially offset by declines in K12, reflecting delayed adoptions and funding pressures.

English Language Learning revenue declined 4% for the nine-month period with third quarter revenue down 5% impacted by a strong comparator in Pearson Test of English given test enhancements implemented last year, alongside continued challenging underlying market conditions.

Enterprise Learning & Skills revenue increased 7% in the nine-month period and 6% in the quarter, driven by a solid performance in Vocational Qualifications and growth in Enterprise Solutions, supported by the continued monetisation of our strategic partnerships.

Effective from the start of 2027, Pearson said it is "simplifying" the business through the "creation of four larger, more balanced, customer-focused business units".

These are US K12, US Higher Education, UK & International Education and Enterprise.

UK & International Education will include the Qualifications and Learning & Assessment Services businesses. Enterprise will incorporate the Professional Assessments, Talent & Clinical Assessments and Workforce Skilling segments.

The changes will result in one-off reorganisation costs of around £50 million in total to be booked across financial 2026 and 2027, which will be excluded from adjusted operating profit.

Shares in Pearson were down 2.3% at 1,329.00 pence each in London on Thursday.

Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-cutting plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.

The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year.

The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.”

When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes.

“That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology.

“We have been focusing on the infrastructure build, and where the infrastructure is modern, we’ve been applying AI.”

The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs over the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030.

Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to shareholders after reporting a jump in quarterly profits.

The lender said it logged £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year.

Venkatakrishnan said he would be passing more cash to investors through a £500m share buyback, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn.

The chancellor, John Healey, is due to announce a hike on banks in the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.

Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax. It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.

The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills.

The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well at the same time – but their windfall profits have been underpinned by mortgage misery for millions. That’s why it’s time for banks to pay a fairer share.

“At a time when the chancellor needs to raise more revenue to support households and businesses through a looming energy bill crunch, Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.”

Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”.

One market estimate suggests that the bank surcharge will be returned to 8% from the current 3% which in turn would reduce earnings by a possible 6%, although whatever the outcome some of the uncertainty which has been overhanging the banks would be removed.

On balance, these concerns have blemished the investor confidence which was clearly in evidence at the interim results, even though the longer-term picture remains solid and where Barclays has maintained its guidance for this year and next. Prospects for its three largest units, the Investment Bank, Barclays UK and Barclays US Consumer Bank are the main drivers and it may yet emerge that this quarter’s slightly uninspiring update is a blip rather than establishing a weaker trend.

Despite the quarterly share price weakness and the heightened expectations which have resulted in a weaker opening price today, the direction of travel remains intact, with the shares having posted a gain of 15% over the last year, as compared to a hike of 13% for the wider FTSE100. Over the last two years, the price is ahead by 74% and there seems little doubt that the group’s financial strength, alongside its geographical and business diversity are factors which keeps the stock in demand among investors, such that the market consensus of the shares as a buy should remain untroubled.

Share

Richard Hunter, head of markets at the trading platform interactive investor, said the Barclays results are a bit “a mixed bag which is unlikely to blow away the clouds which have been hovering over the sector”.

In the investment bank, which accounts for 42% of group revenues, the recent US experience of the large names was echoed, he noted. Equity income rose by 47%, but Fixed Income, Currencies and Commodities (FICC) was 19% lower, leading to an overall 4% gain. Investment banking fees and advisory rose by 13%, with other highlights coming from Barclays UK Corporate.

Hunter added:

double quotation markA cautious impairment provision of £500m was 20% lower than the previous year, with defaults remaining stable and far from ringing any alarm bells.

More broadly, the group reiterated its financial muscle with a further £500m share buyback, in addition to the £1bn announced at the interim results. This is part of the group’s ambitious aim of £10bn of returns between 2024 and 2026, and then £15bn of returns between 2026 and 2028.

At a more granular level, there are pockets which may raise the eyebrows of some investors. The US Consumer Bank saw income decline by 1%… although the numbers were muddied by the inclusion of Best Egg numbers, which Barclays acquired in May for £600m. Barclays UK saw income growth of 4% largely due to the impact of the structural hedge, but numbers were contained by ongoing investment into its wealth proposition, where income nonetheless managed a 10% gain.

Share

Here’s our full story on Barclays:

Barclays is giving a further £500m to shareholders after reporting a jump in quarterly profits, as the lender steels itself for an increase in UK bank taxes at next week’s budget.

It comes only days before the chancellor, John Healey, is due to announce a hike on banks in the 28 October budget, as the prime minister Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.

Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax. It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.

Share

Barclays' bumper profits show need for bank windfall tax at budget, TUC says

Barclays third-quarter profits of £2.3bn – bring its profits so far this year to £8.4bn, up 15% on the year.

The TUC called the government for higher bank taxes, to fund a social energy tariff.

At the moment, the bank surcharge is an additional 3% corporation tax on the profits of banking companies above £100m. The Conservatives slashed the surcharge from 8% to 3% in 2023, just as interest rates were reaching their peak – a move that has cost the Treasury £6bn, the union body argued.

The TUC is calling for the government to increase the surcharge to raise up to £60bn over the next four years. Even just reversing the Tory cuts and setting it at 8% would raise £9bn over four years.

TUC general secretary Paul Nowak said:

double quotation markBarclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well at the same time – but their windfall profits have been underpinned by mortgage misery for millions. That’s why it’s time for banks to pay a fairer share.

At a time when the chancellor needs to raise more revenue to support households and businesses through a looming energy bill crunch, Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can - and should - pay more tax.

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Barclays’ profits jumped in the last quarter and it handed more cash to shareholders as further bank taxes loom in John Healey’s budget next Wednesday.

The UK lender reported a 12% rise in pre-tax profits to £2.3bn for the three months to 30 September. Income rose 3% to £7.4bn, ahead of expectations. In the UK, loans grew 7% year on year with particular strength in its corporate business, up 14%.

It announced a new £500m share buyback, bringing the amount handed back to shareholders so far this year to £2.8bn, up 46% year on year.

C. S. Venkatakrishnan, the Barclays chief executive, said:

double quotation markI am pleased with the ongoing momentum of Barclays’ operational and financial performance.

With one quarter to go before the end of our original three-year plan, we have either achieved or are on track to achieve all of our 2026 group targets. We are confident in and committed to the 2028 targets that we laid out earlier in the year.

The investment bank delivered strong equities performance, offsetting a challenging environment for FICC [Fixed Income, Currencies and Commodities].

Barclays’ investment bank reported income of £3.1bn, lower than analysts had forecast. Income from fixed income trading slid 19%, worse than a 5% drop among US banks.

The TUC urged the chancellor to increase taxes on banks at next week’s budget.

The union body wants the government to use the money to pay for a social energy tariff that brings down energy bills by up to £559 a year for those on low and middle incomes.

double quotation markA UK bank tax risk is now a base case. If it is confirmed on 28 October, it’ll be the size and timing that will be key. The yield, or interest rate, on France’s 10-year bonds rose 4 basis points to 5.039%, the highest since July 2002, after breaking through the 5% mark on Wednesday.

text:
Abu Dhabi, UAE: Eli Lilly and Company and Mubadala Bio announced an agreement on 20 October 2026 to localise packaging and logistics operations for Lilly’s GLP-1 medicines in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

The collaboration was announced during the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit 2026 by Hamad Almarzooqi, Group Deputy CEO of Mubadala Bio, and Nabil Daoud, President and General Manager, Intercontinental, Eli Lilly and Company.

The signing was witnessed by Dr. Fatima Al Kaabi, Director General of the Emirates Drug Establishment; Dr. Bakheet Al Katheeri, Chairman of Mubadala Bio; and Tayllit Aherdan, Vice President and General Manager, Lilly Gulf.

Planned operations supporting the agreement will be based at a 125,000 sqm site in Khalifa Economic Zones Abu Dhabi (KEZAD). The site includes pharmaceutical packaging and warehousing facilities and supports Mubadala Bio’s contract manufacturing and logistics activities.

The companies said they intend to combine Lilly’s pharmaceutical expertise with Mubadala Bio’s existing infrastructure to develop local capabilities and strengthen connections with international supply chains.

“This agreement represents an important step in strengthening our long-term presence in the UAE and contributing to the continued development of its life sciences ecosystem,” Daoud said.

The announcement follows regulatory and commercial developments involving Lilly medicines in the UAE. On 3 April 2026, the Emirates Drug Establishment approved Foundayo (orforglipron) for chronic weight management, making the UAE the second country to register the treatment.

Foundayo was subsequently introduced for eligible patients under Abu Dhabi’s Personalized Weight Management Program, which was launched in June 2025. The UAE also launched Lilly’s Mounjaro (tirzepatide) in August 2022 following approval by the US Food and Drug Administration.

description:
Orange’s transformation from a traditional Telco to a digital Retailer Orange is an international leader in telecommunications that is driven by a vision of disruptive leadership and bold strategic execution.
In this context, Orange partnered with Capgemini in a collaboration aimed at consolidating its position as a digital leader.
Expanding Orange’s reach Through this project and its collaboration with Capgemini, Orange has consolidated various tools and technology into a new digital model capable of delivering immediate business impact.

text:
When Orange set its sights on growing beyond its traditional portfolio and becoming an omnichannel retailer, Capgemini offered end-to-end support to develop and then execute a plan that would realize this ambition. The partners built a new digital marketplace with prices more in line with the market and a new selection of available products, which played a key role in boosting device sales.

Orange’s transformation from a traditional Telco to a digital Retailer

Orange is an international leader in telecommunications that is driven by a vision of disruptive leadership and bold strategic execution. While the company had historically limited its catalog to mobile phones, smartwatches, computers, and tablets, Orange wanted to extend its influence beyond connectivity through a business model transformation.

This would enable its evolution into a powerful omnichannel retailer and extend its influence beyond connectivity through an eCommerce platform, all with the goal of offering a broad, competitive catalog aligned with eCommerce trends and customer needs. This project has significantly boosted sales through the digital channel, a more cost-efficient and highly scalable channel, which is particularly relevant in a context where traditional channels—brick-and-mortar stores and telemarketing—are showing signs of saturation.

To achieve this, it was necessary to develop a competitive, robust, and scalable marketplace, supported by a profound transformation of processes that enabled the company to evolve from a telco model to one typical of the retail sector. The incorporation of retail-specific tools has provided greater control and responsiveness over key elements of the value proposition, such as product assortment and pricing strategy, thereby reinforcing a differentiated offering. In this context, Orange partnered with Capgemini in a collaboration aimed at consolidating its position as a digital leader.

Learning from the market

This began with an exhaustive market study that analyzed purchasing statistics, trends, top-selling categories and products in Spain, product analysis and average ticket sizes, consumer behaviors, and the positioning of major retailers.

Simultaneously, the project team evaluated user experience as well as key business models, categories, and subcategories in order to define key categories, prioritization criteria, and the new value proposition, including a strategy for opening to the general market. This enabled Orange and Capgemini to establish a benchmark for competencies and industry best practices.

Next, Orange performed an extensive analysis of its supplier ecosystem. This began with an evaluation of its existing strategic suppliers that identified what types of products could provide customer value and the opportunity to expand the catalog in categories where Orange had no presence.

In parallel, Orange and Capgemini launched an active search for new suppliers and key retail brands, during which they selected partners that enabled the incorporation of new categories and higher-value products.

Developing a new pricing model

In order to ensure it could compete in pricing, the telecom provider understood that it needed a pricing tool capable of monitoring competitors while applying dynamic pricing according to business strategy.

Following the analysis of around 10 market tools based on specific criteria, Orange and Capgemini selected Minderest and Reactev as the best fit solutions.

Once selected, the tools were integrated into Orange’s ecosystem, where they unified the business rules established earlier in the project. In particular, the AI integrated in Reactev pricing tool provided a recommended sale price that met business objectives while benefiting the consumer.

And when it became clear that the company also needed to efficiently control and manage product costs and margins individually and specifically, Orange and Capgemini developed a custom tool to monitor products in detail.

These fully integrated tools, powered by artificial intelligence and advanced demand models, automate price management, analyze the market, and update values in real time. With this capability, they ensure the business can optimize prices at any moment to be aligned with strategic business objectives and ensure maximum competitiveness and profitability.

Finally, the partners built a robust ecosystem that connected the eCommerce platform, marketplace, pricing tool, and cost management tool. This enabled the creation of automated data flows, centralized information, and ensured scalability.

Expanding Orange’s reach

Through this project and its collaboration with Capgemini, Orange has consolidated various tools and technology into a new digital model capable of delivering immediate business impact.

The launch of the marketplace, which is driven by intelligent pricing processes optimized with AI and competitive analysis, improved the competitiveness of the company’s offers and immediately accelerated growth. Moreover, this complete systems integration made Orange more agile and efficient while ensuring greater future scalability.

This new platform represents a key evolution in how the company connects with its customers and manages its value proposition in the digital environment. As a result, more than 700 new products were added to Orange’s eCommerce catalog, expanding the value proposition and multiplying customer options.

This new platform represents a major step forward in how Orange interacts with its customers and manages its value proposition in the digital environment. As a result:

Launching a new driver of digital growth.

Over 1,200 new products added to the catalog

Tripling the number of product categories available online.

The partnership with Capgemini enabled Orange to diversify its product lineup, establish itself as a leader in omnichannel retail, and cement its position as a major player in e-commerce.

With its greater market presence, expanded catalog, and more precise pricing, Orange has firmly established itself as a digital leader in the telecoms industry.

Next steps

Looking ahead, the team will continue to expand and strengthen the business model, extending the brand’s presence to other channels—including physical retail locations and customer service—to ensure a consistent experience that aligns with its value proposition.

description:
China’s online beauty market contracted by 6% year on year in September 2026, with multinational cosmetics companies reporting widespread sales declines, according to Jefferies’ China online beauty tracker.
THE DETAILS Skincare sales fell 6.1%, while colour cosmetics declined 5.2%, with the two categories accounting for more than 80% of China’s beauty market.
Beiersdorf and Galderma were the only multinational groups to achieve growth, supported by strong performances from Nivea and Cetaphil.
Individual brands showed significant differences, with CeraVe growing 35% and Cetaphil rising 58%, while Bobbi Brown fell 31%.
The figures highlight the increasingly competitive nature of China’s online cosmetics market and the diverging performance of international and domestic beauty brands.
text:
THE WHAT? China’s online beauty market contracted by 6% year on year in September 2026, with multinational cosmetics companies reporting widespread sales declines, according to Jefferies’ China online beauty tracker.

THE DETAILS Skincare sales fell 6.1%, while colour cosmetics declined 5.2%, with the two categories accounting for more than 80% of China’s beauty market. Among international groups, L’Oréal recorded a 5% decline, Estée Lauder fell 8%, P&G dropped 20%, Shiseido declined 24% and LVMH contracted 26%. Beiersdorf and Galderma were the only multinational groups to achieve growth, supported by strong performances from Nivea and Cetaphil. Individual brands showed significant differences, with CeraVe growing 35% and Cetaphil rising 58%, while Bobbi Brown fell 31%. Among domestic players, Mao Geping increased sales by 26%, while Proya recorded 1% growth.

THE WHY? The figures highlight the increasingly competitive nature of China’s online cosmetics market and the diverging performance of international and domestic beauty brands. Strong growth among selected dermatological skincare brands and local competitors suggests that consumer demand is becoming more selective, placing pressure on multinational companies to refine their product portfolios, pricing and digital retail strategies.

title: Microsoft and Alphabet opt out of tokenized stocks in latest blow to ambitious plan from ... - Fortune
description:
OKX did not respond to questions about when trading would begin or whether the objections had changed its launch plans.
The veto’s limits Under these rules, trading platforms do not need a company’s permission to offer tokenized versions of its shares.
Instead, they must notify the company, which then has 30 days from receiving the notice to object before the platform can proceed.
It does not stop other firms from offering tokenized versions of its shares overseas or through other legal arrangements.
A new era of stock trading?
text:
The two tech giants joined Goldman Sachs, Caterpillar, McDonald’s, Qualcomm, and Western Digital in a new batch of objections disclosed Monday. They joined nine companies—Cerebras Systems, AppLovin, Applied Digital, Rocket Lab, CoreWeave, Verizon, Applied Optoelectronics, Broadcom, and UnitedHealth Group—whose objections were disclosed last week.

Cuomo downplayed the wave of objections, framing the pushback as a predictable reaction to a major market shift.

“We always anticipated that—because this is such a dramatic and revolutionary change—many companies would want to wait and see how it goes rather than be the first to participate,” he said in a written statement to Fortune.

OKX did not respond to questions about when trading would begin or whether the objections had changed its launch plans.

The objections come two weeks after Cuomo announced plans to launch OKXICE’s tokenized stock-trading platform. The venture, a partnership between crypto exchange OKX and ICE, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, would offer round-the-clock trading in blockchain-based versions of 63 U.S.-listed stocks.

The venture is seeking to use a temporary exemption granted by the Securities and Exchange Commission last month that allows qualifying platforms to offer trading in tokenized stocks without registering as national securities exchanges, provided they meet certain conditions.

The veto’s limits

Under these rules, trading platforms do not need a company’s permission to offer tokenized versions of its shares. Instead, they must notify the company, which then has 30 days from receiving the notice to object before the platform can proceed.

“There’s not a proactive consent right. Rather, it is a reactive right to object,” said Erin Martin, a partner and co-lead of fintech and digital assets at law firm Morgan Lewis, who spent over a decade as a senior lawyer at the SEC. “If they don’t object within that 30-day notice period, the [venue] can go ahead and start to tokenize and list those securities.”

Applied Optoelectronics, a technology company that makes equipment for high-speed networks, said it objected because the framework is new and its potential effects on the pricing, liquidity, and volatility of its stock remain uncertain.

“At this stage, we don’t see a clear benefit to AOI or our shareholders that justifies these uncertainties,” a spokesperson told Fortune. The company also said investors could mistakenly believe it backed the offering, which it neither sponsored nor endorsed.

The other 15 companies declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment.

But a company’s objection only blocks trading on that platform under the SEC exemption. It does not stop other firms from offering tokenized versions of its shares overseas or through other legal arrangements.

The 30-day deadline can also create practical problems. Under the SEC’s rules, platforms must send notices to a company’s main executive office, where they could get buried in other mail before reaching its legal team, Martin noted. An unanswered notice lets the platform proceed after the deadline. “It has not been contemplated in the existing SEC order,” Martin said regarding whether a company can pull its stock after the 30-day window closes.

A new era of stock trading?

OKXICE’s push to tokenize stocks aims to tap into a $35 billion market, offering investors round-the-clock trading without some of the delays associated with traditional stock markets.

“The market never sleeps, so why should trading? Ownership shouldn’t have office hours,” Cuomo said when he first announced the venture.

But the benefits are less clear for the companies whose shares would be traded.

One concern is that the digital tokens could trade at different prices from the shares they represent on the NYSE or Nasdaq, especially when few people are buying and selling.

Martin, the digital assets specialist at Morgan Lewis, notes that companies have an additional concern when it comes to 24/7 trading. Namely, she points out, they would lose the pause they normally have to announce earnings or other important news while markets are closed, which allows investors time to digest the implications.

Protecting investors also presents hurdles if the software handling trades fails or the firms holding the underlying shares run into trouble, according to risk disclosures detailed in OKXICE’s public notice with the SEC.

Meanwhile, Apple, Nvidia, and Amazon are among the remaining 47 companies that have not yet publicly objected to plans to trade tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE. As of Wednesday, those that received notices in early October could have until early November to respond, depending on when they received them.

If all 60-plus companies in OKXICE’s planned lineup object within the 30-day window, the platform would have no stocks left from that list to offer under the exemption. Ignoring those objections would mean losing the exemption, Martin said.

Eléonore Crespo And Romain Niccoli, Co-Founders Of Pigment

Rising electricity demand and delays in expanding power infrastructure are creating investment opportunities that can help ease grid constraints, David Foley, global head of Blackstone Energy Transition Partners, said Wednesday at the Dow Jones Energy Forum in New York City.

Foley said investment opportunities include ones for manufacturers of grid equipment that can increase the capacity of existing transmission lines, as well as for engineering firms that can help address skilled-labor shortages.

He added that lengthy regulatory processes remain a major obstacle to expanding U.S. power supplies. “Our biggest challenge in the U.S. to solve this power shortage is permitting,” Foley said. “In China, if you have a project, they bring a bunch of engineers. In the U.S., the first people to show up seem to be lawyers.”

Artificial intelligence and data centers account for about a third of the average annual increase in electricity demand, Foley estimated.

Natural gas will remain important as power systems add more renewable energy because gas-fired plants can supply electricity when wind and solar generation fall short, Foley said. He projected that U.S. natural gas demand, including exports, will rise about 22% over the next five years, with a third of that growth coming from domestic power demand. Planned U.S. gas-fired power development is set to increase from 4 gigawatts built over the past five years to 48 gigawatts over the next five, though growth is constrained by turbine manufacturing limits.

Doug Peterson, former president and chief executive of S&P Global, added that the energy transition has progressed more slowly than many expected, with projections for peak oil demand pushing outward to 2045–2050 as oil and coal use continues to grow in countries including China and India.

—Reporting by Allegra Fradkin; Editing by Dean Visser

text:
Five days before Hungary was reported to be exploring replacements for its Russian nuclear contractor, the government said substantive contact with international partners would have to wait until it completed a review of the €12.5 billion Paks II project.

Rosatom, meanwhile, says its requests for government-level discussions have gone unanswered, even as construction work continues.

The difference matters in Budapest’s reassessment of the two-reactor expansion. Reuters reported Wednesday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Hungary had begun sounding out other suppliers. One source said the government was leaning toward proceeding with the expansion without Rosatom.

On October 16, Hungary’s Economy and Energy Ministry told Hungarian outlet Telex that a legal, financial, and technical examination of Paks II was underway and might not finish before the end of 2026. Any substantive engagement with international partners, the ministry said, depended on first establishing a complete picture of the inherited project.

The same day, Rosatom chief Alexei Likhachev told reporters in Moscow that his company lacked government-level dialogue with Hungary’s new administration, according to Interfax.

He said work with technical counterparts was continuing, including discussions of next year’s production programme, and that Rosatom was receiving contractual payments as work milestones were completed.

Hungary had already spent more than €2 billion on Paks II when the first concrete was poured in February, according to Reuters. About €1.1 billion had been paid to Rosatom.

Terminating its role could create additional contractual liabilities, although no penalty amount has been established.

The construction agreement, awarded without a competitive tender under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in 2014, has been amended five times. A proposed sixth amendment remains unsigned, Reuters reported.

There is also an unresolved European regulatory issue. In September 2025, the European Court of Justice annulled the European Commission’s state-aid approval because the Commission had not examined whether the direct award complied with EU procurement rules.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has questioned the project’s cost without rejecting nuclear expansion. The government is also considering extending the licences of Paks’ four existing reactors, which expire between 2032 and 2037, Reuters reported.

text:
By Krystal Hu

Oct 21 (Reuters) – OpenAI will make its frontier artificial intelligence models and Codex coding agent available through Google Cloud in the coming weeks, the companies said on Wednesday, deepening ties between two ​rivals and underscoring how major cloud providers are becoming key distributors ‌of top AI models.

The partnership will bring OpenAI’s latest models such as GPT-6 Astra to Google Cloud’s Model Garden. It will allow customers to buy them through Google Cloud Marketplace and use existing cloud spending commitments for the purchases, according to a company blog post, as OpenAI ‌tries to ​sell its models to more enterprise customers.

It will ⁠also allow customers in regulated ⁠industries to access OpenAI models through Google Cloud’s access controls, data governance tools and infrastructure to build so-called agentic AI workflows.

Alphabet’s Google has become the latest major hyperscaler to offer OpenAI models to its customers, after OpenAI’s exclusive distribution arrangement ​with Microsoft expired in April.

OpenAI has since expanded distribution to Amazon Web Services and now to Google Cloud, each a major hyperscaler vying for AI market share.

The deal ⁠adds another layer to an increasingly complex ⁠relationship between OpenAI and Google, which compete in core AI ​products and search even as the economics of building and deploying large models push ​them toward cooperation.

Google has moved to position its cloud unit as ‌a neutral platform offering customers a broader choice of models, after it struck a cloud deal with OpenAI to offer it more computing capacity last year.

For Google Cloud, adding OpenAI’s models strengthens a strategy of offering customers a wider range ⁠of third-party models rather than relying only on its own.

Thomas Kurian, chief executive of Google Cloud, has told Reuters in a previous interview that the Google cloud platform is ⁠an open platform and ‌it welcomes any model popular with developers in it.

The arrangement ⁠also fits a broader industry shift in which hyperscalers ​are becoming ‌the main commercial channels for frontier AI labs. Cloud ​providers usually ⁠take a cut from sales through its platform.

Anthropic, an OpenAI rival backed by Amazon and Google, has seen 47% of its 2025 revenue coming from cloud providers Amazon and Google’s cloud platforms, according to its IPO filing reviewed by Reuters.

(Reporting by Krystal Hu in San Francisco; additional reporting by Kenrick Cai in San Francisco; ​editing by Lincoln Feast.)

EBay has set itself apart from rivals by pushing into authenticated luxury goods, collectibles and refurbished products, which draw enthusiasts willing to pay more for valuable items. That has helped its shares rise nearly 40% this year, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500's around 12% gain.

"Our strategy is working," Iannone said in the memo, adding that "continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest."

He said affected staff would be informed in the coming days.

Shares of eBay rose about 1% in early trading.

The company has this year also benefited from its $1.4 billion deal for ​fashion resale platform Depop, which expanded its reach among younger consumers ​and strengthened its position in the growing re-commerce market.

That helped eBay forecast third-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates when it last posted results, in August. The company is slated to report latest earnings next week.

Those efforts have also caught the eye of GameStop GME.O CEO Ryan Cohen, who made an unsolicited $56 billion bid for the much larger eBay in May. EBay had rejected the offer, saying that it was "neither credible nor attractive."

text:
The federal government reached a $5 million settlement with Instacart after the company was accused of discriminating against American workers during the hiring process.

Instacart was advertising jobs through the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program. The program lets employers hire temporary visa holders and sponsor them for permanent resident status provided they have also made a good-faith effort to hire U.S. workers, according to the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

The agencies accused Instacart of creating a burden by requiring U.S. workers to physically mail applications to the company for jobs listed as part of its PERM recruitment program. Meanwhile, the company did allow electronic applications for its standard job recruitment process. This meant many U.S. workers who applied were not “timely considered,” per the DOJ.

The settlement requires Instacart to establish a fund of up to $4 million to “compensate Instacart applicants as well as deterred applicants affected by the discriminatory practices from December 2023 to February 2026,” according to the DOJ. The company will also pay $1 million in civil penalties to the federal government.

“This significant resolution marks the fifteenth settlement agreement the Civil Rights Division has reached under my leadership to protect U.S. workers,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said of the settlement. “Our record demonstrates that the Justice Department is holding companies who prefer workers with temporary employment visas accountable. We will not stop fighting for U.S. workers until there is a fair playing field.”

“Today’s settlement makes clear that when employers erect unlawful barriers that harm American workers, the EEOC will act decisively,” said Chair Andrea Lucas of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. “The EEOC is committed to holding companies accountable when they deny equal work opportunities to U.S. workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs. Discrimination against workers based on their American national origin has no place in our economy.”

Instacart released a statement on Tuesday saying that its hiring practices complied with U.S. laws and regulations. The company said it agreed to the settlement to remain focused on business.

Instacart is the latest tech company to reach a settlement with the government over allegations that it favors foreign workers for certain jobs.

In 2023, Apple agreed to a $25 million settlement after federal regulators said its hiring practices discriminated against U.S. candidates for jobs that went to immigrant workers seeking permanent resident status in the country. title: Abbott plans to spin out its nutrition business | MedTech Dive
description:
Dive Brief: Abbott said Wednesday it plans to spin out its nutrition business into an independent, publicly traded company.
Abbott’s nutrition business has been at the center of lawsuits as well as a federal investigation into the manufacturing and handling of a recall of powdered infant formula in 2022 due to potential contamination.
Medtronic separated its diabetes business earlier this year, and Johnson & Johnson is planning to spin out its orthopedics business.
Abbott expects to complete the spin off at the end of 2027, subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions.
There are lawsuits still pending over the nutrition business.
text:
Dive Brief:

Abbott said Wednesday it plans to spin out its nutrition business into an independent, publicly traded company.

The business has approximately $8.5 billion in annual sales and includes brands like Pedialyte, Similac and Ensure. In Abbott’s third quarter, nutrition brought in revenue of $2.26 billion, representing year-over-year growth of about 5%.

Abbott’s nutrition business has been at the center of lawsuits as well as a federal investigation into the manufacturing and handling of a recall of powdered infant formula in 2022 due to potential contamination. In September, the company announced a $385 million settlement with the Department of Justice to resolve claims as well as lawsuits filed by certain relators and the attorneys general in several states.

Dive Insight:

Abbott is the latest major medtech company to turn to the spinout strategy. Medtronic separated its diabetes business earlier this year, and Johnson & Johnson is planning to spin out its orthopedics business.

Abbott CEO Robert Ford framed the decision as a benefit for both companies and a way to “maximize success” in their markets, as well as a way for the remaining company to focus on higher-growth markets.

“Our Nutrition business has a unique opportunity to capitalize on the growing demand for healthy nutrition, and it will be better positioned as an independent company to more effectively direct its strategic resources across its priorities,” Ford said in the announcement. “At the same time, Abbott’s core higher-growth, innovation-driven portfolio of medical devices, diagnostics and established medicines has compelling growth opportunities to improve the health and lives of people around the world.”

After the spin, Abbott’s remaining businesses will be diagnostics, established pharmaceuticals and medical devices. The company will have approximately $42 billion in sales.

Abbott expects to complete the spin off at the end of 2027, subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions. When the deal is complete, Abbott stockholders will own shares in both Abbott and the new company.

The planned separation will not have an impact on Abbott’s guidance for 2026 or 2027, which the company plans to provide in January.

J.P. Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus said that the spinout should be a good strategy for Abbott’s overall business going forward.

“We think the value proposition of the separation is clear - it should improve top-line growth and margins, and remove what’s been a difficult business of late, both for Abbott specifically and the packaged goods/nutrition market overall, “ Marcus wrote in a note to investors.

BTIG analyst Marie Thibault wrote that the “Nutrition business had sometimes weighed on total company sales growth, its margins are below the corporate average, and liabilities tied to infant formula litigation remain an overhang.”

In 2022, Abbott recalled several brands of baby formula due to potential contamination. The recall, as well as the temporary closing of a large manufacturing plant in Michigan, contributed to a shortage of powdered baby formula.

In announcing the DOJ settlement in September, Abbott said the government had closed its criminal investigation into the company. Abbott maintained that the settlement does not represent a finding of fault or liability, and the company said that no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive for the Cronobacter sakazakii bacteria.

In August, Abbott announced a separate agreement to resolve a lawsuit and claims involving about 2,000 other individuals relating to certain specialty formulas for preterm infants made by the company and an alleged connection to necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious gastrointestinal problem that mostly affects premature babies. Abbott agreed to pay an aggregate amount of approximately $670 million. The company said the agreement is not an admission of liability.

There are lawsuits still pending over the nutrition business. However, Ford said on a Wednesday earnings call that fully resolving litigation matters is not a “prerequisite for completing the separation.”

title: Elevance gains self-funded employers as fully insured group risk book shrinks
description:
But buried in the membership table is a trend that says more about where the employer health market is heading than any earnings-per-share figure: the company’s fully insured employer group risk book fell 6.9% year over year, while its employer group fee-based membership grew.

At the same time, Elevance’s employer group fee-based membership, the self-funded book it administers for employers who carry their own claims risk, grew 1.9% to 21 million.

text:
Elevance Health posted third-quarter operating revenue of $50.4 billion, reported results ahead of expectations, and raised its full-year guidance for the third consecutive quarter. The headline numbers were solid. But buried in the membership table is a trend that says more about where the employer health market is heading than any earnings-per-share figure: the company’s fully insured employer group risk book fell 6.9% year over year, while its employer group fee-based membership grew.

Employer group risk-based enrollment stood at 3.366 million as of September 30, down from 3.616 million a year earlier. That 250,000-member decline follows attrition of a similar scale through Q1 and Q2, and lands as the group risk book approaches the high single-digit percentage decline Kaye projected at the start of the year. At the same time, Elevance’s employer group fee-based membership, the self-funded book it administers for employers who carry their own claims risk, grew 1.9% to 21 million.

Chief financial officer Mark Kaye told analysts as far back as the Q4 2025 earnings call that the company expected its employer group risk membership to end 2026 down in the high single-digit percentage range, driven by deliberate pricing decisions on lower-margin public-sector business.

Health benefits margin under pressure

The operating margin in Elevance’s health benefits segment came in at 1% in Q3 2026, down from 1.4% a year earlier. That contraction reflects both the drag of lower risk-based membership and the targeted investments Elevance said it is making to support its long-term operating model. Premium revenue on the commercial side did grow, driven by higher yields across all lines, but higher yields on a shrinking risk book only go so far.

The company’s benefit expense ratio improved 70 basis points year over year to 90.6%, helped by better performance in Medicare Advantage and individual ACA. But operating expense as a percentage of revenue rose 90 basis points to 11.4%, partly reflecting those one-time investments. The net result was a sharp year-over-year decline in Health Benefits operating gain, reflecting the combined pressure of lower risk-based membership and higher operating costs.

While the insurance side compressed, Carelon, Elevance’s services and pharmacy arm, expanded. CarelonRx’s operating gain rose 10.8% year over year and Carelon Services grew 33.3%, with Carelon’s overall margin widening from 4.2% to 4.7%. CarelonRx’s operating gain rose 10.8%, while Carelon Services grew 33.3%. Carelon is carrying an increasing share of the company’s operating gain as health benefits margins narrow. CEO Gail Boudreaux said the company remains confident in returning to at least 12% adjusted diluted EPS growth in 2027 off a higher earnings baseline.

What’s driving the self-funding switch

Elevance’s numbers reflect a market-level shift that has accelerated throughout 2026. Industry-wide data tracking employer health coverage enrollment trends and the self-funding shift shows fully insured employer-group risk plans shed approximately two million members as self-funded arrangements grew.

Administrative services only (ASO) plans now account for 43.5% of total US health enrollment, the largest single segment in the country, according to Mark Farrah Associates’ mid-2026 enrollment analysis. The same dynamic showed up in UnitedHealth Group’s Q3 results, where risk-based commercial enrollment fell from 8.165 million at year-end 2025 to 7.575 million by September 30, a drop of 590,000 over nine months.

Each employer that migrates from a fully insured plan to a self-funded arrangement changes the nature of the advisory relationship. The carrier absorbs less risk; the employer absorbs more; and the conversation shifts toward plan design, stop-loss procurement, and claims management in ways a traditional fully insured renewal does not require. Elevance’s fee-based membership growth, the fastest-growing segment in its commercial book, measures exactly that migration in progress.

Those membership and margin dynamics sit against a broader financial picture that remained ahead of expectations. The company’s full-year adjusted diluted EPS guidance now stands at least $29.00, raised from at least $27.00 following Q2. Operating cash flow guidance was lifted to at least $6.5 billion. On a GAAP basis, year-to-date results continue to carry the impact of a $935 million accrual booked in Q1 related to a Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) notice concerning historical Medicare Advantage risk adjustment data.

GTC Berlin—NVIDIA today announced plans with a group of supply chain partners to expand global manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and full-stack AI factory platform.

Working with Amkor Technology, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology Corporation, NVIDIA is enabling new and existing suppliers to expand critical manufacturing capabilities across substrates, advanced packaging, testing and optical engines, strengthening the resiliency and redundancy of NVIDIA’s global supply chain.

“We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Our supply chain partners are the world’s best manufacturers. I’m grateful they are expanding capacity around the globe to scale production and help us deliver the AI supercomputing systems powering this new industrial revolution.”

Expanding Substrate Capacity to Support Volume Growth

NVIDIA plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. The agreements below will contribute to this capacity expansion, with more underway.

Under an agreement signed and announced earlier this year by IBIDEN, NVIDIA is providing a multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to support IBIDEN’s Ono Plant in Japan. The expansion targets capacity reaching 3x current levels at the plant, with additional capacity expected to begin ramping in the first quarter of 2028.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is joining NVIDIA’s substrate supply chain, bringing immediate capacity from its existing operations in South Korea. The collaboration also supports facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan, South Korea. By 2028, production allocated to NVIDIA is projected to account for a significant portion of Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ total annual package substrate production capacity.

NVIDIA is supporting Unimicron’s KF substrate manufacturing expansion in Taiwan with a capacity reservation agreement. The expansion is expected to begin adding capacity in the second quarter of 2027 and reach full capacity by mid-2028.

Scaling Advanced Packaging for Next-Generation Platforms

description:

The partners plan to pair METiS' generative and predictive AI capabilities with Lilly's scientific and development know-how to discover and refine new LNP architectures.
Lilly continues to pursue its push towards the AI sector, signing a larger AI deal with another Hong Kong-listed company earlier this year.

text:
Hong Kong-listed METiS TechBio (HKEX:7666) could collect up to US$1.1 billion in milestone payments from Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE:LLY) under a new research pact to design lipid nanoparticles that carry medicines to specific tissues in the body.

Lipid nanoparticles, or LNPs, carry therapeutic payloads to target tissues and cells. METiS will apply AiLNP, its proprietary AI platform for discovering and optimizing ionizable lipids, to develop delivery technologies that could improve how accurately LNPs reach their targets and how they distribute through the body.

The partners plan to pair METiS' generative and predictive AI capabilities with Lilly's scientific and development know-how to discover and refine new LNP architectures.

METiS says those designs may improve tissue specificity and therapeutic performance, with potential applications across multiple disease areas.

"Delivery remains a critical determinant of therapeutic success, particularly as the industry expands into increasingly sophisticated modalities," METiS Chairman and CEO Chris Lai said in the announcement.

"By combining METiS' AI-powered platform with Lilly's scientific expertise and development capabilities, we aim to unlock a new generation of tissue-targeted delivery technologies that have the potential to transform how medicines reach patients," Lai added.

The announcement did not name the diseases or therapeutic modalities the partners will pursue first, or how the milestone payments are staged.

Lilly continues to pursue its push towards the AI sector, signing a larger AI deal with another Hong Kong-listed company earlier this year. Insilico Medicine (HKEX:3696) is a clinical-stage biotech that uses generative AI and automation in drug discovery.

That agreement gives Lilly an exclusive worldwide license to develop, manufacture and commercialize novel oral therapeutics in preclinical development for certain indications. The two companies will also run multiple R&D programs on targets Lilly selects, using Insilico's Pharma.AI platforms.

"Insilico's AI-enabled discovery capabilities represent a powerful complement to Lilly's deep expertise in clinical development across multiple therapeutic areas," Andrew Adams, Lilly's group vice president of molecule discovery, said in Insilico's announcement of the deal.

Lilly has also invested in its own AI computing infrastructure. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) said in October 2025 that Lilly was deploying a DGX SuperPOD with DGX B300 systems, built with 1,016 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, and described it as the "largest, most powerful AI factory wholly owned and operated by a pharmaceutical company."

Lilly will use the system to train large-scale biomedical foundation and frontier models for drug discovery and development. Select models will go on Lilly TuneLab, a platform that gives biotech companies access to drug discovery models built on US$1 billion worth of Lilly's proprietary data.

text:
Joel Kaplan has announced his decision to leave his position as Chief Global Affairs Officer at Meta after more than 15 years with the company. He will remain with the organisation for the next few months to support the transition before moving on.

Sharing the development in a LinkedIn post, Kaplan reflected on his tenure at the company and acknowledged the people who supported his journey.

“After more than 15 years at Meta, I’ve decided the time is right for me to move on from my role as Chief Global Affairs Officer. It’s been an extraordinary journey and opportunity, and I’m very proud of the team we built and work we did. I will always be grateful to Mark Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg for bringing me in all those years ago and supporting me and my work all along the way,” the post said.

Kaplan joined Meta in 2011, bringing experience from public service and the legal profession. Before joining the company, he served as Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy under former US President George W. Bush. He had also held the positions of Deputy Director of the Office of Management and Budget and Special Assistant to the President for Policy.

His professional background includes military service as well. Kaplan spent four years as an artillery officer in the United States Marine Corps.

He began his career in law, working as a law clerk for Judge J. Michael Luttig of the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit before serving as a law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia.

Kaplan’s departure marks the end of a tenure spanning more than a decade and a half at Meta, where he served in a senior global affairs role. His transition period is expected to continue for several months as he assists the company with the handover.

Wednesday’s announced expansion brings ChatGPT Ads to a total of 89 countries worldwide, OpenAI said.
Anthropic made OpenAI’s ads push the focus of its first Super Bowl campaign and pledged to keep its competing chatbot, Claude, ad free.
OpenAI said it plans to continue developing additional ChatGPT Ads formats, measurement capabilities and buying options during its next phase of growth.
