text:
OpenAI on Wednesday announced it will roll out ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, its latest push to build out its nascent advertising unit.

The artificial intelligence company has been touting its 8-month-old ads product as a new pillar of its business, which also includes enterprise contracts, consumer subscriptions and usage-based application programming interfaces, or APIs. Digital ads have long been a major revenue stream for other big tech companies, including Google and Meta .

OpenAI said its free users and Go subscribers in countries including Argentina, Peru, Nigeria, South Africa and Ukraine will start to see ads in ChatGPT. The ads are separate from ChatGPT’s response to prompts, don’t influence its answers and are clearly labeled, the company said.

“Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions — and effective for the businesses that advertise with us,” OpenAI said in a release.

OpenAI’s ad business hit $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate in August, up from $100 million in March, as CNBC previously reported. The company said Wednesday that more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on the platform.

Wednesday’s announced expansion brings ChatGPT Ads to a total of 89 countries worldwide, OpenAI said. The company began testing ads in the U.S. in February, a decision that was ridiculed by chief rival Anthropic. Anthropic made OpenAI’s ads push the focus of its first Super Bowl campaign and pledged to keep its competing chatbot, Claude, ad free.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are gearing up for what are widely expected to be blockbuster initial public offerings, though they have not publicly disclosed when they plan to debut. OpenAI executives have signaled that they are eyeing a 2027 listing, while Anthropic’s leaders have been actively meeting with prospective investors in recent weeks.

OpenAI said it plans to continue developing additional ChatGPT Ads formats, measurement capabilities and buying options during its next phase of growth. The company is also looking at new ways for businesses to natively interact with ChatGPT consumers.

“As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services — and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive,” OpenAI said.

text:
OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google’s cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.

For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That’s critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI’s models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.

Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models.

Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI’s GPT products to its cloud’s model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.

“Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them,” OpenAI said in a blog post.

Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42%, respectively. All three report quarterly results next week.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google’s Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.

OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google’s cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.

name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft expands sovereign cloud offerings as data control concerns grow - CIO
description:
“Governments and enterprises want greater control over where their data is stored, who can access it, and whether critical systems can operate during disruptions.
Additionally, DocumentDB and Blob Storage are entering public preview on Azure Local, while SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments.
While these additions give enterprises greater flexibility, industry analysts emphasize that localized deployments do not automatically erase vendor dependency.
The new measures introduced under Microsoft Sovereign Cloud do reduce risks but cannot eliminate them.
Furthermore, while sovereign cloud capabilities can offer greater control over data, infrastructure, and operations, this often comes with trade-offs in cost, performance, scalability, and access to services.
text:
Microsoft expanded its sovereign cloud offerings on Tuesday, adding new security, governance and AI capabilities as customers, particularly in Europe, demand greater assurance over where data is stored, who can access it and how critical services operate during disruptions.

The announcement builds on Microsoft’s ongoing digital sovereignty efforts, assisting organizations in applying appropriate levels of control to each workload rather than forcing a rigid, one-size-fits-all approach.

“Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change,” Douglas Phillips, president and CTO at Microsoft Specialized Clouds, said in a blog post.

The developments come amid growing international scrutiny of how global tech providers handle sensitive data and the extent of control customers retain over their digital infrastructure.

“Three factors are driving this, including stricter data regulations, rising geopolitical tensions, and growing AI adoption,” said Pareekh Jain, CEO at EIIRTrend & Pareekh Consulting. “Governments and enterprises want greater control over where their data is stored, who can access it, and whether critical systems can operate during disruptions. For instance, governments and big enterprises in Europe are worried about keeping their important data on an American company’s computers. Europe has proposed a new law that would limit the use of US cloud companies for sensitive government data in many areas. Microsoft is responding to these concerns while competing with local sovereign cloud providers.”

New controls across cloud and AI workloads

Microsoft is introducing the Sovereign Control Panel, a unified Azure portal experience that will allow organizations to assess their sovereignty posture, identify risks and gaps, apply controls, and evaluate workload portability. The panel is scheduled to enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite.

Expanding on Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM), which gives customers dedicated protection over encryption keys, Microsoft is now extending control beyond its own infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, enabling organizations to keep root encryption keys in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party.

In limited preview, Azure Confidential Clean Rooms will use confidential computing to support collaboration involving sensitive data, where participants will be able to analyse shared information while limiting broader exposure of the underlying data.

Microsoft is also expanding Azure Local to bring more cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments. The ability to transition workloads between connected and disconnected states is entering public preview. Additionally, DocumentDB and Blob Storage are entering public preview on Azure Local, while SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments.

On the AI front, Foundry Local is scheduled to become generally available at Microsoft Ignite for connected and disconnected operations on Azure Local. It will support local inference and agentic retrieval in natural language, backed by an expanded model catalog from Microsoft, partner networks, and the open-source community.

To further protect data during processing, Confidential Virtual Machines on Azure Local is now generally available, leveraging hardware-encrypted memory and isolation alongside workload attestation before sensitive keys or data are released.

While these additions give enterprises greater flexibility, industry analysts emphasize that localized deployments do not automatically erase vendor dependency.

“Depending upon the deployment model, in the public cloud, enterprises get better visibility, stronger access controls, and more control over encryption keys,” said Ashish Banerjee, senior principal analyst at Gartner. “In the Sovereign Private Cloud, they can operate infrastructure locally and even disconnect selected workloads from Azure. But I would not call this complete control. Enterprises still need to check whether Microsoft remains involved in identity, software updates, management, or technical support for the services they use.”

European oversight and partner options

For customers in the EU and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), Microsoft is rolling out Data Guardian. Under this model, a trusted regional partner will provide independent oversight of remote access requests by Microsoft engineers. Simultaneously, a Production Touch Ledger will create tamper-evident logs of all technical actions performed.

Microsoft is also broadening its Sovereign Partner Ecosystem, highlighting regional operators like Bleu Cloud in France and Delos Cloud in Germany, alongside independent software vendors specializing in security, identity, observability, and backup.

Geopolitical realities and market limits

Despite these additions, analysts note that technical controls cannot eliminate geopolitical dependence entirely. US hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) continue to account for roughly 70% of the European cloud market, whereas European providers’ market share has contracted over the last decade.

The new measures introduced under Microsoft Sovereign Cloud do reduce risks but cannot eliminate them. “Local infrastructure, independent encryption keys, and disconnected operations make it harder for external parties to access data or disrupt services. However, Microsoft remains subject to applicable US laws, sanctions, and export restrictions. Enterprises gain greater operational independence but not complete legal or technological independence,” added Jain.

Furthermore, while sovereign cloud capabilities can offer greater control over data, infrastructure, and operations, this often comes with trade-offs in cost, performance, scalability, and access to services.

Banerjee noted that sovereignty should be assessed workload by workload, rather than applied as a label to the entire cloud environment. Greater sovereignty generally comes with greater cost and responsibility. Local or disconnected environments may not receive every Azure service at the same time. Enterprises may also need dedicated infrastructure, specialist skills and separate continuity arrangements. On top of that, they may lose some elasticity and economies of scale.

“So, I would not recommend maximum sovereignty for every workload. Reserve it for workloads where the legal, operational or geopolitical risk genuinely justifies the additional complexity,” added Banerjee.

text:
Oct 21 (Reuters) – Elevance Health on Wednesday raised its annual profit forecast after posting better-than-expected quarterly results due to higher premiums and lower medical costs, driving the health insurer’s ​shares 2.1% higher in premarket trading.

Health insurers have been grappling ‌with declining membership, as well as rising costs from elevated demand for behavioral health services and specialty drugs in government-backed plans.

Elevance, like other health insurers, has adjusted its pricing to reflect higher medical costs. For the third quarter, the ‌company ​said higher premium yields and service fees ⁠offset lower membership, helping ⁠the company’s insurance business post a $1.1 billion rise in revenue from a year earlier.

Last week, larger rival UnitedHealth Group also raised its full-year profit forecast, attributing the improvement to plan design and ​new pricing on products.

Elevance’s upbeat quarterly performance reflects “stronger execution across our diversified portfolio and underscore the earnings power of the business,” ⁠CEO Gail K. Boudreaux said.

Medical membership of ⁠about 44.9 million as of September 30 decreased ​by 487,000 compared to the prior year, the company said.

For the third ​quarter, the health insurer reported a medical loss ratio, the ‌percentage of premiums spent on medical care, of 90.6%, lower than analysts’ expectations of 91.17%.

The company said lower costs were due to better performance in its Medicare Advantage plans for older Americans and ⁠those with disabilities as well as Obamacare plans compared to the prior year.

The company also said it plans to deliver at least 12% growth ⁠in 2027 adjusted profit ‌from an earnings baseline of at least $26.75 per ⁠share.

Elevance forecast full-year adjusted profit to be at ​least $29 ‌per share, compared with its previous outlook of ​at least $27 per ⁠share. Analysts on average estimate an annual profit of $27.23 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG.

On an adjusted basis, the company earned a profit of $6.99 per share, compared with analysts’ average estimate of $4.68 per share.

name: HP Inc
title: Explained - AI On Moon: Why HP Wants To Land A Supercomputer On The Lunar Surface
authors: ETV Bharat Tech Team, ETV Bharat
description:
FLIP will be deployed via Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) lunar lander.
It will study the images taken during the Griffin-1 space mission and help with independent observations.
HPE said an AI services container will show that AI services can be setup on the Moon reliably and at scale.
What else does the Griffin-1 mission carry on-board?
Griffin-1 will be the first flight of the robotic Griffin moon lander, built by a Pittsburgh-based firm, Astrobotic.
text:
What is FLIP?

FLIP will be deployed via Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) lunar lander. The flight is part of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASA) Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS)initiative, a foundational component of the broader Artemis programme aimed at establishing long-term infrastructure on the Moonto prepare for future human exploration of Mars.

According to Astrolab, FLIP will deliver commercial technologies and science payloads to the Moon's South Pole. The robotic lunar rover will gather "valuable science data" to reduce the risks caused by lunar dust on vehicles, infrastructure, and spacecraft systems on the Moon's surface.

The mission will also enable Astrolab to improve its batteries, tyres, avionics systems, sensors, and software across the broader FLEX range.

What will the HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 do?

The HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 is a light, compact, self-contained, and fanless supercomputer. It has a low-power 64-bit Central Processing Unit (CPU) with a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU). It will be linked to FLIP's cooling system and run on power from the rover's batteries and solar cells. The supercomputer will also use solid-state drives (SSDs) from the company KIOXIA to store data.

If everything goes to plan, the Spaceborne Computer-4 will do more than simply survive. It will study the images taken during the Griffin-1 space mission and help with independent observations. The supercomputer will also handle navigation, mapping, and terrain checks.

The mission also promises to test Artificial Intelligence (AI). It is not clear which uses will be observed using this technology. HPE said an AI services container will show that AI services can be setup on the Moon reliably and at scale.

It is also unclear how these tools might be used on future crewed missions. Astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) already use computers for communication, science work, and daily tasks. But how they might use such tools on the Moon, especially with AI, is not yet known.

Why does the supercomputer use an aluminium chassis?

The system is placed in a compact aluminium chassis, mainly for thermal management and weight reduction in the extreme environment of the south pole of the Moon.

This region is notoriously known to feature one of the most unforgiving environments in the solar system. This is because the Sun hits the polar region of the Moon at a very low, glancing angle, creating an extreme landscape filled with intense darkness, sweeping thermal shifts, and rough terrain.

What else does the Griffin-1 mission carry on-board?

Griffin-1 will be the first flight of the robotic Griffin moon lander, built by a Pittsburgh-based firm, Astrobotic. This company will fly the mission for NASA under its CLPS programme.

In addition to FLIP, the lander will carry Astrobotic's CubeRover, a small uncrewed rover. It will also take LandCam-X, a navigation system that uses optical sensors. The third item is Nanofiche GLPH, short for Galactic Library to Preserve Humanity, a tiny archive of human history.

title: GTC Berlin 2026: Live Updates From NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's Keynote
description:

text:
Founded in a tent near the Berlin Wall in 1980, the Tempodrom moved several times before settling near Anhalter Bahnhof in 2001. Its permanent home has since hosted concerts, galas and political events.

Today, it hosts a different kind of spectacle.

GTC Berlin runs three days, with more than 100 sessions on agentic AI, robotics, physical AI, open models and accelerated computing underway at STATION-Berlin down the road. Here, journalists, analysts and partners have gathered for the main event: NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s keynote.

Huang Takes the Stage

Huang opened with a question: What do L’Oréal, Revolut, Spotify, Merck, Vodafone, Zara, Porsche, Nestlé and HSBC have in common? They’re all European companies and they’re all working with NVIDIA on AI, he said.

The keynote comes on the heels of NVIDIA’s weeklong road across Europe — Paris, London, Stockholm, Dublin — with the company committing nearly $10 billion to the technology ecosystem across Europe and working with 12,000+ partners.“After decades of advancement in the computer industry, we are now at the beginnings of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said.

AI is a five-layer cake, Huang explained. Energy powers advanced computers that are part of an AI factory, which generates tokens and digital intelligence from the models that run on it, which are then integrated into every application.

“Long before the AI models emerge, the infrastructure has to exist,” he said, highlighting how, similarly, the internet first needed networking, and electricity first required the grid.

“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI; you want to be producing the AI,” Huang said. “We could do all of that here in Europe, and in fact, we’ve already started.”

The AI Factory Gets a New Form Factor

Huang framed NVIDIA’s full-stack AI factory — spanning hardware, system software, CUDA-X libraries and models — as a broad platform for building and operating AI infrastructure.

“This now represents the breadth of technology necessary to create the AI factory,” Huang said. “This is what NVIDIA builds today, and this is the foundation by which we can enable Europe to be part of the AI ecosystem, the AI economy.”

He said Vera Rubin, in full production, extends NVIDIA’s computing platform beyond models and large language models to process the entire AI agent. He also showed several of NVIDIA’s latest rack-scale hardware offerings.

Next, Huang announced NVIDIA DSX POD, a reference design for complete NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery. With DSX POD, onsite deployment can shrink from six months to just 14 days once site utilities are ready.

“This is a complete transformation of the world supply chain,” Huang said. “This will change the way that people install and build data centers, and hopefully, as a result, velocity goes up.”

The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform enables companies to reduce water consumption for cooling by up to 100% and generate the same AI output with up to 30% less power.

Agents Are the New Computing Platform — and Safety Is an Engineering Problem

Huang said agents think, reason, iterate and use tools, driving token consumption as they become more useful.

He described an agent as comprising five elements: a model, a harness that orchestrates its work and memory, a sandbox that isolates the harness, knowledge and tools. In that framing, an agent is more than a model answering questions; it can draw on knowledge and act through tools.

“The most important thing is to make sure the agent is secure,” Huang said. The autonomous agent can access files, resources, networks and tools, so its privileges should be minimal and it should be monitored.

NVIDIA’s answer is the new NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe AI Agents, a full-stack design built on NVIDIA OpenShell — an open source, policy-controlled runtime with kernel-level sandboxing that sits between an agent and the systems it can affect.

That means privileges, policy enforcement and monitoring must adapt dynamically. “Every single time an agent is launched, the privileges are different,” Huang said.

Open Models Turn Expertise Into an Advantage

Huang presented NVIDIA’s open models as a starting point for building AI tailored to specific needs.

NVIDIA’s frontier, open models are available for use across industries: Nemotron for language, Cosmos for world foundation models, GR00T for humanoid robotics, Alpamayo for autonomous vehicles, Ising for quantum-classical computing and Earth-2 for physics AI.

“We are the frontier,” Huang said. “So in all of these different areas, we offer you all of the models, and we’re continuously working on it. We’ve been working on it for a decade, and we’ll continue to work on this forever.”

NVIDIA provides the models, data and scripts to reproduce them, and companies can post-train a model on their own data for a particular use case — turning proprietary data into what he called “sovereign intelligence.”

“You could start with an open model, something that’s incredibly good like Nemotron, and with your own data, post-train it for your use case and achieve, of course, super intelligence,” Huang said. “That is a very sensible thing to do, and all the technology exists today.”

NVIDIA Gives Agents a Knowledge Layer

Huang then introduced the NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation as a set of models and libraries for connecting agents to enterprise data, whether it’s unstructured information in documents or structured data in databases.

He highlighted Nemotron tools for parsing documents, embedding queries and reranking relevant information, along with new NVIDIA Kumo models for making predictions from structured data.

“Ultimately, what turns these super agents, these agents into super agents, is that you give them access to your company’s knowledge,” Huang said.

NVIDIA CUDA-X — Accelerated Tools for Agents

Huang then described NVIDIA CUDA-X as a collection of accelerated libraries used across science, engineering, research and creative work.

NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform has more than 11 million developers building on it.

Huang said those libraries can accelerate simulators, solvers and data-processing engines — the kinds of tools agents may draw on to do useful work.

“CUDA-X tools are what gives agents the tools of the trade,” Huang said.

Agents Go to Work in Labs, Factories and Engineering

A video showcased NVIDIA Agent Toolkit bringing company knowledge, models and tools together in three industry examples:

At Lila Sciences, agents help design a potential B-cell lymphoma therapy, using virtual experiments to guide work in an automated lab.

At Siemens’ Erlangen factory, agents help prepare new products for production, testing plans in a digital twin before changes reach the factory floor.

And at Dassault Systèmes, engineering agents adapt vehicle design, using simulation to identify a problem and refine the design.

“And [all this] knowledge and tools belong to you,” Huang said after the video rolled. “That’s your expertise, and so all of this is now possible to do.”

Telcos as Distributed AI Infrastructure

Huang said AI is transforming telecommunications, improving spectrum efficiency and turning cell towers into distributed AI infrastructure.

He cited 100,000 sites and about 100 gigawatts of distributed data centers, and said NVIDIA has made its first commercial phone call on T-Mobile’s network with Nokia after nearly eight years of work.

“Now CUDA makes phone calls,” Huang said. “AI will revolutionize the way we do telecommunications. It will enhance our spectrum efficiency tremendously.”

AI Moves Into the Treatment Room

Healthcare and life sciences leaders are building on NVIDIA technologies to advance drug discovery and expand patient care.

NVIDIA and Siemens Healthineers are developing AI-enabled radiation therapy.

Nemotron agents coordinate treatment planning, the Isaac for Healthcare platform and Omniverse libraries create a digital twin of the device and patient anatomy to simulate tumor targeting. Holoscan with IGX Thor connects live imaging and sensor data to enable real-time adaptive delivery as the patient moves.

Huang described adaptive radiotherapy as a physical-AI application: as the patient’s body and tumor change during treatment, the system must track the changes and adjust the radiation targeting.

“The tumor is changing in shape. The physical body is changing while you’re in therapy,” Huang said. “The robot, this radio adaptive radiotherapy system, has to perceive the changing environment, understand where the tumor is, segment it just perfectly and direct the radiotherapy accordingly.”

The Road Ahead: Mobility Leaders Join NVIDIA’s Automotive Ecosystem

Huang said the NVIDIA Hyperion computing platform is being designed into more vehicle fleets, with autonomous-driving software connecting robotaxis to ride-hailing services.

Bolt with Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles and Einride are showcasing selected autonomous-mobility use cases on the NVIDIA Hyperion computing platform, demonstrating potential applications for level 3 and level 4 vehicles as well as future robotaxi fleets.

In addition, Volvo Cars is adopting Hyperion and NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack software for safe automated driving. NVIDIA also introduced new AI and safety technologies to help developers build, validate and deploy autonomous vehicles at scale.

Volkswagen’s van, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes-Benz’s next-generation vehicles will be Hyperion-compatible, Huang announced, saying, “Welcome to Hyperion.”

A Reference Humanoid for Robotics Researchers

Huang then announced Agile ONE SN, a reference humanoid built on Isaac GR00T — a 31-degree-of-freedom body, expected to be available next year, designed to cut researcher setup time from weeks to days.

The platform is modular: researchers can use the full workflow or pull in selected components.

“This is a great starting point,” Huang said.

It builds on NVIDIA’s open physical AI stack — Isaac Capture for data collection, GR00T models for robot intelligence, Isaac Lab for simulation-based training, Isaac OS for runtime — and NVIDIA’s open physical AI dataset. Partners including Agility Robotics, Figure, KUKA and NEURA Robotics are already building on the same platform.

Personal AI Gets a New Machine

Huang closed by discussing RTX Spark laptops, which launched last week, bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI.

He compared its 1 petaflops of performance and 128GB of memory with the DGX-1 he delivered to OpenAI in 2016 — then made the difference in size the punchline:

“In the year 2016, I delivered 1 petaflops and 128GB … to a small company called OpenAI,” Huang said, holding up the compact machine in front of the audience. “This is 1 petaflops and 128GB. The only difference, of course, is that I can hold this like this, and DGX-1 took two people to carry upstairs.”

Huang then showed a video of an agent helping train Hugging Face’s Microduck: it set up a course and simulated the robot in Isaac Sim, sent training jobs to the cloud, then brought the learned policy back to RTX Spark for evaluation before deploying it to the physical robot.

A flock of four Microducks joined Huang onstage, sitting down, standing up and even taking a nap on cue. He explained that they were created on RTX Spark, trained in the cloud and learned their skills in simulation.

“You were created on RTX Spark … [we] trained you in the cloud on a whole bunch of NVIDIA supercomputers, and you learned your skills right here on RTX Spark and the digital twin,” Huang told them.

The Full Lineup

With the Microducks gathered around him, Huang recapped the keynote: Europe is building its AI economy, AI factories are evolving to run agents and physical AI is the next frontier.

“So that’s it,” Huang said. “Everybody can build agents. Every company in Europe will become an AI company … and we’re going to have a thriving AI economy here in Europe.”

To close, Huang had one more surprise: a Eurovision-style musical send-off that turned the keynote’s themes into a comic recap.

The lyrics raced from OpenShell’s guardrails — “No credentials. Access dismissed” and “Sentry on BlueField never clocks off” — to physical AI, where robot training was likened to “college for robots without student loans.”

The punchline: “You can’t spell fungible without fun.” A saxophone solo led into a rousing “We are Europa” chorus.

“Let’s work together to build Europe’s AI economy and put AI to work,” Huang said, closing out his talk. “Have a great GTC.”

text:
What does FactSet Research Systems do?

FactSet Research Systems Inc. is a financial data, analytics, workflow, and enterprise software company serving investment professionals. Its core product is not a single database; it is a connected platform used by portfolio managers, analysts, bankers, wealth advisors, risk teams, data engineers, and market-infrastructure clients to research securities, manage portfolios, run analytics, distribute data, and support reporting. The company is headquartered in Norwalk, Connecticut, and trades under FDS on both the NYSE and Nasdaq, according to its fiscal 2025 annual report.

FactSet matters because it sits inside recurring decision workflows rather than one-off information searches. The company says its purpose is to deliver trusted, connected financial data and analytics for confident decisions, and its investor site summarizes the model with more than $2.3B of annual revenue, more than 95% ASV retention, and roughly 240K global users on its platform, as described on the FactSet investor-relations page.

Which clients and workflows does it serve?

FactSet’s client base is broader than a desktop-terminal story. It serves institutional buy-side firms, dealmakers, wealth-management teams, and market-infrastructure clients. The workflow range is also wide: investment research, portfolio construction, performance measurement, risk, trade execution, reporting, security master data, and managed services. That breadth is important for student and investor analysis because it makes FactSet a subscription software and data platform with financial-market cyclicality, not a conventional advertising, transaction, or hardware company.

How does FactSet make money?

FactSet earns most of its revenue through subscriptions. Clients pay for access to data, analytics, applications, workstations, APIs, enterprise feeds, portfolio tools, and managed services. The model is attractive when clients expand users, add datasets, renew contracts, or adopt additional workflow products. It is pressured when asset managers cut budgets, consolidate vendors, reduce headcount, or replace parts of the stack with internal or competing tools.

Why ASV is the core economic metric

The company’s most important operating metric is annual subscription value, or ASV. ASV approximates the next twelve months of recurring subscription revenue from clients and therefore connects commercial momentum to future revenue. In Q3 FY2026, FactSet reported $2.4856B of organic ASV, up 7.1% year over year and up $35.4M over the prior three months, in its Q3 fiscal 2026 earnings release.

1. License data

FactSet sources, normalizes, and licenses financial, company, market, benchmark, identifier, and alternative datasets.

2. Embed workflow

Users access research, portfolio, wealth, risk, and reporting tools through workstations, APIs, feeds, and managed services.

3. Renew and expand

Contracts convert into ASV; expansion comes from more seats, more content, more enterprise use cases, and price increases.

4. Convert to cash

Recurring revenue, high retention, and moderate capital intensity support operating cash flow and shareholder returns.

How do client type revenues translate into growth?

FactSet’s Q3 FY2026 presentation separated ASV by firm type: Institutional Buy-Side was $1.207B, Dealmakers $470M, Wealth $392M, and Market Infrastructure $417M. That mix is useful because buy-side demand anchors the platform, while wealth and market-infrastructure workflows extend FactSet into advisor technology, identifiers, and enterprise data delivery.

A research analyst may know the workstation, a data team may license feeds, an advisor may use wealth dashboards, and a market-infrastructure client may need identifiers. That multi-product relationship is the center of the business model.

Which segments, clients, and geographies matter most?

FactSet reports three operating segments by geography: Americas, EMEA, and Asia Pacific. For FY2025, the Americas generated $1.506B of revenue, or 64.9% of total revenue; EMEA generated $580.3M, or 25.0%; and Asia Pacific generated $235.4M, or 10.1%. For valuation work, the gap matters: a DCF model should not blindly capitalize one quarter’s GAAP margin if the company is absorbing transaction, restructuring, or integration-related items, but it also should not ignore the possibility that AI investment, compensation, data costs, and product development pressure the steady-state margin.

What gives FactSet a durable competitive advantage?

FactSet’s moat is built from workflow integration, data breadth, client trust, and high switching costs. A financial-data platform becomes more valuable when it sits inside a client’s research process, data architecture, portfolio analytics, compliance reporting, and decision records. Replacing a vendor is therefore not just a price comparison; it can require retraining users, rebuilding data pipelines, testing calculations, and renegotiating content rights.

For FactSet, the strategic tension is simple: the subscription base is sticky because clients depend on the workflow, but the same clients are sophisticated enough to demand better data, AI tooling, and price discipline every year.

Why switching costs matter in financial data

The company’s retention data supports the switching-cost argument. FactSet reported annual ASV retention above 95% and client retention of 90% at Q3 FY2026. Those figures are not a guarantee of future growth, but they show that most of the revenue base renews even when markets are volatile. The broader lesson for MBA readers is that FactSet competes less like a commodity data vendor and more like a mission-critical workflow utility for financial institutions.

How AI changes the opportunity and the risk

FactSet is positioning AI as a way to make financial workflows faster, not as a separate consumer application. The Q3 FY2026 release said more than 90% of its top 50 clients used four or more AI products. The opportunity is higher product engagement and more embedded enterprise contracts. The risk is that AI outputs can create accuracy, compliance, reputational, and intellectual-property exposure if results are wrong, biased, insufficiently explainable, or based on data usage that clients or regulators challenge.

How did FactSet become strategically important?

FactSet’s history is best understood as a gradual move from financial-data access into integrated decision infrastructure. The turning points that matter today are those that increased client dependence, broadened the product set, expanded data rights, or changed the capital structure.

Which turning points still matter today?

1978

FactSet was founded. The long operating history matters because trust, data quality, and institutional relationships compound slowly in financial information services.

1996

The company became publicly traded. Public ownership helped fund product expansion while forcing consistent disclosure around subscription economics and profitability.

2015

FactSet completed the Portware acquisition, expanding from analytics into execution-management workflows and covering more of the portfolio lifecycle through the trader’s desk, as described in the official Portware acquisition announcement.

2021

FactSet joined the S&P 500. Index inclusion reflected scale, maturity, and relevance inside U.S. public markets.

2022

FactSet completed its acquisition of CUSIP Global Services for identifier and reference-data capabilities; the company said CGS covered more than 50 million global financial instruments in its official CUSIP Global Services completion release.

2025

Sanoke Viswanathan became CEO in September 2025. The transition increases attention on AI, enterprise relationships, execution discipline, and capital allocation under new leadership.

2026

Q3 FY2026 showed organic ASV growth of 7.1% and revenue growth of 6.4%, suggesting the platform was still expanding despite margin pressure and elevated reinvestment.

The pattern is consistent: FactSet has used product development and acquisitions to move deeper into financial workflows. The strategic question is whether that depth can keep compounding while clients review vendor stacks, test AI-native tools, and demand measurable productivity gains.

How financially strong is FactSet?

FactSet’s financial profile combines high recurring revenue, strong margins, and meaningful cash generation with debt from acquisitions and shareholder returns. In FY2025, revenue was $2.3217B, operating income was $748.3M, net income was $597.0M, and diluted EPS was $15.55. At Q3 FY2026, the company had $288.1M of cash and equivalents, $16.1M of investments, and total debt of about $1.3897B.

How does capital allocation affect the story?

FactSet returns cash through dividends and repurchases while also funding acquisitions, product development, AI investment, and data infrastructure. Who owns FactSet stock, and why does governance matter?

FactSet has a conventional public-company ownership profile: no founder-class voting control, no dual-class structure, and significant influence from large institutions. That matters because capital allocation, executive incentives, and board oversight are shaped more by broad institutional expectations than by a controlling founder or strategic shareholder.

Is control concentrated?

Vanguard beneficially owned 4,559,571 shares, or 12.2%; BlackRock owned 3,473,642, or 9.3%; BAMCO owned 2,478,027, or 6.6%; Morgan Stanley owned 2,167,472, or 5.8%; and State Street owned 1,932,533, or 5.2%, according to FactSet’s 2025 proxy statement.

What does the board structure signal?

The proxy also said ten of eleven current directors were independent and that the company separates the roles of Chair and CEO. Malcolm Frank became independent Board Chair in September 2025, while Sanoke Viswanathan became CEO. For investors, that governance profile suggests oversight of a leadership transition rather than a controlled-company dynamic. The relevant question is whether the board balances AI investment, acquisition integration, margin discipline, and shareholder returns without over-optimizing for one metric.

Competitors, data dependency, and client budgets shape the risk map

FactSet competes in a market where customers are sophisticated, data is expensive, and workflows are critical. The strongest competitors include Bloomberg, LSEG Workspace and Refinitiv assets, S&P Global Market Intelligence, MSCI, Morningstar, PitchBook, Envestnet, and specialized data, analytics, and AI vendors. The rivalry is not only about price; it is about content depth, data rights, analytics accuracy, workflow integration, API quality, enterprise reliability, and client service.

Which filing risks are most material?

FactSet’s own filings point to several company-specific risks. First, client demand depends on the health of asset managers, banks, wealth platforms, and corporate deal activity. Second, the company relies on third-party data providers; the annual report said two suppliers each represented more than 10% of total data costs in FY2025. Third, AI products introduce accuracy, compliance, reputational, and intellectual-property risk. Fourth, privacy and cross-border data rules such as GDPR and other country-level regimes can increase compliance costs and constrain product design.

Why does FactSet's business model matter for valuation?

FactSet is a useful DCF case because the central variables are not mysterious: subscription revenue growth, ASV retention, pricing power, margin sustainability, capital intensity, cash conversion, debt cost, and capital allocation. The challenge is judging durability. If FactSet keeps expanding ASV at mid-single-digit or better rates while protecting adjusted operating margins in the mid-30% range, the platform can compound cash flows. If competition, AI disruption, data costs, or client budget pressure compress growth and margins together, valuation sensitivity increases quickly.

The company’s own FY2026 outlook in the Q3 presentation called for GAAP revenue of $2.450B to $2.470B, organic ASV growth of $130M to $160M, GAAP operating margin of 29.5% to 31.0%, and adjusted operating margin of 34.0% to 35.5%, according to the Q3 FY2026 earnings presentation. What is the key takeaway from FactSet analysis?

FactSet is best understood as a recurring-revenue financial workflow company whose value depends on data trust, client retention, product expansion, and disciplined reinvestment. It is not immune to competition or market cycles, but its placement inside investment workflows gives it a stronger recurring base than many financial-services suppliers. The Q3 FY2026 evidence is mixed but constructive: revenue, ASV, users, and free cash flow grew, while GAAP margins and net income declined from the prior-year quarter.

What should students and investors remember?

For a student, FactSet is a strong case study in switching costs, data licensing, enterprise subscriptions, and workflow strategy. For an investor or analyst, the research question is whether ASV growth and AI-enabled product expansion can offset higher costs, competitive pressure, and debt-funded capital allocation. The company’s story should be monitored through ASV retention, organic ASV growth, regional revenue, adjusted margin quality, free cash flow, debt, and the pace at which AI products become revenue-expanding rather than merely cost-increasing.

Final synthesis

FactSet’s durable advantage is not simply that it sells financial data; it sells trusted data, analytics, identifiers, and workflow infrastructure that investment professionals use repeatedly. The strongest version of the thesis is sustained ASV growth with high retention, stable mid-30% adjusted operating margins, and cash flow that supports dividends, buybacks, and product investment. The weaker version is a market where client budgets tighten, AI competitors reduce differentiation, data costs rise, and the margin gap between GAAP and adjusted results remains wide. The essential watch item is whether FactSet’s platform becomes more embedded as financial institutions modernize data and AI workflows.

Highlights

Former Medtronic chairman and CEO Omar Ishrak joins as Chair of its board.

Its software uses computer vision and deep learning to combine live surgical video, navigation data and CT and MRI scans into one real-time view.

€7.48M Seed Round

XRlabs, a London-based surgical intelligence company founded in 2024 by practising neurosurgeon Dr Ali Haddad, has raised €7.48 million ($8.4 million) in seed funding.

Playground Global, a Palo Alto deeptech venture firm, led the round, with London HealthTech investor Eka Ventures taking part. Omar Ishrak, who led Medtronic as chairman and CEO from 2011 to 2020 and previously chaired Intel’s board, has joined as chair of XRlabs’ board. The source gives no valuation.

The Technology

XRlabs develops modular, device-agnostic software that sits as an external AI layer across surgical systems hospitals already own.

It says the platform uses computer vision and deep learning to turn live video from surgical scopes, navigation telemetry and pre-operative CT and MRI imaging into a single real-time, anatomy-aware view of each procedure.

It has two core products. XRlabs SIM is a patient-specific planning and rehearsal tool that turns standard scans into interactive 3D models, or digital twins. SurgicalOS is an intraoperative layer that brings that digital twin into the live operative view. XRlabs calls the combination a “Pyramid of Surgical Intelligence”.

Clinical Claims

XRlabs says its platform has been deployed across more than 100 surgical cases on three continents.

It says it achieved first-in-human use of physical AI in cranial neurosurgery, integrated with an ORBEYE 4K 3D exoscope under research conditions, and a world-first in AI-designed patient-specific implants used in separating craniopagus twins. These are company claims, and the source gives no independent confirmation.

Use of Funds

The money will build out XRlabs’ engineering and clinical teams, advance its products through regulatory pathways in the UK, Europe and the US, and extend the clinical evidence base at partner institutions. XRlabs has also been awarded a compute allocation on the UK AI Research Resource (AIRR). Dr Haddad said: “The operating room is the next frontier for physical AI.”

text:
The share of firms publicly committed to protecting biodiversity has more than doubled, from 14% in 2022 to 35% in 2025, new data from the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment has shown.

S&P Global‘s analysis covered 7,425 companies that participated in both the 2022 and 2025 research cycles.

As it noted, the year 2022 marked the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), which saw 196 countries set 23 targets to address nature and biodiversity loss.

Latin America leads the way

According to the data, Latin America had the highest share of companies with biodiversity commitments as of last year, at 63%. As S&P Global put it, Latin American firms ‘appear to recognise their role in protecting what is a uniquely important hotspot for global biodiversity’, given that the region is home to some of the world’s most important ecosystems.

Asia-Pacific recorded the largest increase, with the percentage of companies committed to addressing biodiversity more than tripling between 2022 and 2025. Commitment levels also doubled in North America, although both regions remained behind Europe.

Utilities and energy companies were the sectors most likely to have biodiversity commitments, followed by materials and consumer staples. Almost half of companies assessed in these sectors had some form of commitment in 2025, compared with around one-fifth in 2022.

On a sector-by-sector basis, meanwhile, utilities and energy companies were the most likely to have biodiversity commitments in place, followed by the materials and consumer staples sectors.

Of the 1,801 companies that conducted biodiversity risk assessments last year, 96% assessed their own operations, while 37% examined upstream suppliers and 24% considered downstream activities.

Tackling deforestation

Elsewhere, deforestation commitments have increased but remain relatively limited. As S&P Global noted, the share of companies with public commitments to stop deforestation rose from 6% in 2022 to 12% in 2025. However, Latin America recorded a rate of 32%.

Europe is likely to see an increase in deforestation commitments in the coming months, with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) entering its enforcement period in December 2026.

‘ Large and medium-sized European companies will come under new pressure to certify that the supply chains behind their products have not contributed to deforestation, wherever their suppliers are located,’ S&P Global noted, adding that recent data indicates that around three-quarters of European companies with deforestation commitments already include their supply chain in that commitment.

‘Significant momentum’

‘Corporate attention to nature has gained significant momentum since the GBF was adopted, with commitments to biodiversity and halting deforestation doubling since 2022,’ S&P Global noted. ‘The maturation of disclosure frameworks and stronger policymaking in some regions could push adoption of corporate commitments higher still.

‘The full picture is more complex, however. Among companies with nature-related commitments, few look beyond their own operations or conduct risk assessments, potentially leaving gaps in their strategies and exposing them to risk. Corporate engagement on nature issues is also expanding more in some regions and sectors than others.’

text:

The Florentine fashion house’s income statement is supported by the Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) channel, which largely offsets the strategic rationalisation of the wholesale division and the persistent weakness in consumer spending in the Asia-Pacific region.

In the third quarter alone, the group’s total revenue amounted to €207 million, down by 3.5% at constant exchange rates and by 6.2% at current exchange rates, reflecting the impact of a complex macroeconomic and geopolitical backdrop that led to a general weakening of consumer confidence over the summer period.

Direct-to-Consumer in good shape, wholesale network streamlined

The figures highlight the gradual reorganisation of the distribution model undertaken by the fashion house. The DTC channel reported net sales of €537 million in the first nine months, up by 4.0% at constant exchange rates and 1.9% at current exchange rates, driven by an increase in full-price sales in primary retail. In the third quarter, the direct channel remained stable at constant exchange rates and grew by 2.3% at current exchange rates, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of positive execution.

By contrast, the wholesale channel slowed, with sales declining to €123 million over the nine-month period, down by 13.4% at constant exchange rates and 15.0% at current exchange rates, with a particularly sharp fall in the third quarter - a drop of 19.1% at constant exchange rates. The company attributes this decline to the deliberate process of selecting and discontinuing partnerships with non-strategic partners in order to protect and strengthen brand equity.

Geographies: boost from North America and Europe, China underperforms

The geographical breakdown reflects a pronounced polarisation in global luxury consumption. North America stands out as the brand’s most dynamic market. Over the nine-month period, revenue in the region grew by 11.2% at constant exchange rates and by 7.3% at current exchange rates, supported by both the DTC and wholesale channels, each posting double-digit growth. The third quarter closed up 2.4% at constant exchange rates.
